We present SynthAVE, a large-scale benchmark for attribute-value verification spanning 12,726 products across 229 product types, 792 attributes, and 4 languages (Spanish, French, Italian, German). To validate synthetic labels at scale, we introduce a multi-LLM arena framework where each sample is evaluated by 21 judge configurations (7 model families \times 3 prompts), with final labels determined via majority voting; disagreements with the synthetic label are expert-adjudicated and agreement cases are audited on a stratified sample. The majority vote ensemble agrees with expert labels at Cohen’s \kappa = 0.92 (95.0% agreement), while individual judges agree with one another only moderately (Fleiss’ \kappa = 0.76)—by design, since we select for diversity. This demonstrates that diverse models with varying individual judgments aggregate into highly reliable predictions, enabling cost-effective validation at scale while concentrating expert effort on the cases where it changes the label. We estimate the resulting label quality at 97.9%.

paper.title: Data Scout: Targeted Web Crawling for Domain-Specific Pretraining Corpora
paper.abstract: The dominant approach to building domain-specific pretraining corpora is to filter large web archives such as CommonCrawl. This works well for popular domains but breaks down for specialized ones, where relevant content is sparse and often beyond the reach of popularity-driven crawlers. We present **Data Scout**, which inverts this: instead of filtering an archive, it directs a targeted crawl. An LLM expands a root topic into a taxonomy and thousands of search queries; the returned URLs (*seeds*) are grouped by subdomain and screened with a user-supplied classifier (the *probe*), admitting each subdomain on the basis of a small sample. This works because relevance has a sharp boundary at the subdomain level: in mathematics, a page is 21x more likely to be relevant than one on a sibling subdomain. With the FineMath classifier as the probe, **21.9%** of crawled pages are high-quality math content, **70x** the 0.31% rate from filtering a comparable web sample, so the crawl wastes far less effort. But the payoff is not just efficiency: 63.2% of these pages are missing from CommonCrawl altogether, yet just as useful for training. Continued pretraining of Llama-3.2-3B on 1.9B Data Scout tokens matches FineMath corpus on GSM8k. Because the probe is the only domain-specific component, Data Scout can in principle apply to any domain with such a classifier.

paper.title: Interactor: Agentic RL oriented Iterative Creation for Ad Description Generation in Sponsored Search
paper.abstract: This paper focuses on automatically generating informative ad descriptions in sponsored search. Unlike ad titles which are usually optimized to attract user click feedbacks, ad descriptions have a longer text span and possess the potential of incorporating world knowledge to address user search intents while presenting the fine-grained selling points of the ads. We propose Interactor, a multi-turn iterative creation framework optimized with agentic RL for ad description generation. The generation model acts as a policy that interacts with a customized environment consisting of multiple generative reward models. Given initial generations by the policy, the customized GenRMs evaluate qualities including knowledge capacity and landing page consistency, providing both binary signals and detailed feedbacks. The policy then iteratively refines the descriptions based on such feedbacks to ensure continuous improvement. Experiments show that it significantly outperforms state-of-the-art ad text generation approaches in generating knowledge-rich and faithful ad descriptions. Since late May 2026, it has been deployed online in a leading search ads system, where the framework serves over 140k advertisers, contributing to both ad revenue and user experience.

paper.title: Mosaic: Automated Intent Description Generation for Multi-Label Classification
paper.abstract: Traditional intent classifiers map utterances directly to intent categories using labeled examples. In contrast, LLM-assisted zero-shot intent classifiers rely on natural language descriptions alongside intent labels to determine the most appropriate categories for a given utterance. As intent taxonomies grow and evolve, descriptions must define clear boundaries among overlapping intent categories. Maintaining them is costly because it requires domain expertise and continual updates to keep pace with changing product and user behavior. We present MOSAIC (Multi-label Ontology Synthesis for Automated Intent Classification), a deployed system that automatically generates and updates intent descriptions for an existing taxonomy. MOSAIC analyzes unlabeled user utterances to identify coherent clusters. It associates cluster-level evidence with the existing intent taxonomy. Then, it synthesizes discriminative descriptions that define each category’s semantic boundary. On a 140-class production deployment, MOSAIC approaches the quality of expert-written descriptions while reducing taxonomy revision time from 2-4 weeks to less than 30 minutes. On the public NLU++ and Multi³NLU++ benchmark datasets, MOSAIC-generated descriptions do match or exceed the performance of expert-written descriptions.

paper.title: Tracing Target Answers in Poisoned Retrieval Corpora via Token Influence Attribution

author.affiliation: National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University
National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University
National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University
National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University

paper.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems are vulnerable to corpus poisoning attacks that manipulate model outputs through malicious retrieved documents. Existing detection methods typically rely on auxiliary classifiers or additional LLM-based verification, introducing substantial computational overhead. We present TRACE, a lightweight detection framework that identifies poisoning attacks by tracing answer-related tokens through token influence attribution. TRACE first discovers recurrent high-influence keywords across retrieved documents and then performs a secondary verification to confirm their influence on model predictions. Experiments on three QA benchmarks and six LLMs demonstrate strong detection performance while simultaneously uncovering attacker-specified target answers.

paper.title: FinSTaR: Towards Financial Reasoning with Time Series Reasoning Models
paper.abstract: Time series (TS) reasoning models (TSRMs) have shown promising capabilities in general domains, yet they consistently fail on financial domain, which exhibit unique characteristics. We propose a general 2 x 2 capability taxonomy for TSRMs by crossing 1) single-entity vs. multi-entity analysis with 2) assessment of the current state vs. prediction of future behavior. We instantiate this taxonomy in the financial domain—where the distinction between deterministic assessment and stochastic prediction is particularly critical—as ten financial reasoning tasks, forming the FinTSRBench benchmark based on S P stocks. To this end, we propose FinSTaR (Financial Time Series Thinking and Reasoning), trained on FinTSR-Bench with distinct chain-of-thought (CoT) strategies tailored to each category. For assessment, which is deterministic, we employ Compute-in-CoT, a programmatic CoT that enables models to derive answers directly from raw prices. For prediction, which is inherently stochastic, we adopt Scenario-Aware CoT, which generates diverse scenarios before making a judgment, mirroring how financial analysts reason under uncertainty. FinSTaR achieves 78.9% average accuracy on FinTSRBench, substantially outperforming LLM and TSRM baselines. Furthermore, we show that the four capability categories are complementary and mutually reinforcing through joint training. Code is publicly available at: https://github.com/seunghan96/FinSTaR.

paper.title: Towards Fluid Consultations: Design and Real-World Evaluation of a Multi-Agent, Full-Duplex Health AI Assistant
paper.abstract: Access to reliable health consultation is a critical global challenge. While large language models show promise, their practical utility is typically limited by high input barriers, lack of adaptive response strategies for complex scenarios, and insufficient real-world evaluation. To address these gaps, we present a novel health AI assistant that integrates a low-latency full-duplex voice interface with a Multi-Agent System (MAS). The full-duplex design supports natural turn-taking, significantly lowering interaction barriers and quadrupling average conversation depth from 2.62 to 10.16 turns compared to text-based baselines. Furthermore, our MAS architecture decouples clinical reasoning from general conversation, effectively managing complex queries and boosting clinical performance scores by over 30% compared to single-agent baselines. We conducted the first large-scale analysis of an LLM-based health assistant deployed to the general public (N > 5,000), demonstrating superior user engagement and providing empirical evidence on the safety and utility of deploying such systems in realistic environments.

paper.title: Quantization Breaks the Format: How Weight Compression Undermines Chat Format Safety in On-Device LLM
paper.abstract: On-device LLM deployment routinely serves GGUF-quantized models whose safety is ver- ified at full precision rather than on the llama.cpp/GGUF stack end users actually run. We stress-test nine production mod- els across four GGUF levels against seven CHATBUG chat-format attacks on 520 Ad- vBench instructions, served through the same llama.cpp binary that powers Ollama, and report three deployment-relevant findings. (1) Q2_K vulnerability concentrates in the smallest on-device models: Llama-3.2-1B reaches 75.3% ASR-R at Q2_K (+26.9 pp vs. Q8_0) while Gemma-3-4B is essentially un- affected (+3.0 pp), so model choice dominates quantization-level choice within the on-device regime. (2) The vulnerability is a property of the deployed system: a subset reproduces end- to-end through Ollama (median |∆|= 2.7 pp). (3) Keyword- and moderator-based metrics diverge in magnitude: Llama-2 Mismatch-∅ shifts ASR-R +55.8 pp but ASR-M−1.7 pp at Q2_K, while Llama-2 Overflow-FS is con- firmed unsafe by both (+16.8 pp ASR-M). We release a one-page deployment-safety checklist and GGUF-native diagnostic probes, and iden- tify single-layer probes as insufficient cross- model predictors of ASR change, motivating per-layer llama.cpp instrumentation.

paper.title: Beyond Semantic IDs: Encoding Business-Value Ranking into Document Identifiers for Generative Retrieval
paper.abstract: Generative Retrieval (GR) formulates retrieval as a sequence-to-sequence generation task, assigning each document a document identifier (DocID) and retrieving it through autoregressive decoding, making DocID design a critical factor in retrieval quality. However, existing schemes based on discrete representation learning suffer from inherent collision issues and create a mismatch between the DocID’s encoding objective and the system’s business optimization target. To address these limitations, we propose Cluster-Ranked Identifier (CRID), which decouples DocID into semantic clustering and business-value ranking, yielding collision-free identifiers that support incremental updates via intra-cluster reranking. We further introduce an analytical framework that decomposes retrieval gains into personalized preference and statistical prior generalization, revealing how semantic cluster size governs the balance between the two components. Experiments on a Taobao e-commerce corpus of over 300M items show that CRID surpasses the strongest embedding-based retrieval baseline on top-K Hitrate, and delivers +1.06% GMV in full-traffic deployment.

paper.title: PULSAR: Pooled Unified Late-interaction Search And Retrieval for Enterprise Visual Document RAG
paper.abstract: Institutional investors search visually dense pitch decks, board packs, and diligence materials that change hourly near deal closing. OCR followed by figure verbalisation is costly to refresh at this scale and can lose chart detail. We present PULSAR, a production vision-first retrieval system deployed at Mubadala Investment Company. PULSAR indexes page images with a frozen ColPali-style backbone and uses a pooled two-stage late-interaction index: compact page summaries support initial retrieval, followed by exact MaxSim rescoring over a finer pooled representation. On ViDoRe V3, this design reduces median vector-search latency by 15.1 times against an unpooled configuration with less than 0.01 absolute NDCG@10 and Recall@10 loss; production median vector-search latency is 156 ms. Under concurrent load, the pooled index sustains approximately 88 times higher QPS than an unpooled index. The event-driven ingestion path is estimated to be approximately 20 times cheaper per page than the OCR+verbalisation baseline it replaced. Since March 2026, PULSAR has served 78 thousand documents and approximately 2.4 million pages across more than 3,000 deals. At the production top K, it more than doubles answer-fact recall over the OCR+verbalisation baseline.

paper.title: Longitudinal-aware Evaluation of Retrieval-Augmented Generation over Evolving Credit Policy Documents
paper.abstract: We present a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system in production since April 2026 for credit policy question answering, a setting in which the corpus is revised several times per quarter: a single revision changes thresholds, narrows scopes, and restructures tables. Static test sets silently decay under this regime, and scores computed against successive corpus versions cannot separate system drift from corpus drift. We propose a longitudinal-aware evaluation framework that makes RAG quality over an evolving corpus both measurable and attributable. It combines (i) a change-type taxonomy — Stable, Evolved, Added, Removed — built on a deterministic, model-independent alignment of document subsections keyed to how each gold-supporting provision changed between versions, making explicit which scores remain comparable across releases; (ii) a versioned, class-stratified synthetic QA pipeline that keeps the test set current at revision cadence; and (iii) a statement-level LLM judge for compound policy answers; each component is calibrated against subject-matter experts. Across three corpus versions, a conventional longitudinal-unaware protocol would report a recall decline of up to 25.7 points. However, paired comparisons on answer-invariant items show no evidence of regression in the unchanged system.

paper.title: ASSERT: A Measurement Pipeline for GenAI Audits
paper.abstract: Audits of generative AI (GenAI) systems often summarize behavior as a reported rate: how often the audited system complies with policy. Researchers and stakeholders use that rate to compare systems, track regressions, and gate deployment. A reported rate reflects both the system under audit and the measurement choices behind it, so a change in the rate can leave it unclear whether the system or those choices moved. We introduce ASSERT, a specification-driven measurement pipeline for GenAI audits that ties each reported rate to a written specification of the measurement choices used to produce it. ASSERT helps draft a behavioral rubric and test cases, then runs the audit against a GenAI system and returns a reported rate. In a case study on conversational deception, we observe that the reported rate moves substantially with the dialogue setup, the simulated user, the judge, and the evidence bar for non-compliance. These measurement choices substantially change the reported rate and can reorder GenAI system rankings. Because each reported rate is tied to an explicit specification, differences across audits are easier to attribute and interpret.

paper.title: From Benchmarks to Production: A Text-to-SQL System for Complex Financial Data
paper.abstract: General-purpose Text-to-SQL systems achieve strong performance on academic benchmarks like Spider and BIRD, where schemas are relatively shallow and column values are often human readable. In production financial databases, where concepts are stored as opaque integer keys rather than human-readable strings, these methods fall below 50%, as even simple queries require multiple joins and filter predicates reference opaque IDs. We present FLINT, a domain-specialized Text-to-SQL system that closes this gap through three key components: (1) a lookup agent that dynamically resolves natural-language concepts to question-specific reference table constraints, (2) embedding-based retrieval of structurally similar query templates from a compact, expert-authored bank, and (3) schema linking that prunes a large table schema to the relevant subset by traversing foreign-key chains, rather than relying on name similarity alone. We evaluate on two datasets totaling 359 questions over production financial schemas. FLINT outperforms various state-of-the-art baselines using the same LLM. The system is deployed in production as part of a financial data retrieval service.

paper.title: SWE-Tester: Training Open-Source LLMs for Issue Reproduction in Real-World Repositories
paper.abstract: Software testing is essential for maintaining software reliability, yet issue reproduction tests are often missing when bugs are reported. Automatically generating such tests can accelerate debugging, support test-driven development, and improve automated software engineering systems that rely on execution-based verification. Existing approaches largely depend on proprietary language models, limiting accessibility and reproducibility. We present SWE-Tester a framework for training open-source large language models to generate issue reproduction tests from natural language issue reports. To support this task, we curate a dataset of 41K training instances from 2.6K open-source GitHub repositories. Fine-tuning on this dataset improves issue reproduction performance across multiple model families, yielding gains of up to 10% points in success rate and 21% in change coverage on SWT-Bench Verified. We further study the effects of model size, training data scale, and inference-time compute, observing consistent improvements along all three axes. Our results demonstrate that open-source models can be effectively specialized for issue reproduction test generation and provide a scalable foundation for future software testing and automated issue-resolution systems.

paper.title: Fidelity Is Not Enough: Dispatch-Level Instrumentation for Agentic Datasheet Extraction
paper.abstract: One model passed our fidelity check without ever opening the datasheet. We found it while qualifying models for an internal extraction service: a structured-output constraint had silently disabled tool use, and the model answered anyway, with fabricated source text. Only the per-tool trace exposed it. Fidelity—whether an extracted value matches the source—is the standard measure for agentic document extraction, and it scores that run a success. We therefore log every tool call in an agentic benchmark of 25 hand-curated claims over three components, with 12 more on a fourth, 37 in all. From that dispatch record we build two instruments: a rule-based failure- attribution classifier, and a silent-failure detector whose two rules check only which tools were called, never the extracted value. The detector raises no flag on 207 clean fidelity-passing extractions across three model families, and recovers all 50 planted faults that withhold exactly the tools its rules check. The two results are not symmetric: the first bounds the false-positive rate, the second is recall by construction, and detection power against runs that call their tools and still answer wrongly is unmeasured. A second, independent oracle, a causal chamber that tests whether the datasheet’s claims hold under physical measurement, is intentionally partial: it confirms only what the apparatus can exercise, a verifiable envelope of 2 of those 37 claims, and we give a taxonomy of why the rest are not physically gradable. Under a controlled perturbation, fidelity passes throughout while the chamber verdict flips exactly at the measurement uncertainty. Across three deployed model stacks (one destabilised by its serving stack, not by any capability gap) the tool layer buys portability and observability rather than accuracy, and earns its premium only once a document outgrows the context window. We distil the lessons into a checklist of cheap dispatch-level signals.

paper.title: Quality Over Clicks: Iterative Reinforcement Learning for Early-Stage E-Commerce Query Suggestion
paper.abstract: Existing dialogue systems rely on query suggestion to enhance user engagement. Recent approaches mainly optimize generative models using click-through rate (CTR) models to align with user preferences. However, these methods are less effective in early-stage deployment scenarios, where click feedback is sparse and insufficient for training a reliable CTR model. To bridge this gap, we propose QualEQS, a quality-first iterative reinforcement learning framework for e-commerce query suggestion. We formalize actionable suggestion quality along three dimensions that directly affect downstream usability: answerability, factuality, and information gain. To continuously improve from online traffic without click supervision, we further propose group-level disagreement among candidate suggestions to identify ambiguous query contexts and mine hard training cases for iterative refinement. We also introduce EQS-Benchmark, a dataset of 16,949 real-world e-commerce queries for offline training and evaluation. Experiments show that our quality-based offline metrics correlate strongly with online performance, providing a practical evaluation recipe for sparse-feedback deployment. In both offline and online settings, QualEQS consistently outperforms strong baselines, yielding a 6.81% improvement in online ChatPV in a real-world enterprise-level conversational shopping assistant system.

paper.title: From Simulation to Reality: Validating Automated Evaluation of Conversational Agents
paper.abstract: Evaluating conversational agents typically requires human participants, a process that is costly and difficult to scale. LLM-based user simulators and LLM-as-a-judge evaluators offer a promising alternative, but how close they are to replacing real users remains unclear. We study this through a human user study (52 participants) and a simulated user study (four LLM-based simulators) applied to an experimental conversational sales agent, comparing LLM-as-a-judge assessments against human self-reported ratings. The results show that none of our simulators fully replicates human interaction patterns, and none of the LLM-based evaluators shows strong correlation with human ratings on real dialogues. We provide practical guidelines for combining automated and human evaluation, identifying key areas for improvement and highlighting when real-user studies remain essential.

paper.title: The Blocker Beasts and How to Tame Them: Schema-Driven Extraction in the Connective AI Layer of Network Operation
paper.abstract: In the Microsoft Azure datacenter network, a technician repairs a link and an on-call engineer, on a different shift and a different continent, decides whether the repair holds. The only channel between them is the technician’s free-text note. When the note omits the measurements the engineer needs, the ticket stalls: the median blocked ticket took 7.0 days to resolve, of which roughly one hour was engineering work. The rest was waiting for an account of the work that the note did not carry.We treat the note as the object to be repaired. A pipeline in production for ten months parses each note at write time into two lightweight schemas, STAR and ECO, using deterministic rules for measurements and a language model for prose. It reaches 0.913 F1 against a 2,141-note gold standard, above a stronger frontier model working alone, and across a staggered rollout of 450+ datacenters the deployed package cuts time-to-repair by 3.4 days. Resolution time falls steeply in a completeness score, at a rate that holds across five physically unrelated failure types, which is what we would expect if the constraint were in the handoff rather than in the physical work.

paper.title: MixEmb: Importance-Aware Quantization and Caching Co-Design for Industrial Decentralized Embedding Training

author.affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China
University of Science and Technology of China

paper.abstract: Industrial recommendation training increasingly relies on decentralized multi-GPU infrastructure, yet sparse embedding tables remain a major bottleneck due to significant storage, lookup, and communication overhead. Most existing works typically optimize only one of these bottlenecks or are designed for parameter server architectures, making them less effective in industrial decentralized training stacks. To tackle these challenges, we propose MixEmb, a practical framework for efficient decentralized embedding training through importance-aware quantization and caching. We first design a novel importance metric, i.e., embedding score, which can distinguish the contribution of embedding vectors based on spatial heterogeneity and temporal dynamics. Guided by embedding scores, MixEmb employs mixed precision quantization and hierarchical caching at fine-grained vector level. Besides, our key finding is that quantization and caching decisions are tightly coupled. Instead of naive combination, we delicately integrate them into a unified training framework through coupled co-design. A theoretical convergence analysis is also provided for MixEmb. We implement and evaluate MixEmb in real-world training scenarios. Across three workloads, MixEmb attains up to 1.55× speedup and 3.54× compression ratio compared to state-of-the-art methods.

paper.title: Session-Guided Pre-training for Query Understanding: Constraining Mask Prediction and Improving Query Fine-tunability

author.affiliation: Institute of Industrial Science, the University of Tokyo

paper.abstract: Large-scale search systems must process vast numbers of diverse, short queries for query understanding (QU) tasks such as named entity recognition (NER) and query classification, under strict latency constraints. Yet general-purpose language models (LMs), trained largely on context-rich open-domain text, are poorly matched to context-poor queries; large generative LMs also incur high serving costs. To achieve accurate and efficient QU, we introduce SEG-QU, a session-guided continual pre-training framework that tailors standard encoder pre-training objectives to search queries. It jointly optimizes token- and query-level objectives over session-derived query pairs: Session-Guided Masked Language Modeling (SG-MLM) reduces uncertainty in single-query MLM, while Same-Session Query Prediction (SSQP) improves downstream fine-tunability. On commercial-search NER and classification tasks, SEG-QU outperforms encoder baselines and fine-tuned generative LMs up to 43\times larger, while requiring substantially lower latency and energy. SEG-QU also transfers effectively to a public e-commerce benchmark. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/lycorp-jp/segqu.

paper.title: Configurable Clinical Information Extraction with Agentic RAG: What Works, What Breaks, and Why

author.affiliation: IKIM – Institute for Artificial Intelligence in Medicine
Institute for AI in Medicine (IKIM), University Medicine Essen

paper.abstract: Patient contexts span hundreds of heterogeneous documents and thousands of structured data points, yet the document-level metadata that AI systems need for retrieval and triage is absent or incomplete. Standard retrieval-augmented generation fails on this data, mishandling temporal reasoning, cross-document dependencies, and missing metadata. We report on the deployment of ACIE (Agentic Clinical Information Extraction) at University Medicine Essen: an on-premise agentic RAG pipeline that reasons over complete patient contexts and grounds every answer in source passages for clinician verification. We quantify the metadata gap, trace the architectural decisions it shaped, and evaluate extraction alongside an independent retrospective lymphoma registry study, in which nuclear-medicine physicians verify every extracted value against its cited sources. Across 7,326 clinician judgments on this lymphoma-registry workflow, 96.5% of extractions were accepted, with per-type acceptance ranging from 80% to 99%.

paper.title: FLASH-MAXSIM: IO-Aware Fused Kernels for Late-Interaction Retrieval
paper.abstract: Late-interaction retrieval (ColBERT, ColPali) scores a query against a document via the MaxSim operator. The standard PyTorch implementation materialises the full query-token \times document-token similarity tensor only to reduce it away. At ColPali scale this is the single largest tensor in the pipeline (e.g. 21 GB in FP16 for 10K documents) and limits both candidate set size at inference and batch size during contrastive training. We present Flash-MaxSim (FM), an IO-aware fused GPU kernel that computes the same MaxSim scores without ever materialising the tensor, and extends the same principle to the training backward. At ColPali scale on A100, FM reduces inference peak memory by 1.4-2.6\times relative to the deployed chunked baseline (4.9-8.9\times relative to unchunked eager execution) and reduces MaxSim-operator training memory by two orders of magnitude, enabling exact reranking over larger resident candidate pools and contrastive batch sizes that vanilla autograd cannot fit on a single GPU. The kernel is a drop-in replacement, exact up to floating-point evaluation order under its stated FP32-accumulation protocol: nDCG@10 differs from the FP32 reference by at most 5{\times}10^{-4} on BEIR and REAL-MM-RAG. A separate INT8 path trades exactness for halved index storage at high fidelity. Released open-source at https://github.com/roipony/flash-maxsim.

paper.title: Trains but Doesn’t Learn: A Post-Training Delivery Benchmark for LLM Agents as Forward-Deployed Engineers
paper.abstract: Post-training is becoming a service (PTaaS): a customer hands an operator data and a goal, and a forward-deployed engineer (FDE) returns a fine-tuned, evaluated, and deployed model under a budget, a human-approval gate, and reproducibility requirements. Seating an LLM agent in the FDE seat raises a question existing benchmarks cannot answer: not whether an agent can raise a metric, but whether it can be trusted to deliver. We answer it on a governed delivery plane, where an agent drives ten stages and an oracle scores each stage from platform-recorded facts. The central silent failure is the run that trains but does not learn (TBDL): loss falls, every signal stays green, and the delivered model is no better than the base. A detector calibrated on known-corrupted runs flags every such run before payment. We ran four frontier agents (Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6-luna, Gemini 3.7 Flash, DeepSeek-V4-Pro) end to end on metered L40S, A100, and H200 GPUs across 8B to 70B open bases, certifying every scenario before scoring. We also ran a human FDE arm under the same oracle and compare every agent against it.

paper.title: Loom: Weaving Diagnostic Strands into Free-Text Consensus via Embedding-Space Reweighting
paper.abstract: Aggregating noisy, conflicting textual hypotheses into a reliable consensus is a fundamental challenge when deploying NLP systems in real-world industrial settings. While monolithic Large Language Model (LLM) agents offer unbounded expressivity for tasks like Root Cause Analysis (RCA), they suffer from context limits, compounding hallucinations, and prohibitive inference latency. Traditional weak supervision offers statistical rigor but is mathematically restricted to discrete classes. We present Loom, a generative consensus framework deployed for real-world RCA that bridges these paradigms. Loom aggregates open-form hypotheses emitted by modular heuristics (diagnostic templates dynamically populated with episode-specific entities, times, and metrics) by projecting them into a continuous embedding space, and resolves conflicting signals with an iterative centroid-based reweighting algorithm. The resulting consensus weights ground a single lightweight LLM synthesis step. Evaluated on the OpenRCA benchmark, Loom occupies the accuracy–efficiency Pareto frontier: it matches a state-of-the-art autonomous agent on Bank and Market-2 and trails on Market-1 and Telecom, while using a single LLM call per incident on all four datasets (\sim26\times faster; \sim33\times with an 8B-parameter synthesizer). We discuss our deployment experience, highlighting lessons learned regarding the trade-offs between agentic depth and inference latency, negative results in redundancy detection, and how deterministic consensus fosters trust among Subject Matter Experts (SMEs).

paper.title: SPAR: Experience-Driven Strategy Evolution in Multi-Session B2B Sales
paper.abstract: B2B outbound sales involves high transaction values and relationship-based trust, so closing a deal typically requires multiple rounds of outreach building on prior context. Existing LLM-based sales agents operate within single sessions and cannot carry forward context or refine strategies from experience. Methods that do learn from experience store lessons as unstructured text and treat all outcomes as equally informative, with no mechanism to distinguish a flawed strategy from an external factor. We propose SPAR, a self-evolving framework that models selling strategies as testable hypotheses and refines them without parameter updates. A double-loop architecture lets an inner loop adapt to individual merchants through episodic memory while an outer loop evolves a shared strategy playbook through causal attribution and hypothesis-driven evolution. In a live A/B test on the 1688 platform with over 200,000 merchants, SPAR achieves +15.8% conversion lift and +35.8% high-intent merchant growth. Human evaluation by domain experts rates SPAR at 4.62 out of 5 on overall sales quality, the highest among all methods.

paper.title: RAW: Refusal Aversion in the Wild, A Causal Measurement Method for Deployed LLMs

author.affiliation: London School of Economics and Political Science, University of London

paper.abstract: Deployed LLMs field hundreds of millions of conversations a day and refuse a non-trivial fraction of user requests, yet the user-side cost of refusal, whether users disengage and by how much, is unmeasured on any production model: a blind spot for the consumer-facing platforms built on them. A/B-testing refusal is ethically and operationally constrained on frontier-lab products and unavailable to third-party platforms deploying these models through a fixed API. We introduce RAW, a method that uses LLM stochasticity as a natural experiment: at near-identical prompts in any existing log, the same model sometimes refuses and sometimes does not, and that variation identifies the causal user-side effect of refusal. Applying the method to 15 deployed LLMs in LMSYS-Chat-1M and WildChat, with user-clustered inference, we find that for about half of the models we can measure precisely, a refusal costs 3 to 17 pp of subsequent re-engagement; the rest show no distinguishable effect, among them one deployment whose positive point estimate we trace to persistent users retrying the refused request. Our contribution is the measurement method, which runs on any deployed model from logs alone for about 0.30 per 1,000 conversations. We release labels, moderation scores, prompt embeddings, and pipeline code.

paper.title: What 1,114 Documents Reveal About Schema-Driven Extraction: Models, Pipelines, and the Real-vs-Synthetic Gap
paper.abstract: Extracting structured data from documents is a core task in finance, insurance, legal, and healthcare, yet empirical studies comparing extraction approaches across domains remain scarce. We assemble a corpus of 1,114 documents across 12 categories spanning 8 domains, with 7,197 fields annotated with ground-truth values, and use it to study how extraction accuracy varies across models, pipeline architectures, and document sources. We evaluate with a type-aware methodology that scores every field as a correct extraction, a miss, a hallucination, or a correct absence, so that declining to extract is distinguished from extracting wrongly. Our central finding is that aggregate accuracy conceals critical divergence along every axis: synthetic documents overestimate accuracy by 38–45pp on insurance certificates (n=18 real documents); three models score within 1pp overall but diverge by 31pp per category; and two pipeline architectures diverge by 26pp on contracts—with the advantage not predicted by document length. An independently built extraction system, run under a protocol fixed in advance, agrees with our ground truth on 82–87% of fields across three models spanning two providers, providing evidence that the corpus is not calibrated to a single implementation. The corpus and evaluation tooling are released to enable reproducible comparison.

paper.title: PriceBench: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Price, Quality, and Brand Preferences in LLM Booking Agents

author.affiliation: London School of Economics and Political Science, University of London

paper.abstract: LLMs increasingly act as purchasing agents, which makes the LLM, not the user, the one choosing among the options that satisfy a request; its preferences quietly fix what gets bought and what it costs. Hotel booking is a clean instance: a high-volume choice settled on a few comparable attributes, where the pick reveals those preferences. We introduce PriceBench, a diagnostic benchmark that recovers an LLM’s price, quality, and brand preferences from its booking choices with a logit choice model, applied to 28 LLMs from 8 providers on 3,600 hotel tasks from 179 real New York City properties. We find that capability is associated with how consistently an LLM chooses, not with what it chooses: more capable LLMs hold stronger, more consistent preferences, while weaker ones either lock onto one position, exploitable by whoever controls listing order, or choose almost indifferently. What those preferences favor varies sharply across providers and even within one family: price sensitivity spans more than an order of magnitude, and the price/quality trade-off moves mean booked nightly price from USD 247 to USD 393 on identical tasks. What an agent buys must therefore be measured per LLM, not inferred, and we release the tasks, code, and all 28 response sets.

paper.title: Towards Autopilot Labeling for Short Video Content Governance
paper.abstract: The explosive growth of short videos has presented significant challenges to content governance. Traditional manual labeling is inefficient, slow to iterate, and costly. Therefore, we explore and develop a multi-stage autopilot labeling framework aimed at progressively increasing the level of automation in short video content annotation. To move beyond the heavy reliance on human expert labeling at the initial L0 stage, we first introduce a discriminative MLLM labeler at the L1 stage, which is fine-tuned with supervised data to directly predict labels for short videos. Advancing to the L2 stage, we shift to a domain-adaptive MLLM pretrained on short video data and use it for zero-shot labeling, enabling flexible generalization without task-specific supervision. In the L3 stage, we propose an agentic annotation workflow, and equip the agent with several key tools, which empower the agent to handle complex, unfamiliar, or vaguely defined cases, significantly reducing the need for human intervention. We conduct extensive experiments across various content issues, and results demonstrate that each stage of the autopilot labeling framework progressively improves labeling accuracy, and has significantly reduced manual labor costs in real-world applications by up to 85%. This automated labeling approach is poised to gradually replace manual annotation, emerging as the new paradigm for short video content labeling.

paper.title: A Practitioner’s Guide to Systematic Prompt Evaluation for Information Extraction
paper.abstract: Practitioners across industries increasingly use large language models to extract information from unstructured documents such as financial filings, legal contracts, and sustainability reports, yet typically rely on generic online recommendations for prompt design that lack empirical grounding in their target setting. We address this gap with a practical methodology for systematically varying individual prompt components (prompt structure, contextual information, and model selection) and measuring their effect on extraction quality. We use greenhouse gas emissions extraction from corporate sustainability reports as a case study of fixed numeric extraction from high-stakes PDF documents that vary widely in structure and presentation and are dispersed across company websites. Instantiated in a retrieval-augmented generation pipeline, our evaluation shows that best practices from industry-facing prompting guides do not always hold: a structured prompt incorporating roles, definitions, extraction rules, and JSON formatting unexpectedly underperforms a simpler question-style prompt, while the benefit of adding tabular context proves both prompt- and model-specific. We condense our evaluation procedure and findings into a practitioner’s decision guide for systematically testing design choices on task-specific data rather than adopting generic recommendations by default.

paper.title: Closing the Operational Gap in Semantic Caching
paper.abstract: Semantic caching cuts LLM inference costs by serving a cached response to semantically similar queries. Standard practice evaluates these systems using PR-AUC, a metric that only measures how well scores rank and ignores whether they are usable at a fixed threshold. We show this mismatch leads to systematically poor deployment choices, as models with the highest PR-AUC are often the worst in operation. We introduce Precision-Cache Hit Ratio (P-CHR) AUC, a cache-aware metric that measures precision across cache utilization levels, and Operational Retention Rate (ORR), which captures how much offline ranking quality survives at deployment. We decompose the operational gap between offline and deployed quality into a recoverable threshold-utility component and an irreducible structural component fixed by the dataset’s positive rate. Our experiments show that the threshold-utility gap is governed by the training objective rather than data scale, and yields only to re-normalizing scores over the candidate pool or changing the training objective. Ultimately, model selection for semantic caching is a threshold-utility problem, not a ranking one, and measuring it is the first step to closing the gap.

paper.title: EComAgentBench: Benchmarking Shopping Agents on Long-Horizon Tasks with Distributed Hidden Intent
paper.abstract: As LLM-based shopping agents enter production, existing benchmarks fail to capture how a shopper’s requirements arrive: stated implicitly in the query, recorded in a profile, or revealed only when the right question is asked. Benchmarks that expose full intent upfront and grade only the final choice can neither pose this long-horizon challenge nor explain which requirement an agent missed. To address this gap, we introduce EComAgentBench, a benchmark of 662 tasks grounded in real Amazon products and reviews. Each task scatters these requirements across a visible query, a tool-gated profile, and scripted clarification; an agent must uncover hidden intent, verify candidates against attributes and review evidence, and commit to a single product within 100 tool calls. Moreover, typed, source-tagged rubrics grade every task, attributing each failure to a requirement and its source. Construction is automated yet reliable, with every answer fixed in code before any text is generated and every sample validated. Our evaluation of seven models reveals that even the strongest attains only 57.1% overall accuracy, and rubric satisfaction degrades from visible to hidden sources. Overall, we believe EComAgentBench will serve as a reproducible foundation for moving shopping agents from single-query search toward dependable assistance over long horizons.

paper.title: TripScore: Aligning LLMs for Real-World Travel Planning via Expert-Calibrated Reward
paper.abstract: In our deployed travel-planning service, most users give minimal inputs or free-form requests rather than the structured constraint checklists assumed by existing benchmarks. We therefore present TripScore, a behavior-grounded benchmark and evaluation framework built from real user logs and calibrated against 1,468 pairwise judgments by 203 travel experts. TripScore couples a hierarchical feasibility gate (format and commonsense) with a unified, point-wise reward that aggregates soft quality and preference fulfillment. Using TripScore as both evaluator and reward signal, we benchmark direct prompting, test-time compute, neuro-symbolic solvers, code agents, and fine-tuning. We find that reinforcement learning fine-tuning (e.g., GRPO) provides consistent gains over other approaches under the same base model and practical latency.

paper.title: SkillChain: Closing the Loop on Skill Evolution for Image-Based E-Commerce AI Assistants
paper.abstract: Image-based AI assistants are now deployed at production scale on e-commerce platforms, where a single uploaded image can trigger fundamentally different user intents: product search, style recommendation, visual encyclopedia, or utility tool calls, each demanding its own response format, tool invocation, and domain knowledge. Without per-intent behavioral constraints, LLM-based systems conflate these heterogeneous modes and fall short of domain quality standards, while the breadth and dynamism of the intent space render manual engineering infeasible. To address this, we present SkillChain, which closes the production feedback loop on Skill evolution, automating the lifecycle of Skills through three stages: Skill Creator for bootstrapping from task specs and trajectories, Route Optimizer for routing alignment, and Body Refiner for iterative Skill Body refinement via dual-path LLM-Judge evaluation. Deployed on a production-scale e-commerce image assistant, SkillChain substantially improves aggregate response quality, with the strongest gains on structural compliance and content quality; a one-week online A/B experiment further confirms significant gains in user engagement, content consumption, and long-term retention.

paper.title: OpenDC-Infer-LC: Benchmarking Production-Valid Long-Context and RAG LLM Serving
paper.abstract: Long-context and RAG workloads expose production bottlenecks that raw tokens/s and offline accuracy do not capture, including prefill cost, KV-cache pressure, prefix reuse, routing, and latency SLOs. We introduce OpenDC-Infer-LC, a hardware- and backend-neutral benchmark for evaluating complete data-center LLM serving stacks under long-context and retrieved-context workloads. The benchmark ranks systems by SLO-qualified, quality-preserving goodput: valid output-token throughput at the highest load satisfying p95 TTFT, p95 TPOT, p95 end-to-end latency, and success-rate targets. Because RAG and LongBench quality depends on model ability, retrieval difficulty, and task difficulty, OpenDC-Infer-LC uses a relative quality guardrail against a low-load reference run for the same model and workload, while reporting absolute quality separately. Pilot results on AMD MI355X and NVIDIA B200 show that deployable capacity depends strongly on backend scheduling, cache reuse, context length, routing, quantization, and runtime maturity.

paper.title: From Historical Queries to Actionable Rubrics: Category-Aware Rubric Generation for Local-Life AI Search

author.affiliation: Beijing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics
Beijing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics
School of Artificial Intelligence, Beihang University

paper.abstract: Rubric generation improves the interpretability and actionability of large language model evaluation, but in online-to-offline (O2O) local-life AI search, user queries often reflect more complex needs, such as consumption intent, location constraints, and scenario preferences. Directly generating rubrics from a single query tends to produce generic criteria that fail to satisfy AI search evaluation needs, while leveraging candidate responses, preference samples, or external evidence at scale remains challenging. To address these limitations, we propose Category-Aware Rubric Generation (CaRG), a category-aware evaluation dimension candidate pool framework. Through embedding-based clustering, representative selection, and iterative LLM-based consolidation, CaRG constructs reusable candidate pools of both general and category-specific evaluation dimensions from representative historical queries. Subsequently, these candidate pools are leveraged to generate query-level rubrics with concrete positive and negative scoring criteria for target queries. Experimental results demonstrate that CaRG consistently outperforms Direct-Rubric and shows more stable overall quality than existing query-only baselines, while achieving the strongest overall agreement with production golden rubric rankings. Our repository is available at https://github.com/PlussLe/CaRG.

paper.title: PeopleSearchBench: Evaluating AI-Powered People Search Platforms with Criteria-Grounded Verification
paper.abstract: Al-powered people search platforms are increasingly deployed for recruiting, sales prospecting, and professional networking, yet no standardized benchmark exists for their rigorous evaluation. We present PEOPLESEARCHBENCH, an open-source benchmark comprising 119 multilingual queries across four scenarios: corporate recruiting, B2B sales prospecting, expert search, and influencer discovery. A central contribution is Criteria-Grounded Verification, an evaluation methodology that decomposes each query into explicit, independently checkable criteria and verifies each returned individual via live web search, producing factual relevance judgments rather than subjective LLM-as-judge scores. We evaluate four architecturally diverse platforms along three complementary dimensions-Relevance Precision, Effective Coverage, and Information Utility-and find that multi-source search agents significantly outperform single-domain systems, particularly in influencer discovery where the performance gap is largest. Platform rankings are robust across ablations on scoring thresholds, dimension weights, and judge models. All code, queries, and evaluation prompts are publicly available.

paper.title: Telco-GAIA: Bilingual Benchmark for Agents in Telecom Domain

author.affiliation: King Abdullah University of Science and Technology
King Abdullah University of Science and Technology
King Abdullah University of Science and Technology
King Abdullah University of Science and Technology
King Abdullah University of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: We introduce Telco-GAIA, a bilingual, multi-modal benchmark for evaluating tool-using agents on the data of a real-world telecommunications operator. Telco-GAIA comprises 100 human-verified question-answering tasks, in English and Arabic, that each demand multi-hop reasoning (4.2 hops on average) over three heterogeneous sources: a static website snapshot (HTML, images, and linked PDFs), a synthetic relational SQL database, and external web archives, spanning text, image, and tabular modalities. The benchmark is delivered as a sandboxed Docker environment and scored by normalized exact string matching, making evaluation objective, deterministic, and reproducible over time without any LLM-as-a-Judge. Evaluating a purpose-built reference agent across twelve commercial and open LLMs, we find Telco-GAIA challenging: even the strongest model solves only 71% of tasks; under a moderate cost budget, this falls to about 40%, and the visually grounded categories remain the weakest, where the average backend scores below 30%, leaving substantial headroom in document and image understanding. Telco-GAIA offers a rigorous, reproducible testbed for enterprise agents and a template for constructing closed-domain benchmarks.

paper.title: Same Gains, Half the Cost: Selector Choice in Automatic Prompt Optimization for Financial Question Answering
paper.abstract: Agentic pipelines assign a separately optimized system prompt to each step, so the cost of automatic prompt optimization (APO) multiplies across the pipeline. In this setting, the strategy for selecting candidate prompts cannot ignore budgetary constraints. We study the selection step of a textual gradient APO framework (Pryzant et al., 2023) in financial question answering with retrieval-augmented generation, a domain that stresses both the prompt and the reward signal. We compare the framework’s stateless Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) selector against two learned alternatives, PPO and DPO, with BEM as the shared reward. Across 135 experiments spanning three benchmarks, three budgets, and five random seeds, the selectors differ little in average accuracy gain (UCB 13.5% vs. DPO 13.4% vs. PPO 11.2%). Averaging over seeds erases these gaps and cost becomes the differentiating factor. PPO runs in under half the time of UCB (76 vs. 182 minutes per experiment) and its cost stays nearly flat as budget grows. For cost-sensitive deployments, selection has to consider efficiency in addition to accuracy, and PPO emerges as a promising low-cost selector within this APO setup. This design was shaped by an in-progress deployment at a consulting firm that assigns one system prompt to each step of an agentic data-cleaning pipeline.

paper.title: EvidenT: Building Trustworthy Enterprise Assistants through Evidence Groundedness and Traceability
paper.abstract: Enterprise AI assistants must produce responses that are verifiable and traceable to source evidence. However, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over heterogeneous enterprise data can suffer from citation drift, unsupported content, and weak source traceability. We present EvidenT (T = Trust + Transparency + Traceability), a lightweight pipeline that verifies extracted evidence against retrieved documents before answer generation, without model retraining. EvidenT combines structured passage extraction with deterministic lexical alignment to filter unsupported content, correct citation drift, and preserve source-span traceability. On approximately 500 real enterprise queries, EvidenT improves gold-source hit rate by an average of 29% over prompting baselines, produces no citations to non-retrieved urls, and achieves near-saturated answer-to-source lexical coverage.

paper.title: RainbowPlus: Enhancing Adversarial Prompt Generation via Evolutionary Quality-Diversity Search
paper.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to adversarial prompts that exploit safety mechanisms. Existing red-teaming methods face scalability challenges, computational bottlenecks, or limited attack diversity. We propose , a framework that reconceptualizes adversarial prompt generation as evolutionary quality-diversity search, where diverse attack strategies co-evolve across behavioral niches. introduces two synergistic innovations: (1) multi-element archives that maintain populations of elite solutions per niche, and (2) parallel fitness evaluation that replaces pairwise comparisons with efficient probabilistic scoring, achieving \Theta(M) speedup (from \Theta(M^2N) to \Theta(MN)). Experiments demonstrate superior performance: compared to Rainbow Teaming, generates 100\times more prompts (10,418 vs. 100) with higher attack success rates. Against nine state-of-the-art methods on HarmBench with 12 LLMs, achieves 81.1% average ASR - surpassing AutoDAN-Turbo by 3.9 points - while being 9\times faster (1.45 vs. 13.50 hours). Code: https://github.com/knoveleng/rainbowplus

paper.title: Building Interpretable Feature Representations for Resume–Vacancy Matching by Distilling Production LLM Signals
paper.abstract: Matching candidates to vacancies is central to recruitment, and a recruiter needs to see why a candidate fits, not only a single opaque relevance score. We provide this evidence as named, interpretable matching dimensions recruiters can act on — eight in our current deployment. We propose a two-part approach. The first is an LLM-based labeler whose prompts and feature definitions were refined from recruiter feedback while it served as an earlier production matching stage. In the current architecture, it is used only for offline labeling and is not called on online requests. The second is a feature bi-encoder distilled from it: a LoRAadapted embedding backbone with compact per-dimension heads that runs on CPU and serves all online requests. Both parts keep improving: prompts are revised as feedback arrives, and the bi-encoder is retrained on the updated labels. The model is trained on 168,772 labeled vacancy–resume pairs (17,921 vacancies and 180,030 resumes). Recruiters using the service can confirm or revise surfaced feature predictions. On 927 recruiter-recorded values from this selected production-feedback subset, the deployed student agrees with the recorded decisions in 888 cases (95.79%). This is operational, non-blinded agreement rather than an independent human evaluation.

paper.title: MortarBench: Evaluating Mortgage Loan Origination Agents
paper.abstract: Loan origination is the process by which a lender creates a new loan, from application and underwriting through approval and funding. This process serves a critical role in evaluating the eligibility and level of risk posed by an applicant. Recently, firms have begun using mortgage loan agents to augment human loan officers, despite a lack of any public benchmark. To fill this gap, we present MortarBench, a loan origination agent benchmark. MortarBench uses a financial data synthesis and mutation pipeline to generate examples with broad edge case coverage that match real-world distributions and questions. We find that state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs) perform poorly, with closed-source models achieving at most 80.8% F1 accuracy. We also discover systematic biases in LLM perception of foreignness related to non-English names. Noting these weaknesses, we introduce CRIT, a confidence calibration framework. Our method increases peak F1 accuracy to 83.6% while improving risk management steering and reducing bias.

paper.title: Retrieval-GRPO: Reinforcement Learning for Dense Retrieval in Taobao Search
paper.abstract: Dense retrieval is a fundamental component of e-commerce search, projecting user queries and items into a shared semantic representation space for large-scale, real-time retrieval. While LLM-based embedding models are increasingly replacing BERT-style encoders, prevalent training pipelines still largely rely on BERT-like supervised fine-tuning and hard negative mining. Such paradigms require intricate offline negative construction, thereby constraining model iteration efficiency and limiting the evolution of learned semantic representations. We propose Retrieval-GRPO, a dense retrieval framework based on reinforcement learning. It dispenses with offline hard negative mining by performing dynamic Top-K candidates retrieval during training. Moreover, we introduce a relevance-oriented LLM as a reward model to provide real-time supervisory signals. Guided by the resulting reinforcement learning objective, the retriever updates embeddings to better capture semantic correspondence and achieve improved generalization on complex long-tail queries. Extensive offline and online experiments substantiate the effectiveness of Retrieval-GRPO in Taobao Search, which serves China’s largest e-commerce platform.

paper.title: ACE: A Self-Correcting Agentic Canvas Editor for Multi-Slide Presentation Automation
paper.abstract: Commercial design platforms increasingly edit documents through large language model (LLM) agents, but two practical problems block reliable deployment: legacy document formats expose only flat, absolutely positioned elements, so agents must recompute coordinates and routinely break layouts; and design has no unique ground truth, so diff-against-reference metrics penalize valid-but-different outputs. We present ACE, an agentic canvas editor over a hierarchical scene-graph with a presentation-specialized action space (98 tools), paired with CARE, a content-aware router that feeds the agent only the relevant slice of each deck (avg. \sim 89\% input-token reduction), and a self-correction loop driven by a ground-truth-free instruction-following (IF) judge whose natural-language critique is fed back as the next-turn instruction. On a multi-slide benchmark and with a fixed backbone, a scene-graph editor in a single turn already matches a same-backbone agentic HTML pipeline that iterates internally; adding self-correction lifts ACE clearly above it on quality (IF 4.45 vs. 4.09; VQ 4.02 vs. 3.89) while remaining 1.75\times faster and \sim 44\% cheaper. Self-correction contributes +0.41 IF / +0.27 VQ, and 66% of cases halt after one pass, keeping it cheap.

paper.title: Safe and Sufficient Caching: Validated Evidence Reuse for Production Retrieval-Augmented Generation
paper.abstract: Production Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems serve repeated queries over evolving document corpora under user-specific access constraints. Standard pipelines perform full retrieval and generation for every request, wasting computation on recurring queries. Naive caching reduces latency but introduces safety failures: stale evidence from updated documents, unauthorized content crossing access boundaries, and superseded passages no longer reflecting source truth. These violations are invisible on academic benchmarks yet unacceptable in enterprise deployment. We introduce SSC (Safe and Sufficient Caching), a validated evidence reuse framework for production RAG. SSC caches evidence chunks (not generated answers) with perchunk provenance metadata, and enforces hard validity constraints before reuse: access-control gating ensures user authorization, and freshness verification confirms source-document currency. Only evidence passing both checks enters a utility-based ranking stage balancing relevance, source trust, historical utility, and serving cost. This separation of safety from efficiency is the central contribution. On WebQuestions and HotpotQA, SSC maintains full quality parity with unrestricted retrieval baselines, confirming zero degradation from evidence reuse. On a proprietary InternalQA workload with role based access control and document versioning, it reduces end-to-end latency by 22% and retrieval cost by 34% while achieving zero invalid reuse, compared to 3.4-9.8% violation rates for standard caching and 0.3-8.2% for TTL-based invalidation. The method is training-free, retriever-agnostic, and deploys as a thin validation layer in existing RAG pipelines.

paper.title: TaxCE : A Framework for Automated Taxonomy Construction and Evaluation at Scale
paper.abstract: Organizing unstructured feedback text into hierarchical taxonomy is a fundamental challenge in NLP, particularly in domains where feedback arrives at massive scale in varied forms such as reviews, transcripts, and surveys. Existing approaches either produce shallow hierarchies, neglect long-tail topics, or lack rigorous evaluation frameworks. We present TaxCE, a fully automated framework that constructs multi-level hierarchical taxonomies from raw text through progressive condensation of corpus content into actionable segments, deduplicated semantic units, and granular topics with definitions, which are then organized bottom-up into a hierarchy with corpus-groundedness. We also introduce three corpus-grounded evaluation metrics, Exclusivity, Exhaustivity, and Granularity (EEG), and integrate them into a metrics-in-the-loop iterative refinement mechanism that diagnoses deficiencies and applies targeted corrections until convergence. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TaxCE consistently outperforms existing baselines spanning classical topic models, neural methods, and LLM-based approaches, with average improvements of 11.8, 20.5, and 15.7 percentage points in exclusivity, exhaustivity, and granularity respectively over the strongest baseline. Human evaluation further confirms superior taxonomy quality, actionability, and navigability.

paper.title: Conversation Coach: A Voice-enabled AI System that Helps Practice Difficult Workplace Conversations
paper.abstract: Effective manager-employee communication is critical for retaining high performers and developing underperformers, yet training managers in these skills remains costly. Text-based chatbots offer a scalable approach but cannot provide realistic rehearsal: managers need to practice speaking aloud to build confidence before high-stakes conversations. In this paper, we propose Conversation Coach, a voice-first AI system that enables managers to rehearse difficult workplace conversations in a realistic spoken format. The system addresses three challenges: achieving low-latency interactions with strong language understanding, enabling adaptive conversations through configurable bot personalities that simulate different employee types, and generating personalized feedback on content and policy compliance. We compare an end-to-end speech-to-speech model with a cascaded approach combining automatic speech recognition, a large language model, and text-to-speech synthesis. The end-to-end approach achieves 3\times lower median (P50) latency with native barge-in capability at an estimated 8\times lower cost, while the cascaded approach offers superior reasoning essential for coaching quality. We deployed the cascaded architecture in production, where 40,000+ managers used it over six months, with adoption patterns indicating selective use for difficult conversations.

paper.title: Deploying Programmatic Tool Calling for Large-Scale Agentic Systems
paper.abstract: Production tool calling for agentic systems must satisfy four operational requirements: bounded per-invocation cost, predictable latency, adaptability to evolving tool catalogs, and the ability to catch errors before execution. The ReAct paradigm keeps the large language model (LLM) in the loop, but at production scale, re-processing intermediate results inflates cost and latency and degrades answer quality. Programmatic tool calling (PTC) offers an alternative; the LLM generates a single script that resolves dependencies and extracts relevant fields in one inference pass. PTC is a harder generation task, however, because the LLM must produce code that handles complex, variable responses without observing intermediate results, and existing remedies each fail at least one of the four requirements. We describe a production deployment of PTC serving 26,528 invocations, paired with a three-layer abstract syntax tree (AST)-based validator that rejects invalid scripts before execution and requires no training data, preserving adaptability to evolving tool catalogs. This reduced average input tokens by 77%, latency by 21%, and increased the answered-query rate by 5.6 percentage points across 19 production agents.

paper.title: Data-Driven Persona-Conditioned Agents for A/B Test Simulation
paper.abstract: A/B testing is the gold standard for evaluating product changes, but each experiment requires real user traffic, engineering effort, and weeks of measurement. We propose a simulation framework that predicts A/B test outcomes using LLM-powered agents conditioned on data-driven personas grounded in real user behavioral signals. Unlike prior work that relies on synthetic or rule-based personas, our agents are constructed from anonymized behavioral data—activity patterns, engagement signals, and inferred demographics—enabling more faithful population modeling. We frame A/B test simulation as a structured question task and systematically study (i) question design formats, (ii) the impact of persona data source and domain alignment, (iii) the trade-off between per-persona behavioral depth and population diversity, and (iv) efficient population subsampling. On a benchmark of 40 A/B tests spanning two metric types, our best configuration achieves 0.75–0.90 directional accuracy depending on the test metric, demonstrating that data-driven personas are a viable path toward fast, low-cost experiment pre-screening.

paper.title: SCR-Eval: Evaluating Video Subtitle Translation with a Script-like Context Representation
paper.abstract: The quality of video subtitle translation cannot be assessed from sentence-level semantic equivalence alone. Subtitles are governed by audiovisual cues, speaker relationships, and narrative context that accumulates across scenes, yet existing automatic metrics and text-centric LLM-based evaluation do not reflect these factors.We propose SCR-Eval, a context-aware evaluation framework for video subtitle translation, built on a Script-like Context Representation (SCR) reconstructed from the video. The evaluator aligns the translated subtitles to the SCR’s semantic scenes, then performs MQM error analysis with an LLM judge.On three open movies, we benchmark five English-to-Korean subtitle providers against blind, randomized annotations by seven professional evaluators. The framework’s provider ranking agrees strongly with the experts (system-level Spearman ρ = 0.967). In ablations, agreement weakens stepwise from full context through scene-bounded text to isolated source–translation pairs. Automatic baselines agree less: MetricX and xCOMET correlate negatively with the expert ranking, while RUBRIC-MQM correlates only weakly.With full context, SCR-Eval shows substantially stronger agreement with experts than these baselines.

paper.title: APDMem: Agent-Controlled Progressive Disclosure for Query-Adaptive Long-Term Memory
paper.abstract: Personalized LLM assistants must recover sparse evidence from long conversation histories across queries of varying complexity. We introduce APDMem (Agent-controlled Progressive Disclosure Memory), a hierarchical long-term memory architecture that applies progressive disclosure to memory retrieval. Rather than relying on a flat memory store or fixed retrieval granularity, APDMem represents conversation history as four progressively detailed layers: thematic summaries, personalized key facts, turn-level evidence notes, and raw messages. At inference time, a controller applies progressive disclosure to the memory hierarchy: it first reads high-level summaries and drills into finer evidence only when needed. This creates an adaptive cost-fidelity trade-off: simple queries can terminate early, while complex temporal, multi-hop, or exact-evidence queries trigger deeper inspection. A note synthesizer converts retrieved evidence into a query-focused structure that consolidates facts, orders events, and flags contradictions before final answer generation. Experiments on LongMemEval show that APDMem achieves strong performance for long-context memory reasoning while accessing only 8% of the total conversations.

paper.title: HyDRA: Hybrid Dynamic Routing Architecture for Heterogeneous LLM Pools
paper.abstract: Production LLM deployments maintain heterogeneous model pools spanning order-of-magnitude cost differences, yet existing routers make binary strong-vs-weak decisions coupled to specific model identities, requiring retraining on every catalog change. We present HyDRA (Hybrid Dynamic Routing Architecture), which uses a lightweight ModernBERT encoder to predict capability requirements (reasoning, code generation, debugging, and tool use) for each query. It then selects the cheapest model meeting those requirements through shortfall matching. HyDRA decouples the learned predictor from the model catalog, enabling catalog changes without retraining. On SWE-Bench Verified, HyDRA is 0.3 QR points below always-strong (not statistically significant) at 54.1% cost savings. On a held-out multilingual evaluation set, the same checkpoint retains 80.6% of oracle-routing quality at 37.5% cost savings, tunable to 79.1% retention at 56.1% savings. A 14-day A/B flight with close to 1M users per arm found statistically significant improvements in latency, time-to-first-token, reliability, and user activity. Deployed across GitHub Copilot VS Code Chat, GitHub Copilot CLI, and GitHub Copilot extensions, HyDRA demonstrates cross-lingual routing consistency across 16 languages and 4 language groups.

paper.title: Reasoning vs. Validation in LLM-based Pharmacological Parameter Extraction
paper.abstract: Pharmacokinetic (PK) parameters are critical to drug development, but many remain embedded in free-text biomedical literature rather than a structured form. Existing extraction approaches primarily target explicit parameter mentions, while a substantial proportion of PK values must be inferred from context. We introduce implicit PK parameter extraction, where parameter identity is not explicitly stated but must be resolved through domain-grounded, multi-sentence reasoning. To address this challenge, we propose CORVA, a validation-enhanced LLM-based extraction framework that integrates reasoning and domain constraints to extract structured PK tuples from text. We also construct a labelled dataset from DrugBank absorption descriptions, of which 47.5% involve implicit expressions. Relative to the strongest baseline, the proposed method improves F1 by 35.3% and tuple accuracy by 52.9%. CORVA achieves the highest implicit recognition rate at 45.8%, which is 10.5 points ahead of the runner-up. Our results demonstrate that reliable implicit PK extraction requires validation as a first-class component rather than a post-processing step, which offers a practical framework for scalable knowledge extraction from biomedical literature. The code and data are available at https://github.com/wuqinhao/CORVA.

paper.title: MINCE: Shrinking LLM Evaluation Datasets via Few-Model Monte Carlo Calibration

author.affiliation: International Institute of Information Technology Hyderabad

paper.abstract: Evaluating LLMs across many model variants—quantized, fine-tuned, or deployment-specific—requires running large benchmarks repeatedly, a process that can take tens of hours per model on edge hardware such as NPUs. Existing subset selection methods reduce this cost but depend on large calibration pools or learned prediction layers. We introduce MINCE (Monte Carlo Informed N-sizing for Compact Evaluation), which uses Monte Carlo simulation over per-item logs from a small set of calibration models to find the minimum subset size that bounds accuracy drift and then fixes a randomly sampled subset at that size, with no prediction layer needed. MINCE reduces IFEVAL by 54%, MMLU by 89%, GSM8K by 70%, and MMLU-Pro by 88% with maximum drift \leq2.62 pp on BF16 calibration models. The frozen subsets generalize to held-out GPU models with mean drift \leq1.40 pp and to INT4 NPU models with mean drift of 0.77–3.59 pp, while delivering evaluation speedups of up to 8.1\times on the GPU models and evaluation speedups of 1.7–3.4\times on the NPU models. The method is robust to calibration pool size and achieves lower drift than tinyBenchmarks (12\times lower on MMLU, 3.3\times on GSM8K) while using 42\times fewer calibration models.

paper.title: CHUNDER: Enabling Million-Token Qwen3 Serving on AMD ROCm
paper.abstract: Million-token context serving is becoming a critical requirement for industry LLM systems for real deployments. However, practical 1M-context serving for open-source models has remained heavily CUDA-centric, largely because the required long-context runtime features are not fully available on AMD ROCm. With AMD GPUs now reported at around 19% market share, this gap matters. We address it by enabling 1M-token Qwen3 serving on AMD GPUs with ROCm. We present , a runtime stack that enables million-token serving for the widely used open-source Qwen3 family on AMD ROCm. achieves this by intercepting vLLM’s attention routing at runtime and redirecting queries, keys, and values to JIT-compiled Triton Dual Chunk Attention (DCA) kernels, without forking the serving engine. We then harden the surrounding runtime to make full 1M-token execution practical: DCA-aware paged metadata, tiled single-request chunked prefill, MoE token chunking that reduces per-rank transient memory from approximately 91.6 GiB to 10.6 GiB, and FP8 GEMMs with hardened hipBLASLt kernel selection. We evaluate across multiple million-token context tasks and show consistent serving performance and exact retrieval correctness. To our knowledge, this is the first reported end-to-end Qwen3 million-token serving path on AMD ROCm integrated with vLLM.

paper.title: Beyond Query-Item Matching: Personalized Behavioral Relevance Modeling for E-commerce Search via Rubric-Guided Reinforcement Learning
paper.abstract: E-commerce search systems typically separate query-item relevance matching from downstream personalized ranking. While effective for large-scale serving, this design leaves relevance levels dominated by objective query-item matching, forcing follow-up ranking to operate over candidate structures that may not reflect user behavioral preference. We define a new personalized behavioral relevance task, which predicts whether a relevance-stage candidate item is supported by the user’s behavioral evidence under current query intent. We develop a corresponding framework, BRIDGE, for Behavioral Relevance Inference with Dynamic Guidance from Evidence. It organizes multi-timescale behavioral context from online logs, obtains reliable supervision with multi-perspective annotation and adjudication, and trains an LLM to produce structured evidence-grounded decision rationales. It particularly incorporates sample-specific rubric rewards into GRPO to improve generated reasoning traces. Offline experiments validate that BRIDGE improves both prediction accuracy and reasoning quality. Online A/B tests show gains of 0.19% in active user-days and 0.67% in transaction-related user-days, both significant in statistics.

paper.title: Cognitive Echoes: Deployable Conversational Risk Screening in Automotive Finance on Constrained LLMs
paper.abstract: Automotive-finance screening can fail when individually valid documents are paired with an internally inconsistent applicant narrative. We present the Adversarial Cognitive Probing Framework (ACPF), a theory-motivated staged protocol that scores four ordinal behavioral dimensions and delegates the final decision to a deterministic backend predicate. We evaluate ACPF on a risk-enriched retrospective corpus of 340 officer–applicant dialogues: 72 institutional adjudications of suspected misrepresentation, 138 cases of significant early delinquency, 110 good cases, and 20 non-fraud rejections excluded from the primary metrics. On identical fixed transcripts and the same QWEN3.5-122B carrier, structured scoring raises combined-risk capture from 5.7% to 61.0% while reducing the false-rejection rate from 14.5% to 12.7%.
