With OmniMAX, the selected low-FPR carrier, ACPF captures 58/138 (42.0%) delinquency cases at 6/110 (5.5%) false rejections; current origination review flags none of these delinquency cases. On the institutionally adjudicated stratum, ACPF captures 56/72 (77.8%) versus 72/72 for current review, but we make no comparative claim because the label and reference decision share institutional provenance. A shadow deployment has no adverse-action authority; prospective outcome validation is not yet available.

paper.title: Techniques for Peak Memory Reduction for LoRA Fine-tuning of LLMs on Edge Devices
paper.abstract: Fine-tuning of Large Language Models (LLMs) using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) on an end-user’s data offers personalized experiences while keeping data private, but faces severe memory constraints on consumer hardware. Peak memory during fine-tuning often exceeds device limits, especially for models with billions of parameters and long-context training data. This paper introduces a suite of complementary techniques to reduce memory footprint: (1) base model quantization with on-the-fly dequantization, (2) memory-efficient checkpointing combining selective activation caching and disk offloading, (3) softmax approximation using semantically relevant token subsets, and (4) logits masking. Only softmax approximation alters the training objective and we discuss the resulting quality trade-off both analytically and empirically. Experiments on Llama-3.2 3B and Qwen-2.5 3B demonstrate up to 26\times and 28\times reduction in peak memory, enabling fine-tuning on resource-constrained devices.

paper.title: Open Rubric System: Scaling Reinforcement Learning with Pairwise Adaptive Rubric

author.affiliation: Beijing University of Post and Telecommunications

paper.abstract: We argue that robust alignment for non-verifiable tasks is fundamentally a \textit{principle generalization} problem: reward should be guided by explicit, auditable principles rather than compressed into a learned scalar function. To operationalize this view, we present the \textbf{Open Rubric System (OpenRS)} , a modular, rubrics-based \textit{LLM-as-a-Judge} framework built around \textbf{Pairwise Adaptive Meta-Rubrics (PAMR)} and lightweight \textit{Pointwise Verifiable Rubrics} (PVRs). OpenRS is governed by an explicit \textit{meta-rubric}—not a rubric itself, but a higher-level guideline that specifies \textit{how} rubrics should be generated, which criteria to prioritize, and which failure modes are non-negotiable—and instantiates concrete \textit{adaptive rubrics} on the fly by conditioning on the semantic differences between two candidate responses. It then performs criterion-wise \textit{pairwise} comparisons and aggregates criterion-level preferences externally, avoiding pointwise weighted scalarization while improving discriminability in open-ended settings. Finally, we instantiate OpenRS as reward supervision in pairwise RL training. Empirically, OpenRS achieves state-of-the-art results on four reward-modeling benchmarks and yields stable gains when replacing scalar reward models in end-to-end RL.

paper.title: Retrieval-Conditional Parsing Score (RCPS): Choosing Document Parsers by Retrieval, Not by Appearance
paper.abstract: Document RAG retrieves from parser outputs, yet parsers are commonly selected by intrinsic measures of transcription fidelity and boundary quality rather than by retrieval performance. We introduce the Retrieval-Conditional Parsing Score (RCPS), a training-free protocol that ranks parser–chunker combinations on a fixed held-out Q–A retrieval probe. RCPS averages mean reciprocal rank (MRR) across specified retrievers and retrieval depths, using the same format-normalised exact-span relevance rule for every candidate. On KoGovDoc-RAG, table-enabled MinerU-on has a higher Boundary Clarity score than our production parser, Prod (0.713 versus 0.610). Yet its Hit@1 is 42.6 percentage points lower (0.123 versus 0.549). Across five parsers evaluated on all 294 pages, RCPS ranges from 0.137 to 0.584. With Prod fixed, the four chunkers score between 0.535 and 0.593. A retriever-free coverage diagnostic finds no normalised exact match for 20.2% of reference spans in Prod output. No tested chunker splits more than 2.3%. On source-aligned OHR-Bench data, semantic noise lowers retrieval while Boundary Clarity remains stable or changes non-monotonically. In a secondary parser-training study, two direct preference optimization checkpoints improve Hit@5 by only 0.95 and 1.15 percentage points over Prod on an audited compatibility subset; a matched edit-distance control performs similarly. The workflow therefore selects with RCPS, diagnoses with coverage, and trains only if needed. We release the 663-Q–A KoGovDoc-RAG probe and an RCPS reference implementation.

paper.title: GraphReduce: Coverage-Preserving LLM Aggregation for E-commerce Review Insights

author.affiliation: School of Computer Science and Engineering, Nanyang Technological University

paper.abstract: In e-commerce, product detail pages (PDPs) often contain hundreds or thousands of customer reviews, yet the interface can surface only a small set of concise and reliable insights. A useful review aggregation system must therefore abstract recurring themes while preserving which reviews support each insight. We study this problem as structured review-insight mining: review-level tuples are first extracted and then aggregated into ranked product-level insight clusters with explicit member traceability. We propose GraphReduce, a coverage-preserving framework for product-scale review insight aggregation. It combines a contrastively trained projection layer over frozen sentence embeddings, graph-based clustering on local neighborhood structure, and an LLM reducer/ranker for naming and ordering canonical clusters. By keeping membership accounting outside the generative step, GraphReduce preserves complete tuple coverage and avoids a common failure mode of direct LLM summarization: producing plausible high-level themes while silently dropping long-tail evidence. Across three product-category benchmarks, GraphReduce improves recovery of gold insight clusters over strong lossless embedding-based baselines while maintaining comparable ranking quality. We further show that flat LLM and topic-modeling baselines can appear competitive under ranking metrics despite omitting substantial input evidence, and that an anti-copy reinforcement objective improves the quality of upstream tuple extraction. These results highlight the importance of coverage-aware aggregation for faithful review insight mining in e-commerce settings.

paper.title: Intent-Driven Generative Query Suggestion with Query-Level Credit Assignment

author.affiliation: Beijing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics

paper.abstract: Generative query suggestion aims to enhance user engagement by anticipating user intents and recommending relevant follow-up queries. A central challenge is to generate slates whose individual queries are useful while the slate covers distinct intents. We propose an Intent-Driven Query Suggestion Framework with dual-stage optimization. First, intent-aware diversity modeling constructs intent-aligned supervised fine-tuning (SFT) data and uses an Intent-Aware Diversity Reward to optimize intent coverage. Second, query-level credit assignment routes individual quality signals to the corresponding query tokens while sharing a slate-level diversity signal across the slate. Experiments on a large-scale production dataset, including online A/B testing and offline evaluation, show improvements in click-through rate, query quality, and intent coverage.

paper.title: CACHE-ED2: Compiling LLM Reasoning into Reusable Extraction Programs for Document Extraction at Scale
paper.abstract: Extracting structured information from visually rich documents at enterprise scale demands both the reasoning capability of large language models and the efficiency of deterministic execution. Current approaches either deploy LLMs as instance-level analysts, incurring per-document inference costs that are prohibitive for repetitive templates, or rely on manually authored vendor-specific prompts that do not scale beyond a handful of high-volume vendors. We present CACHE-ED2, a framework that repositions the LLM as a system-level developer: given a novel document format, a multimodal ReAct-based agent synthesizes a reusable Document Extraction DSL (DocExDSL) program encoding the complete extraction logic (strategies, disambiguation, transforms, and automated reasoning validation), then caches it for deterministic, LLM-free execution on all subsequent documents of the same format. A contrastive Document Format Encoder routes incoming documents to cached programs with perfect hit rates, and a HITL Feedback Analysis Agent incorporates analyst corrections to refine programs over time. On public benchmarks (CORD v2, FATURA) and production streams spanning seven business verticals (580,000+ documents, 11,500+ vendors), CACHE-ED2 achieves near-perfect extraction accuracy ({\sim}0.99) with a 1.0 extraction rate on document-present fields and perfect format matching across 50+ benchmark templates, matching or exceeding manually authored vendor-specific prompts, while reducing cumulative token consumption by {\sim}2.6\times over first 1,000 documents.

paper.title: AgentLens: Trajectory Reviews for Coding Agent Evaluation

author.affiliation: Steklov Institute of Mathematics at St. Petersburg

paper.abstract: We present AgentLens, a trajectory-level evaluation framework for interactive code agents, built from production-informed tasks and integrated into continuous regression testing. Most code-agent benchmarks reduce a run to a single bit—did the task pass?—but the people who actually use these agents experience the entire trajectory: how the agent follows instructions, uses its tools, verifies its own work, recovers from mistakes, and talks to them along the way. AgentLens evaluates that whole trajectory, pairing formal verification with LLM-written trajectory reviews and side-by-side comparisons, so that each run yields a readable explanation of the final score. Apart from ranking models, AgentLens can be used to diagnose model behavior, compare successive versions of agents, and catch product regressions in an evaluation pipeline. We release AgentLens at https://github.com/agent-lens/agent-lens-bench.

paper.title: The Cost of Decomposition: Trade-Offs in Long-Context Aspect-Based Scientific Summarization

author.affiliation: University of Kassel, hessian.AI, and ScaDS.AI

paper.abstract: Aspect-based scientific summarization produces a focused summary of a long document for a given aspect (e.g., Approach, Methods). Prior work decomposes the task, assuming a model can neither attend over the full document nor resolve aspect complexity in one pass. We revisit both assumptions now that compact yet capable language models handle long contexts natively. Across three datasets and two primary open long-context models, decomposition provides no reliable quality advantage over direct full-document prompting. With the main 9B model, zero-shot is strongest on aggregate lexical, semantic, and claim-recall/F1 metrics; under the 7B robustness model, simple decomposed variants occasionally edge zero-shot, but gains are small and inconsistent. On these primary models, the multi-role agentic pipeline is never best in aggregate and incurs substantially higher token cost, whereas RAG uses roughly one seventh of zero-shot’s tokens but delivers lower, less consistent quality. We characterize where added complexity loses, quantify the cost–quality trade-off, and distill practical deployment guidance. Code is available on GitHub.

paper.title: Beyond Final Visibility: A Three-Stage Diagnostic Framework for Enterprise Generative Search Optimization
paper.abstract: Generative search introduces failures in query matching, competitive ranking, and grounded generation, while conventional SEO and final mention metrics often cannot locate these failures. We present a controlled Stage-Isolated Evaluation framework that converts stage-specific errors into fact-grounded sitemap revisions. In an industrial study with an anonymized consumer-health company, each version is evaluated against nine fixed competitors using disjoint training, validation, and held-out test queries. The selected checkpoint improves the test score from 58.78 to 69.98, exceeding one-shot rewriting by 6.19 points and same-budget recursion without diagnostics by 3.07 points. Different stages favor different checkpoints, revealing non-monotonic trade-offs. Pilot online results and human annotation provide additional support for the framework as a reproducible diagnostic proxy for enterprise GEO.

paper.title: Querit-Reranker: Training Compact Multilingual Rerankers via Efficient Label-Free Distribution Adaptation

author.affiliation: Insititute Of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
Institute of Computing Technolgy, Chinese Academy of Sciences

paper.abstract: A deployable multilingual reranker must not only generalize across languages, domains, and ranking tasks, but also remain efficient to serve as a second-stage reranker in practical systems. However, adapting it to new target distributions typically requires extensive task-specific relevance annotations. We present Querit-Reranker, a family of multilingual rerankers trained with a data-centric pipeline for label-efficient adaptation. We instantiate it as Querit-Reranker-A0.4B, initialized from an in-house MoE backbone with 0.4B activated parameters, and Querit-Reranker-4B, initialized from Qwen3-Embedding-4B. Our pipeline first learns general relevance modeling from large-scale ranking-oriented data, then adapts to target distributions through synthetic-query mining with teacher scores as continuous soft labels. To consolidate complementary task-adapted strengths, we further merge checkpoints via spherical linear interpolation, obtaining a single deployable model without runtime ensembling overhead. Using Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B as the first-stage retriever, Querit-Reranker-A0.4B improves average nDCG@10 from 54.11 to 59.28 on BEIR and from 59.87 to 67.70 on MIRACL. On MTEB Multilingual v2 Reranking, it also shows competitive performance with larger embedding-based models, while Querit-Reranker-4B further achieves state-of-the-art performance among all evaluated models. We release both models on Hugging Face.

paper.title: CemLit-IE: Schema-Constrained LLM Extraction for Traceable Cement Strength Databases
paper.abstract: Cementitious materials teams need machine-readable databases of compressive strength records to support mix-design optimization. However, manual curation of the literature is too slow and hard to scale. We present CemLit-IE, a five-stage zero-shot pipeline, converting raw PDFs into fully attributed records with provenance. The core challenge is that the relevant information is distributed across tables, text, and figures. Even though table-only extraction produces plausible numbers, the results are not auditable. CemLit-IE addresses this through a series of methods, including keyword-weighted page scoring, structured table injection, value-provenance schema, and review queue. On a benchmark of 20 papers with 655 expert-annotated records, CemLit-IE achieves a recall of 76.3% with 99.2% precision and 100% exact-match accuracy in a text-only model. The recall can be raised to 83.5% when figure reading is enabled. The ablation study shows that each design choice contributes to improving precision. As for the cost, a separate 270-paper journal-batch run extracted 2,039 strength records at $31.28 total API cost. All data and code are publicly released.

paper.title: PRISM: Prompt-Refined In-Context System Modeling for Financial Retrieval
paper.abstract: Deploying LLMs for financial information retrieval demands accuracy, cost efficiency, and reproducibility, yet most approaches require expensive fine-tuning. PRISM is a training-free framework that composes three deployable modules (prompt engineering, in-context learning, and a candidate refinement module) with a boundary-condition study of multi-agent coordination for financial document retrieval. On FiQA-2018, stacked reranking and k-reciprocal encoding raise Recall@100 from 0.7783 to 0.8326. On FinAgentBench, a Cohere-refined top-50 pool yields a higher observed end-to-end NDCG@5, below this evaluation’s minimum detectable effect, while cutting per-query cost by about 35%. Added complexity does not always pay off: k-reciprocal encoding stops helping once the upstream stage is already high-recall, and multi-agent coordination is not a default for fine-grained chunk ranking. Matched pairs that hold prompt, model, and exemplars fixed lose 0.0702 and 0.0681 combined NDCG@5 to their single-path controls, and the whole gap sits at the chunk stage. We release an expert-annotated FinAgentBench evaluation set, together with a label-robustness sweep over 16 alternative ground-truth constructions, restoring a reproducible evaluation path after the original evaluator went offline. Without fine-tuning, PRISM placed third on the official FinAgentBench private leaderboard (leaderboard basis, NDCG@5 0.71181), reaches NDCG@10 0.6197 on FiQA-2018, and 98% accuracy on FinanceBench. We report per-query latency, token, and dollar accounting across roughly 40 configurations, present the quality–cost–latency Pareto frontier, and introduce FACET, a transparent SLA-specific scalarization for choosing among non-dominated configurations. Code and dataset are released at https://bit.ly/prism-ailens.

paper.title: Rethinking Content Moderation via Severity-Aware Ranking

author.affiliation: Shanghai University of Finance and Economics

paper.abstract: Online video content moderation is critical for protecting minors. Violations are increasingly implicit and context-dependent: a swimwear is innocuous in a vlog but high-risk with suggestive posing. Yet, traditional binary systems fundamentally fail to capture this continuous severity spectrum, directly leading to both excessive false positives for context-heavy samples and missing deeply implicit violations. We introduce KUROKO, a content moderation system that acts as a behind-the-scenes assistant, driving a paradigm shift in content moderation from binary classification to severity-aware ranking. Our contributions are threefold: (1) Human-Centric Severity Ranking: KUROKO shifts from rigid binary divides to a continuous risk spectrum, producing nuanced, expert-level rationales closely aligning with human judgment. (2) Verifiable Alignment and Interpretability: By integrating a severity-aware data engine and a verifiable reinforcement learning approach, we replace black-box decisions with transparent, actionable diagnostics. (3) Cost-Efficient Deployment: We engineer a coarse-to-fine inference architecture equipped with a lightweight recall classifier, enabling compact models to rival proprietary VLMs at a fraction of the computational cost. Extensive offline and online A/B tests demonstrate KUROKO’s advantages over traditional binary baselines and its competitiveness with leading commercial APIs at a fraction of their scale. Online, KUROKO yields more human-confirmed enforcement actions under an equal human-review budget, while lowering violative exposure and user negative feedback.

paper.title: FlowTrain: Flow-Based Decoupled Training for Industrial-Grade Vision-Language Models
paper.abstract: Industrial-grade distributed training of vision-language models (VLMs) remains far less efficient than that of unimodal LLMs. Existing solutions either follow a monolithic design that assigns uniform parallelism to heterogeneous modules or adopt a disaggregated deployment that separates modules while executing them as a batch-synchronized pipeline. In this paper, we highlight that the above solutions are still not sufficient, and VLM training can be further decoupled. To this end, we present FlowTrain, a flow-based decoupled training framework that reformulates VLM training as a producer-consumer dataflow coordinated through a unified memory pool. The encoder and backbone can progress independently over a global virtual address space. Since this execution decoupling fundamentally changes the optimization objective of allocation and scheduling, FlowTrain further introduces a heterogeneous parallel allocator that assigns module-specific parallelism strategies by solving a throughput matching problem. The dynamic packing scheduler is used to construct balanced microbatches at runtime according to the actual LLM-side computation cost. Extensive experiments on real-world workloads show that FlowTrain achieves over 50% MFU and up to 1.7× throughput improvement, narrowing the efficiency gap to LLM-only training.

paper.title: Predefined-Tool Execution for Reliable LLM Agents in Semiconductor Lot Analysis
paper.abstract: LLM agents for structured data analysis rely on dynamic query generation, in which the model synthesises tool calls at runtime. This introduces failures such as fabricated dataset references, unsupported operations, and incorrect results, which existing mitigations reduce but do not eliminate. We propose predefined-tool execution as an architectural alternative in which the language model selects and parameterises tools from a fixed, schema-validated registry. We formalise the approach using typed tool specifications and prove executability and hallucination-suppression properties under assumptions. We complement the architecture with a Numerical Faithfulness Checker that verifies quantitative claims against pre-computed ground truth, and evaluate the system on a domain-specific benchmark using four language-model backbones. The suppression property follows from the validation layer under those assumptions, and held across all 276 evaluated agent executions involving 23 queries, four backbones and three runs. Mean exact-plan-match rates ranged from 50.7 to 53.6 per cent, with a between-backbone spread within a single backbone. Because exact plan match penalises valid but non-minimal plans, it is a strict lower bound on task correctness. Given only three runs per backbone, comparisons are descriptive, not evidence of equivalence The on-premise open-weight backbones performed comparably to commercial ones on the measured metrics, supporting confidential deployments.

paper.title: TeleTables: A Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Understanding of Tables in Technical Standards
paper.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to telecom engineering tasks, yet perform poorly on 3GPP specifications. These standards encode much of their technical information in complex tables, but LLM knowledge and interpretation of such tables remain largely unexplored. We introduce TeleTables, a benchmark comprising 2,220 tables from 13 3GPP specifications in four formats and 500 human-verified MCQs spanning direct retrieval to multi-step reasoning. Evaluating 20 open-weight LLMs across non-reasoning, multimodal, reasoning, and table-specialized architectures reveals two distinct performance bottlenecks. In the closed-book setting, domain knowledge is the primary constraint, with no general-purpose model exceeding 41% accuracy. When the table is provided as context, the best models exceed 90%, but performance degrades systematically with reasoning depth, evidence scope, and structural complexity, with a 32.2 pp spread across reasoning skills. Table specialization on non-telecom data provides no consistent benefit, while strong reasoning capabilities remain essential for reliable interpretation of complex technical tables.

paper.title: FINSTRUCT: LLM-Based Logical Structure Recovery for Financial Filings
paper.abstract: Financial-filings workflows depend on more than extracting reported values: each number must be placed in the document context that makes it reviewable, comparable, and auditable. In practice, this logical structure—including the relevant section, note, heading, row, column, period, currency, and surrounding text—is often clear to professional reviewers but only partially encoded in inline XBRL markup. As a result, rule-based parsers can work on familiar layouts yet fail silently when document structure departs from expected templates. We present FINSTRUCT, an on-premise LLM system designed for confidential financial-document workflows. FINSTRUCT runs locally on a single 16 GB GPU, requires no task-specific fine-tuning, predicts nine structural fields for each reported fact, and provides reviewer-facing rationales together with repeated-sample agreement signals for human-in-the-loop review. On 1,493 manually annotated facts from five UK FRS 102 filings produced by a single accounts-production stack, FINSTRUCT raises macro accuracy from 50.6% to 74.8% and micro accuracy from 63.1% to 85.1% over a deterministic parser. More importantly for deployment, it recovers structure at 83.5% accuracy on a filing where the rule-based parser silently misses whole sections, and its agreement signal separates more reliable predictions from cases requiring review. These results position logical structure recovery as a practical document-understanding layer for regulated financial automation, rather than a conventional parsing problem alone.

paper.title: SkillHone: A Harness for Continual Agent Skill Evolution Through Persistent Decision History
paper.abstract: Agent skills extend language-model agents with task-specific procedures, scripts, and references, but the tasks and environments they target continually change. Existing methods improve skills in bounded runs and retain only the final artifact, discarding the decision history that later agents need to interpret prior revisions, evaluations, and rejected alternatives. We introduce SkillHone, a harness for continual agent skill evolution grounded in persistent decision history. SkillHone pairs skill revisions with evaluation-side evidence that supplies practice feedback, recording structured histories of diagnoses, revisions, evidence, and outcomes. Role-separated subagents run candidate skills on practice probes with redacted reporting and propose revisions informed by prior decisions, enabling cross-session refinement without rediscovering past rationale. On deep-research benchmarks, SkillHone runs without a pre-integrated search stack and outperforms the commercially backed deep-research agent by 15.8 points on GAIA and 3.2 points on WebWalkerQA-EN, while also exceeding prior skill-evolution methods. We further deploy SkillHone on internal tool-mediated analysis scenarios, where it improves accuracy by an average of 18.8 points across seven settings.

paper.title: GRAM-V2: Generative Reasoning and Ranking Alignment for Large-Scale E-commerce Search

author.affiliation: University of Chinese Academy of Sciences

paper.abstract: Click-through rate (CTR) prediction is a critical task for e-commerce advertising systems. However, industrial ranking models still rely on sparse IDs and historical behavior signals, which limits their generalization to cold-start products, long-tail queries, and complex user intents. Although large language models (LLMs) provide strong semantic understanding and can generate behavioral rationales, directly using them for online ranking is impractical under strict latency constraints.We propose GRAM-V2, a rationale-supervised ranking framework that transfers LLM-generated behavioral rationales into an efficient CTR model. GRAM-V2 uses a Teacher LLM to generate click-oriented rationales, distills them into a lightweight Student LLM, and aligns a two-tower CTR model with the Student’s representations and rationale signals. During online serving, GRAM-V2 uses only distilled representations and cached item embeddings, without generating rationales autoregressively. Large-scale offline experiments and online A/B testing show that GRAM-V2 improves CTR prediction accuracy, CTR, and advertising revenue while satisfying production latency constraints.

paper.title: D2GS: A Data-Centric Framework for LLM-based Creative Game Script Generation
paper.abstract: Although Large Language Models (LLMs) offer significant advantages for creative tasks like game narrative design, their application remains largely confined to academic exploration. Existing methods often fail to integrate with specific game assets, production constraints, and iterative workflows essential for industrial development, limiting real deployment in professional studios. To bridge this gap, we present D2GS, a data-centric framework for LLM-based game script generation designed for industry. D2GS supports narrative designers end-to-end, from ideation to engine-ready scripts. It grounds creation in multi-source, game-specific data and mimics human iterative refinement. The framework includes four modules: (1) knowledge augmentation for multi-source data preparation; (2) logline and plot outline generation with a critic-feedback revision loop; (3) character and world enrichment using role-assigned LLM agents to simulate interactions; and (4) script rephrasing to ensure game-engine compatibility. Experiments show D2GS outperforms strong baselines in coherence, relevance, creativity, and overall writing quality, while staying faithful to predefined settings and assets. Industrial-scale validation further confirms its practicality for real-world narrative design pipelines.

paper.title: DiagFlowBench: Evaluating How Language Models Handle Off-Procedure Inputs in Grounded Diagnostic Dialogue
paper.abstract: Language models increasingly serve as advisory systems in maintenance operations. To prevent hallucination, established approaches ground these models in procedural documentation, constraining them to prescribed sequences. In practice, however, operators may stray from these steps, requiring models to recognise unscripted, off-procedure utterances. Current benchmarks rarely prioritise this capability. We introduce DiagFlowBench, a dataset of 50 industrial diagnostic flowcharts from a consumer manufacturer converted into 1,676 multi-turn conversations that contrast compliant with off-procedure utterances. Evaluating a panel of ten commercial and open-weight models reveals high variability in abstention rates, with models often selecting a real but contextually inadequate step rather than fabricating facts. The inherent plausibility and authority of this mapped but wrong advice exposes a challenging vulnerability for grounding systems.

paper.title: Style as a Confound: False Positives in AI Detection of Non-Native Academic Writing
paper.abstract: AI text detectors are increasingly employed in academic settings, but it remains unclear whether their outputs reflect AI authorship itself or broader linguistic features associated with polished academic English. Previous studies have reported high false-positive rates (FPRs) for non-native English writing, but population-level comparisons confound authorship with differences in topic, domain, and writing style. Professional editing provides a useful setting for examining this issue because it changes the linguistic form of manuscripts while preserving authorship and content. We examined 135,389 document pairs from a professional English editing service (2018–2025), comprising non-native manuscripts and their native-edited versions, to assess how editing affects detector responses controlling for content and authorship. For the 13 AI text detectors, FPRs for human-written texts varied widely, from 0.0% to 100.0%. Responses varied across detectors: the same edits increased AI scores in some detectors but decreased them in others. Notably, score changes correlated with the extent of editing. The findings identify professional editing style as a key confounding variable in AI detector outputs, rather than establishing a full separation of text origin from linguistic style, raising concerns about fairness and reliability in academic settings.

paper.title: When Not to Think: Mitigating the Overthinking Effect in Content Moderation
paper.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has become a default paradigm across reasoning-intensive tasks and is widely assumed to be, at worst, harmless. Recent efficient-reasoning work treats unnecessary CoT purely as a cost to be reduced. We show that in boundary-dense classification tasks such as content moderation and toxicity detection, CoT is instead actively harmful. We identify the overthinking effect: extended reasoning amplifies weak surface signals into false evidence of violation, inflating false positive rates on ambiguous non-violating samples while its gains on ambiguous violating samples mask the harm in aggregate metrics. To address this, we propose Oreki, an adaptive CoT framework that uses K-fold cross-probing to label per-sample reasoning necessity and fine-tunes on a mixture of full-reasoning and reasoning-skipped formats. Across four base models on video moderation and multi-label toxicity detection, Oreki preserves CoT’s recall gains while suppressing its false positive inflation, outperforming both Always-CoT and Never-CoT. On toxicity detection, it cuts low-agreement false positive rate from 0.467 to 0.257 while raising overall F1 from 0.792 to 0.851.

paper.title: EAGER: Enrich-and-Align Generative Query Recommendation from Clicked Items in E-commerce Search

author.affiliation: Huazhong University of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: E-commerce platforms increasingly display clickable query suggestions alongside items in the user feed, enabling users to refine or expand their intent without manually reformulating queries. Existing approaches either mine suggestions from historical logs—limited to past behavior and blind to long-tail, personalized intents or rely on off-the-shelf LLMs whose lack of platform-specific knowledge yields fluent but generic queries disconnected from real click behavior. We propose EAGER (Enrich-and-Align Generative Query Recommendation), a two-stage framework for generating query suggestions from clicked items. In the enrichment stage, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) follows a four-stage curriculum that scales information richness (from item-only to user-conditioned) and reasoning depth (from direct to chain-of-thought). Each stage incorporates rationale augmentation, diversity regularization, and self-distillation. In the alignment stage, we post-train via GRPO with a hybrid reward of multiple rule-based business signals and a preference-aware click reward. Extensive offline experiments and online A/B test demonstrate the effectiveness of EAGER, which has been deployed in production at a major e-commerce platform.

paper.title: Perceptually Better, Semantically Worse: Measuring Speech Enhancement Impact on LLM-Based Voice Systems
paper.abstract: Speech enhancement (SE) is commonly applied as a preprocessing step in spoken AI pipelines under the assumption that better audio quality improves downstream task performance. Whether SE-induced distortions propagate to downstream LLM task performance remains an open question. We introduce Output Divergence Rate (ODR), which measures how often SE changes an LLM’s intent classification relative to clean speech, and benchmark five conditions on 2,974 SLURP clips using Whisper large-v3 and wav2vec2-large cascades. Every condition produces ODR significantly above zero (p < 0.001, binomial test). MetricGAN+ more than doubles ODR versus unenhanced noisy speech (0.318 vs. 0.135) despite improving PESQ, and unmitigated echo reaches an ODR of 0.836 through speaker substitution, a failure WER cannot capture. Audio quality metrics range from near-zero to moderate correlation with ODR (SQUIM-MOS \rho\=\-0.068, PESQ \rho\=\-0.467). The MetricGAN+ and echo results replicate across ASR architectures, indicating that standard audio quality metrics are insufficient for LLM pipeline quality.

paper.title: AuDQ: Auditable Data Quality through Agentic Rule Discovery
paper.abstract: High-stakes tabular pipelines rely on scattered, static quality checks that are hard to evolve and audit against policy intent. Regulated domains particularly suffer as the LLM-era automation raises expectations for traceability and accountability. We propose a vision for an ontology-grounded, repository-native data quality layer in which rules are first-class artifacts: versioned, provenance-linked to governance texts, and re-playable through immutable execution traces. As a first step toward validating this vision, we present a concrete implementation of its agentic rule-discovery core with two rule acquisition modes (Full-Agentic and Guided) and a human-in-the-loop (HITL) review interface. We define an evaluation framework and run experiments addressing whether our fully autonomous, divide-and-conquer agentic rule discovery produces rules of the same quality and diversity as those specified by a human expert, reporting preliminary results on two real world industry datasets in the finance and retail domains.

paper.title: Voice of Australian-AI: Learning Australian Assistant Voice Without Caricature
paper.abstract: LLM assistants deployed outside the United States often inherit US-centred interactional defaults. We introduce an Australian-facing assistant, and test whether local voice is better learned during fine-tuning or imposed with an inference-time prompt. We define Australian Voice as pragmatic alignment, directness, modesty, warmth, register control, and task fidelity, rather than slang or spelling substitution. We build a governed dataset from user research, human rewrites, contrastive negatives, reviewed synthetic examples, and replay data. In a blind evaluation by Australian English users (356 question-level ratings over 89 prompts), the raw 50% voice/replay mix scores best on all five dimensions (4.24/5; 102 best-pick wins). Prompted variants underperform every matched fine-tuned model.

paper.title: Less Is More: Graph-free Multimodal RAG via Multi-signal Late Fusion
paper.abstract: Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is widely used for multimodal, cross-document question answering. However, building corpus-level graphs is expensive, slow to query, and difficult to maintain. We present TrioRAG, a graph-free multimodal framework that integrates evidence from three complementary signals: the question, the anchor image, and a VLM-enhanced query generated from both. Each signal retrieves independently over a shared multi-vector index of page text and page images, and the results are combined through late fusion. Further, we introduce AutoQA, a multimodal automotive benchmark whose questions are grounded in noisy, web-sourced images rather than clean document-sourced figures. Its questions require reasoning across manuals. We position it as a model-curated testbed rather than a human-validated gold standard. Across three benchmarks, TrioRAG matches or outperforms graph-based systems while reducing total cost and accelerating per-query inference by 1.6-2.3\times. By construction, AutoQA grounds its questions in out-of-corpus web images. In this setting image retrieval reaches only 19.3% document-level recall, while text-derived signals, especially the VLM-enhanced query, keep retrieval robust.

paper.title: Lightweight Temporal Attention for Video Retrieval over Frozen Image and Text Encoders
paper.abstract: Large-scale visual search platforms maintain production text-image embedding models trained on behaviorally-mined query-image pairs, where the text encoder is implicitly tuned to organisation-specific search vocabulary. Extending such a system to video retrieval is non-trivial: retraining risks disrupting hard-won query understanding, while naive temporal aggregation discards the sequential structure that distinguishes a door opening from a door closing. We add a lightweight temporal attention pooling head over independently encoded frame embeddings, keeping both encoders frozen and training only the pooling head and positional encodings. We train on a large-scale dataset from a commercial creative platform using bidirectional InfoNCE with a two-stage hard negative mining pipeline. Benchmarking against LoRA fine-tuned Gemma 3 (12B) and SmolVLM2, neither matches our approach despite substantially larger parameter counts. We also introduce an evaluation benchmark with graded relevance judgments annotated by a VLM judge, where each query is mapped to all relevant videos in a large corpus rather than a single ground-truth clip, avoiding protocols that greatly underestimate model quality. Our model improves nDCG@1 by 10.1% over mean-pooling overall and 25% on complex action queries. With Matryoshka Representation Learning, 256-dim embeddings retain 95.6% of full performance, and int8 quantization costs under 1% in retrieval quality.

paper.title: From Production Traffic to Post-Training: Building a Self-Hosted LLM That Covers the Corporate Request Mix
paper.abstract: Data-residency constraints force enterprises to self-host LLMs, but continuous adoption of newer models without decommissioning their predecessors expands the serving fleet, fragmenting a finite GPU pool. We consolidate traffic from over 200 internal applications onto a single model by closing quality gaps identified through production error analysis along three axes: instruction following, function-calling, and internal task distribution. Quality is tracked by offline benchmarks stratified to production traffic and scored by deterministic verifiers or calibrated LLM judges. Rather than optimising all objectives jointly, which introduces cross-domain reward interference, we train a separate GRPO expert per axis and merge them via two-stage SLERP. Each expert’s reward exposes a distinct failure mode, namely semantic collapse, over-calling, and verbosity hacking, each requiring a domain-specific fix. In non-reasoning mode the recipe surpasses a {\sim}7\times larger by total parameters baseline on the in-house Arena with 69.6 to 65.8, instruction following with 0.85 to 0.83, and function-calling with 0.79 to 0.77, while lifting general dialogue benchmarks. The model absorbs 50% of platform traffic, 116M requests per month, at a fraction of the serving cost.

paper.title: Closing Cost-Quality Gap in Document VLMs: Difficulty-Aware Data Curation and Quality-Adjusted Deployment Economics
paper.abstract: Extracting structured fields from hundreds of millions of documents annually remains costly in regulated industries: bespoke OCR cascades cover only a fraction of workflows, privacy rules preclude external models, and existing open-source VLMs that clear quality thresholds cost more to serve than human annotation. We present a deployed document-understanding system built on a Mixture-of-Experts VLM (35B total, 3B active), fine-tuned on in-house production data mixed with open-domain documents curated by a Difficulty-Aware pipeline for layout diversity, fact-extractability, and cross-model consistency. Fitting on a single H100 and serving heterogeneous workflows via prompting, the model leads all deployable (non-reasoning) baselines up to an order of magnitude larger. A quality-adjusted cost analysis, with confirmation and correction costs calibrated from production telemetry, shows it reduces expected costs by over 80% against the human baseline and by more than 50% against the best competing open-source model, while larger baselines remain economically unviable.

paper.title: Business Compromise Detection with Agentic AI and LLM-driven Knowledge Discovery
paper.abstract: The detection of compromised business ad accounts is a critical challenge in digital advertising, as attackers exploit hijacked accounts to launch fraudulent campaigns. Large Language Model (LLM) agents show promise for integrity violations, but we find that they cause business friction through hallucinated mistakes on hard cases. Through a deployment study we observe that an autonomous LLM agent is a strong, recall-heavy signal extractor but an unreliable final arbiter for ambiguous compromise decisions, conceding substantial precision. We therefore pair the agent with a knowledge-based decision stage: the agent investigates an account and emits a structured, interpretable signal vector, and a neuro-symbolic stage makes the decision in three layers, symbolic rules discovered automatically with an Inductive Logic Programming (FOIL-IE) algorithm, a Naïve Bayes layer that calibrates those rules, and a data-tuned contradiction layer. We evaluate on a large oversampled general population (compromise oversampled, used because hard-case labels are scarce) and a realistic, low-prevalence production sample with subject-matter-expert (SME) labels, benchmarking against tree-ensemble baselines under identical conditions. The knowledge stage restores much of the precision lost by the agent (up to doubling it). On realistic low-prevalence data the full three-layer stage exceeds human expert reviewers and tree-ensemble baselines, with each layer contributing; its rules encode domain priors and generalize from few labels where ensembles overfit, while remaining interpretable and auditable.

paper.title: Benchmarking AI Agents for Hardware Design Automation via MCP Tool Calling
paper.abstract: We ask whether AI agents powered by locally deployed large language models can reliably automate expert-defined hardware design workflows in an industry-realistic tool-calling setting. In these environments, engineers issue repetitive, dependency-ordered operations—such as creating components, adding ports, and wiring connections—through specialised tools. Confidentiality constraints on component specifications and naming conventions often preclude hosted proprietary APIs, motivating the use of locally deployed models. To study this setting, we build a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that reproduces the state and dependency logic of a proprietary hardware design tool used in embedded system development and construct a benchmark covering single-operation edits, multi-step dependency chains, invalid requests, misspelled prompts, and multi-server tool contexts. We evaluate seven open-source models comparing pipeline choices including system prompts, tool-description detail, context scope, and single-agent versus multi-agent architectures. Results show that strong models can achieve near-complete expected-call coverage on the benchmarked workflows, but reliability depends strongly on both task structure and agent configuration. Comprehensive tool descriptions consistently reduce failures, few-shot prompting can cause severe inaction for some models, cumulative context harms constrained models, and multi-agent decomposition helps weak workers or long sessions at the cost of additional calls. These findings provide practical guidance for deploying local LLM agents in stateful hardware design environments.-

paper.title: From Synthetic to Localized: Benchmarking Multilingual Intent Classification in Logistics Customer Service
paper.abstract: Multilingual intent classification is central to logistics customer-service systems, where models must handle noisy user queries across languages and hierarchical labels. Yet many multilingual benchmarks rely on machine-translated text, which is cleaner than real customer requests and can overestimate robustness. We present a public benchmark for hierarchical multilingual intent classification from real logistics logs: approximately 30K de-identified, single-utterance queries curated from 600K records through filtering, LLM-assisted quality control, human privacy review, and sampled label auditing. The dataset uses a two-level taxonomy with 13 parent and 17 leaf intents; English, Spanish, and Arabic are seen languages, while Indonesian, Chinese, and Thai support zero-shot evaluation. To measure the gap between machine-translated and professionally localized evaluation, we provide paired test sets derived from the same source items. We benchmark multilingual encoders, embedding models, and small language models under flat and hierarchical protocols, and find that machine translation tests yield higher accuracy in most settings. [Prompts and sample data are available at <https://github.com/JTExpress-MICCS/MICCS>. A preprint version of this work is available at <https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.23172>.]

paper.title: Adaptation, Not Translation: An Architecture and Evaluation Framework for Long-Form Cross-Cultural Story Localization
paper.abstract: Translating a story renders its words into a new language; adapting it transposes its world into a new culture. Large Language Models (LLMs) translate and adapt individual passages effectively, but long-form novels spanning \sim100 chapters suffer model failures. We formalize long-form cross-cultural story adaptation as a generation task parameterized by source and target language-culture pairs, with three structural axes: A1 identity coherence across narrative arc, A2 cultural-system alignment within scenes, and A3 dependency-chain integrity among related entities. This is addressed through a five-stage agentic adaptation framework comprising entity registry, target-culture plan, dependency-aware batched localization, validation and rewrite. Evaluation is conducted through ablations across three language-culture pairs and two model families; the proposed system outperforms across all three axes, reducing identity errors by 65%, dependency errors by 64%, and cultural misalignment errors by 27% against competitive baselines. Further validation through a production A/B test on a commercial storytelling platform demonstrates listener retention comparable to that for human-adapted content, reflecting viability of the framework.

paper.title: Beyond Accuracy: Robustness, Cost, and Governance Trade-offs for Vision-Language Models in Templated Document Extraction
paper.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used to extract structured fields from business documents, yet most evaluations report accuracy on clean benchmarks and offer little guidance to practitioners choosing an approach for a given task complexity. We address this gap with a measurement-grounded study and an open-source release. Across eleven systems (three commercial, two reasoning, five open-source VLMs in pretrained and fine-tuned form, and a non-LLM OCR→regex floor) scored on a 750-document held-out pool of synthetic checks, fine-tuning on 3K samples lifts the best open-source VLMs above F1 0.98—above every zero-shot commercial system on this task—while GPT-5 leads the commercial pool on F1 and Claude Sonnet 4.5 collapses on Date. To turn these measurements into actionable choices, we introduce a practitioner-oriented selection framework that maps a task profile (quality, latency, governance, volume) to a recommended approach via filtering and total-cost minimization, illustrated on a hypothetical mid-volume document-extraction scenario.

paper.title: Schema-Hierarchical Soft Prompts for Structured Information Extraction
paper.abstract: Structured information extraction at small-language-model scale is a routine production workload, yet each new task added to a serving stack can demand new task-specific model state. We propose a schema-hierarchical soft prompt: a small learned prefix, trained on a frozen backbone, that gives every JSON-schema node its own slot, orders the slots by the schema, and marks tree depth with learned embeddings. Used alone on the open USPTO-ORD patent task, it recovers most of a LoRA reference’s extraction quality while training more than an order of magnitude fewer parameters, and ablations attribute the gain to depth and schema order rather than token count. Used with a LoRA adapter on an internal booking task, the same slots stabilize one of two held-out categories, so we report this as a bounded mechanism study rather than a general gain. Inference-time slot replacement indicates that position supplies the schema scaffold while learned content stabilizes generation. Measured serving gives a far smaller task artifact and higher throughput than multi-LoRA as interleaved tasks grow. The soft-prompt module is available at https://github.com/microsoft/Hierarchical-Soft-Prompt.

paper.title: From Confusion to Clarity: Confusion-Aware Retrieval and Knowledge Injection for Text Classification
paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) struggle to classify text into taxonomies with many semantically similar labels, as the distinctions are domain-specific and not captured by pre-training. To handle large label spaces, a common approach retrieves top-K candidate labels by embedding similarity and prompt the LLM to choose among them. However, top-K retrieval reduces the number of candidates but does not help the model tell similar ones apart. When two similar labels both appear as candidates, the model lacks the signal to choose correctly between them. We propose a framework that (1) identifies which label pairs the model struggles to distinguish, (2) expands the candidate set to include confusable labels, and (3) generates targeted rules to differentiate between similar candidates. The framework requires no fine-tuning, and the generated rules transfer to smaller, cheaper models. On three benchmarks (WOS, Flipkart, LEDGAR), our approach improves Macro F1 by up to 10.0pp over retrieval baselines, with smaller models (2B–20B) gaining up to 11.5pp via cross-model transfer.

paper.title: RLMA: Reinforcement Learning with PolyMetric Alignment
paper.abstract: RLHF, RLAIF, and RLVR align LLMs with human instructions but rely on costly human labels, potentially biased LLM judges, or task-specific verifiers. We propose PolyMetric Alignment (RLMA), a reference-based reward framework for supervised-answer tasks that fuses heterogeneous evaluation metrics against a given reference answer using a Residual Set Transformer (RST) trained with a Bradley-Terry objective. Empirically, RLMA is stronger than all three paradigms, achieving 98.0% of the Pass@K oracle on a 9-pool benchmark, with gains of +17.6 pp over the RLA single-metric baseline and +7.4 to +15.4 pp over RLHF, RLAIF, and RLVR. RLMA also generalizes broadly, reaching 97.2% of oracle on unseen GSM8K and, when used as a DPO reward, improving TriviaQA Pass@1 by +4.80 pp on Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct. Finally, RLMA is efficient to deploy. Its 113K-parameter gate requires only 0.33 ms per candidate, roughly 300x faster than a single 8B reward-model forward.

paper.title: Edit4Agency: Efficiently Enhancing Agent Sub-Capabilities of Small Language Models via Model Editing
paper.abstract: Currently, most agentic systems are driven by mainstream closed-source large language models (LLMs), such as GPT-5 and Gemini 3, resulting in high operational costs. As a result, deploying customized small language models (SLMs) to replace LLMs in agent components has attracted increasing attention. However, the limited capabilities of SLMs often render them inadequate for agent tasks. To address this, we propose \textbf{Edit4Agency}, a novel framework that utilizes model editing to efficiently and effectively enhance agent sub-capabilities of SLMs. By formalizing tasks as a sequence generation problem triggered by specific conditions, the framework embeds task triggers into system prompts and performs model editing through localized parameter updates, eliminating the need for large-scale retraining. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets and case studies in agent systems demonstrate that model editing, with only 50 data samples, enables a base model without instruction tuning to acquire new skills such as tool calling while maintaining its general capabilities. The results show that Edit4Agency outperforms instruction-tuned SLMs, constrained decoding, and SLMs trained with large-scale supervised fine-tuning or reinforcement learning methods.

paper.title: SAFARI: An Industrial Benchmark for LLM-Assisted Hazard Analysis and Risk Assessment
paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly considered for safety-critical engineering, yet their reliability in regulated functional-safety workflows remains underexplored. We introduce SAFARI (Safety-Aware Functional Automotive Risk Inference), the first industrial benchmark for LLM-assisted automotive Hazard Analysis and Risk Assessment (HARA) under ISO 26262. It contains 3,000 de-identified industrial HARA cases and evaluates two coupled tasks: open-ended hazard analysis and standards-grounded risk assessment. To evaluate open-ended HARA artifacts, we propose the first reference-anchored LLM-as-a-judge protocol with high expert correlation. Experiments with nine frontier LLMs show that models often produce plausible hazard narratives but remain weak at ISO 26262 risk classification, with the best ASIL macro-F1 reaching only 0.261. Chain-of-Thought prompting provides limited benefit and often degrades categorical risk assessment. Error analysis further localizes major failures to scenario-critical context omissions during hazard generation and to controllability misjudgments during risk assessment, indicating where expert oversight should be concentrated. The dataset can be obtained from https://github.com/xixi47520-hash/HARA.

paper.title: SCOPE: Stratum-Coordinated Optimization Pipeline for Efficient Agent Context
paper.abstract: LLM agents routinely spend orders of magnitude more tokens on context than on generation, re-sending interaction history, tool schemas, and system prompts at every turn. We introduce **SCOPE**, a unified framework for *context compilation* that compresses these three strata jointly under a fixed token budget while preserving agent behavior. SCOPE combines: 1. A learned *minimal sufficient context* reranker for memory, trained via leave-one-out supervision; 2. A plan-conditioned tool compressor that speculatively loads likely tools while retaining lightweight signatures for the rest; 3. A constraint-aware prompt compressor that preserves instructions. A lightweight planner coordinates these components via a contextual bandit, allocating budget across memory, tools, and prompt to maximize fidelity to full-context execution. On 3142 chat trajectories, SCOPE achieves **96.8%** decision fidelity at **4.46×** compression (60K tokens/turn), matching full-context task success within **0.9%** while using only **22%** of the tokens. Across operating regimes, SCOPE Pareto-dominates strong single-stratum baselines and naive compositions, with gains exceeding **11%** at matched cost. Our results show that optimizing context in isolation is insufficient: coordinated, budget-aware compression is key to scaling LLM agents without sacrificing reliability.

paper.title: Human-Anchored Factuality Evaluation with Strategic Annotation
paper.abstract: LLM-based factuality judges provide scalable evaluation signals, but their metrics are often systematically biased relative to human judgments. We study human-anchored factuality evaluation under limited annotation budgets, where judge predictions on the full dataset are combined with human labels on a small selectively sampled subset to obtain statistically valid estimates. The efficiency of this approach depends critically on which examples receive human annotation: in factuality evaluation, judge-human misalignment is not driven solely by low confidence, but also by structured failure modes such as incomplete evidence, temporal mismatch, unverifiable claims, and rubric misalignment. To exploit this structure, we introduce a factuality-specific annotation policy design pipeline that uses failure-space analysis (FSA) to derive diverse predictive signals for modeling human-judge misalignment. On an internal reference-based factuality evaluation system (AutoFA) and RAGTruth, where judge-predicted estimates substantially underestimate human-judged factual accuracy, our FSA-guided policy improves annotation efficiency over uniform sampling and uncertainty-driven baselines, achieving effective-sample-size gains of 40.3% on AutoFA and 27.1% on RAGTruth.

paper.title: Attention-Weighted Retrieval-Augmented Data Engineering for ADR Severity Classification

author.affiliation: University of Texas at San Antonio
University of Texas at San Antonio
University of Texas at San Antonio

paper.abstract: Adverse drug reaction (ADR) severity prediction is a key task in pharmacovigilance and post-market drug safety surveillance, but is of- ten challenged by noisy and heterogeneous clinical data. We propose a retrieval-augmented learning framework that leverages historical FAERS reports to construct evidence-enriched training instances for ADR severity prediction. Each ADR query, including patient demographics, drug exposure, and indications, is encoded using a fine-tuned BGE-M3 embedding model. We retrieve the top five relevant cases using BM25 lexical search and the top five semantically similar cases using dense vector search, and fuse them via an attention-based aggregation mechanism to produce retrieval-aware representations. These representations are evaluated using machine learning, deep learning, transformer, and fine-tuned large language model approaches for binary severity prediction. Results show that a tree-based ensemble achieves the best performance with an AUC of 82.3%, outperforming the strongest deep learning baseline by 2.3 percentage points and fine-tuned LLMs by 17 percentage points. Overall, the findings demonstrate that retrieval-enhanced data preprocessing can improve representation quality for ADR severity prediction, while the proposed upstream data engineering approach enables classical ensemble methods to remain highly effective for large-scale pharmacovigilance risk prediction.

paper.title: Enrich-Retrieve-Rank: Scaling Capability Discovery Beyond In-Context Routing
paper.abstract: Agent ecosystems now include thousands of MATS components (Models, Agents, Tools, and Skills), yet their discovery still relies on in-context routing. These systems read a registry (names, hints, or descriptions, as context budget permits), pick a candidate, invoke it, and retry on failure. This pattern degrades with scale, and registries are growing fast. We recast capability discovery as search over a registry by defining an offline enrichment step that turns sparse metadata into searchable profiles, and an online retrieve-then-rank pipeline that returns a ranked shortlist without invoking any candidates online. We show that from N=10 to 7,278 capabilities, in-context routing’s top-1 accuracy (Match@1) collapses (0.85 to 0.12), while retrieve-then-rank degrades more gently (0.81 to 0.39) because its reranker still ranks the right capability first 0.70-0.87 of the time once retrieval finds it. In the Nova Micro sweep, the crossover is around N=500. We compare against two in-context baselines. Full-Ctx puts the whole registry in the prompt and asks the LLM to pick. Search Pick gives the LLM a search tool to narrow candidates before it picks. At full scale the pipeline leads Search Pick by 6.5 percentage points (pp) on Match@1 at about half the cost. It reduces cost 70x versus Full-Ctx. We use a fixed configuration (same enrichment, retriever, and scorer weights) across agent, tool, and skill registries. The pipeline runs in production as the default capability-discovery layer of a large-scale multi-agent platform.

paper.title: GLS Chatbot: A Governed Multi-Agent Conversational System for Domain-Specific Customer Service

author.affiliation: UPC - Barcelona School of Informatics, Universidad Politécnica de Cataluna

paper.abstract: Hi, I’m Gisela, GLS’s assistant. How can I help you today? This is how the Spanish deployment of the GLS Chatbot greets its customers. Behind the greeting is a governed multi-agent system for parcel-logistics customer service, built on self-hosted open-source small language models with RAG. An orchestrator separates routing, execution, and generation; probabilistic components are bracketed by deterministic safeguards, customer-impacting actions require explicit user confirmation, and out-of-scope, abusive, or manipulative inputs are refused. In production since November 2025, the system has handled over 1.7 million conversations across Spain and Germany. In Spain, the average realised cost during May 2026 was approximately 0.07€ per conversation, with sub-3-second latency. We describe the architecture, evaluate the Spanish deployment on task completion, routing conformance, and RAG answer quality, and report lessons from production.

paper.title: REPO2ROCM: An Agentic System for Reproducing Research Code on AMD ROCm GPUs

author.affiliation: International Institute of Information Technology, Hyderabad, International Institute of Information Technology Hyderabad

paper.abstract: Machine learning practitioners routinely rely on public code repositories accompanying research papers, libraries, and open-source projects to evaluate, baseline, or build upon prior work. Yet getting such repositories to run and reproduce results often involves non-trivial effort, and is especially challenging when the target software and hardware stack differs from the one the original code was developed on. A prominent instance is running repositories originally built for CUDA-enabled hardware on AMD GPUs supporting the ROCm software stack. Here, successful installation alone is not a sufficient signal: a range of subtler issues may cause the code to either fail outright or silently fall back to inefficient execution. We present Repo2ROCm, an agentic system that migrates CUDA-centric ML repositories to ROCm in an automated manner. Repo2ROCm reconstructs a ROCm-compatible environment, adapts hardware-specific assumptions, executes a real workload, and confirms GPU-backed execution emitting auditable artifacts at every step (environment specs, source patches, execution logs, and verification evidence). We evaluate on ResearchBench, 60 repositories belonging to recent papers from top AI conferences. While only 18/60 run out of the box, Repo2ROCm reaches verified functional reproduction for 59/60 (3.3× improvement). Against popular general-purpose coding agents on a curated ten-repository diagnostic set (with all agents using the same Claude Sonnet 4 backbone), Repo2ROCm achieves the highest Portability Fidelity Score (PFS), a measure of how faithfully a run preserves the accelerator-critical execution path, real workload, and verified environment, scoring 77.3 vs. 61.4 (Claude Code), 58.7 (Mini-SWE-Agent), and 40.3 (Cursor Agent).

paper.title: TRACE: Traceable Root-cause Analysis with Calibrated Evidence-grounded agents
paper.abstract: Root Cause Analysis (RCA) for defects in large e-commerce enterprises is manual and slow: a single defect spanning thousands of microservices and SOPs takes experts one to two weeks to diagnose. Generic agentic RCA frameworks fail on this workload because they stop at proximate causes, cannot verify numeric claims, ignore past reviewer decisions, and return enumerated hypotheses rather than the quantified narratives business teams act on. We present Trace, an end-to-end agentic RCA system that combines supervised hypothesis-driven investigation with recursive why-drilling, an evidence-traceable multi-tool suite with stable artifact identifiers, a feedback retrieval and ingestion pipeline, and a two-layer confidence framework combining six mechanistic checks with an LLM judge - including a novel numerical-traceability score. Across several thousand cohorts spanning eight use cases in three metric categories (cost, quality, and inventory), Trace achieves 65.4% expert acceptance; on a 240-cohort head-to-head benchmark it reaches 67.1% vs. 38.8% for a matched ReAct baseline (+28.3pp, p<0.001) with calibrated confidence (AUC 0.819, ECE 0.041).

paper.title: Mem-LM: An LM-style Model for Reinforced Memory Selection

author.affiliation: Nanjing University of Posts and Telecommunications

paper.abstract: External memory banks can improve test-time reasoning in frozen large language models without updating backbone parameters. Yet similarity-based retrievers and pointwise selectors score memories independently, ignoring interactions and presentation order. We introduce , an LM-style model for reinforced memory selection that casts context construction as autoregressive index decoding. From a densely retrieved candidate pool, a lightweight Transformer encoder–decoder generates an ordered index sequence [i_1,\ldots,i_k], modeling dependencies among memories while leaving the backbone frozen. This formulation supports standard language-model training. For sparse binary verifiable rewards, we further propose , a confidence-aware extension of group-relative policy optimization that promotes correct, low-confidence rollouts, penalizes confidently incorrect ones, and retains learning signals in reward-homogeneous groups. Across three mathematical reasoning and two reasoning-intensive question-answering benchmarks with three Qwen backbones, achieves an average score of 84.9 on Qwen-plus, exceeding the strongest memory-augmented baseline by 2.3 points.

paper.title: From Metrics to Natural Dialogue: French Full-Duplex Benchmark for Spoken Dialogue Models
paper.abstract: Full-duplex spoken dialogue models aim to make voice agents more natural by allowing them to listen, speak, pause, and respond during ongoing conversation. However, it is not clear whether full-duplex benchmarks behave the same way when models are evaluated in a different language. To investigate this, we introduce a French full-duplex benchmark (FDB) with two variants, CALLFC-FDB for Canadian French and MEDIA-FDB for European French, and compare them with an English FDB. Built from real spoken resources, these benchmarks evaluate key full-duplex skills, including pause handling, turn-taking, backchannels, and interruptions. Beyond introducing French FDBs, we evaluate human–human conversations with FDB metrics to better understand the values these metrics take in real-world dialogue. Our analysis reveals that most timing-based metrics behave similarly across languages, while content-based evaluation degrades under language mismatch. We also find a trade-off between optimizing benchmark metrics and preserving conversational naturalness.

paper.title: BIRD-Persona: A Persona-Aware Benchmark for SQL and pandas Analytics Code Generation
paper.abstract: Production text-to-code systems increasingly use LLMs to translate natural-language analytics requests into executable SQL and pandas code, serving both business users, who describe desired results in application terms, and technical users, who name tables and columns directly. Existing Text-to-SQL and Text-to-Python benchmarks provide coverage, but they do not isolate when SQL and pandas performance diverge. We introduce BIRD-Persona, a persona-stratified extension of BIRD-Python that adds novice/expert rewrites (business-style and technical-style phrasing) to tasks with matched SQL and pandas ground truth, plus schema variants and task-structure annotations. Across 1,534 tasks, nine models, and 245,592 evaluations, BIRD-Persona reproduces the previously reported SQL-over-Python gap: SQL outperforms pandas for eight of nine systems. The gap is not uniform: expert, schema-explicit prompts improve both paradigms but help SQL more, schema representations have mixed model-dependent effects, and selected-column burden widens the gap while subqueries do not. By making user phrasing a controlled benchmark dimension, BIRD-Persona provides a foundation for persona-aware and paradigm-aware evaluation of natural-language analytics systems.

paper.title: EGT-KG: Evidence-Grounded Typed KG Retrieval for Practical Scientific QA with Small Language Models
paper.abstract: For emerging scientific research domains, local Small Language Models (SLMs) are becoming more attractive, as they offer stronger privacy control and more stable deployment pipelines than Large Language Models. However, in practice, scientific question-answering on SLMs often operates under inevitable constraints: small literature collections, fragmented evidence, limited context window and reasoning abilities. We propose the Evidence-Grounded Typed Knowledge Graph (EGT-KG), a retrieval framework to improve information retrieval with local SLMs. We assessed three question-answering settings: a vanilla Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) workflow and two EGT-KG workflows: an automatically generated relation schema (AS) and an expert-defined relation schema (ES). Our experiments were evaluated with a six-dimensional evaluation framework (S3CRF: Soundness, Correctness, Completeness, Conciseness, Relevance, Fluency) on a Biopolymer-bound Soil Composite literature benchmark, showing that EGT-KG outperforms the vanilla RAG method in most settings, with the best improvement from llama3:8b: a Final Score of 70.37 (+14.67%) and 68.82 (+12.14%) by AS/ES EGT-KG variants.

paper.title: Small Model, Big Retrieval: Unified Heterogeneous Retrieval via Multi-Label-Aware Contrastive Fine-Tuning
paper.abstract: Contrastive fine-tuning of a single embedding model across heterogeneous retrieval tasks is challenging when the tasks differ in label structure. In product-compliance retrieval, some tasks have multi-label supervision — every item carries a set of compliance categories, and many in-batch items share at least one category with the query, producing frequent in-batch false negatives. Other tasks (e.g., cross-catalog product matching) have no category labels: each query has one canonical match. Existing multi-label contrastive methods require every batch item to carry comparable labels, so they cannot serve a single embedding model trained on both label-bearing and label-free tasks. We propose label-aware false-negative exclusion: a zero-cost binary mask on the InfoNCE denominator that drops same-label candidates from the negative set rather than including them to positives. The mask has no effect on label-free items, so the same loss handles both task types. A 0.6 B-parameter embedding model fine-tuned this way handles four retrieval tasks simultaneously, lifting average Recall by 49% (0.489 \to 0.729) and matching the 13\times larger off-the-shelf Qwen3-Embedding-8B at 32\times lower embedding dimensionality. Fine-tuning further enables learned query fusion: concatenating regulatory text with an example product, which hurts retrieval before fine-tuning, becomes the strongest query type after, beating either alone by 6-11%.

paper.title: An Empirical Study of VLM Pipelines for Long-Document QA

author.affiliation: national university of singaore, National University of Singapore

paper.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are increasingly used for long-document processing, where the inputs combine text with charts, tables, figures, and complex layouts. Deploying them means choosing how to feed the document to the model, which retriever to use when only a subset of pages is sent, and whether to run the model agentically or as a static pipeline. We study these choices on two long-document QA benchmarks with both frontier API and open-weight VLMs. First, on MMLongBench-Doc our six-tool agent with page, table, figure, and search calls pays off only once the answering VLM is large enough: with Qwen3.5-4B and 9B it trails static page input, with Qwen3.5-27B it draws level, and with Sonnet 4.5 it leads. On LongDocURL it is level with or ahead of static input at every reader. Its lead over the strongest static pipeline is clearest with the frontier reader on MMLongBench-Doc and narrows to within noise on LongDocURL. Second, retrieval modality matters more than the specific retriever: the strongest image retriever leads the strongest text pipeline, and on the text side a single off-the-shelf cross-encoder rerank essentially matches a much heavier multi-stage LLM pipeline. Top-k image retrieval is also the most token-efficient input at every reader we paired it with, at roughly a seventh to a quarter of the tokens of sending every page. Third, cutting across all three choices, three of our strongest pipelines succeed on different questions, and an oracle that picks the best pipeline per question gains roughly thirteen points over the best single pipeline, though evidence-type routing recovers almost none of it.

paper.title: StreamCorrect: Self-Supervised Error Correction for Real-Time ASR with Offline Recognizers
paper.abstract: Streaming Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), also known as online or real-time ASR, transcribes speech incrementally while audio is being spoken and is critical for many industry applications. Despite the strong performance of modern offline ASR models, streaming deployment remains challenging because limited future context can cause early recognition errors to propagate across later chunks. We define the task of streaming ASR error correction and propose StreamCorrect, a modular framework that fine-tunes a lightweight error corrector from self-generated streaming ASR errors and integrates it with existing streaming ASR systems. To enable training without human annotation, StreamCorrect introduces a timestamp-free boundary recovery procedure based on Prefix-to-Reference Alignment for generating chunk-level correction data. Across multiple languages and ASR backbones, StreamCorrect achieves up to 39% relative character error rate (CER) reduction with minimal latency overhead. Error propagation analysis further shows increasing benefits over time, with up to 7.2% absolute CER reduction in later audio chunks. StreamCorrect bridges offline ASR models and streaming deployment through a lightweight correction plug-in while preserving the pretrained ASR component without additional tuning or distillation.

paper.title: Better Together: Complementary Query Rewriting Under a Strong RAG Baseline
paper.abstract: A popular way to improve Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is to rewrite the user’s question into several variants and search with all of them. We test whether this actually helps once the underlying search is already strong. Under one fixed, competitive pipeline (BGE dense retrieval, cross-encoder reranking, and MMR diversification), we compare four query-rewriting strategies (S1–S4) against two strong LLM baselines (HyDE, Query2Doc) on three datasets (HotpotQA, AmbigNQ, and the 512K-document EnterpriseRAG-Bench) over three seeds with paired-bootstrap significance tests.Our headline result is that rewriting alone is at best competitive with a strong baseline, but combining methods yields outsized gains because different strategies fail on different questions. A post-hoc union of four methods (S1+S3+S4+HyDE; seed-42 analysis) improves HIT@10 over the dense baseline by +12.5 points on enterprise-style data (51.70 vs 39.22), and a five-method union reaches 52.98 (+13.8 over baseline). Budget-matched controls (TopK-100 reranking, multi-pass HNSW) capture only \sim40% of this gain, confirming that complementarity, not retrieval budget, is the primary driver. On HotpotQA the union adds +1.6 to +1.8 points (p < 0.001), saturating the all-method oracle; on AmbigNQ the same fusion hurts (-2.4 below the best solo, p < 0.001), and we analyze when and why. Because rewriting is expensive (one LLM call each), we turn this into a cost-aware heuristic evaluated in simulation: a confidence-gated router that runs rewriting only when the baseline’s own top-1 score is low.
