To bridge this gap, we propose RoleGen, a framework that synergizes a Conversion Trajectory Reasoner with a Generative Collaborative Executor. Specifically, the LLM-based Reasoner explicitly models the context-dependent Functional Role of items to reconstruct intent evolution. It further uses counterfactual role exploration to mitigate interest collapse and generate diverse conversion-oriented candidates. These reasoned candidate items are then injected into the Executor, which is optimized via a feedback-driven co-training mechanism to ensure grounded execution. Extensive offline experiments and online A/B testing on a large-scale e-commerce platform show a 5.82% gain in Recall@1 and a 6.71% increase in online order volume, confirming RoleGen’s effectiveness in activating dormant users.

paper.title: Do Agents Help? Agentic Document Information Extraction with Enterprise Database Grounding

author.affiliation: Singapore University of Technology and Design

paper.abstract: In enterprise applications, document information extraction (IE) does not operate in isolation: extracted information must match the systems of record (SoR) for the process to work. While reliable IE demands entity extraction, SoR grounding, and iterative refinement, existing methods rely on single-pass inference. To address this gap, we propose a SoR-grounded agentic pipeline and evaluate four agentic paradigms (Agentic Workflow, ReAct, Plan-Execute-Critic, and Dynamic Agent Collaboration) on real-world enterprise data. We focus on the goods receipt and invoice settlement processes as representative use cases, where delivery notes and invoices must be matched and verified against purchase order SoR. Our results show that agentic approaches generally match or exceed non-agentic baselines, with simpler paradigms matching or outperforming complex alternatives. Paired with systematic error analysis, this work provides actionable guidance for deploying agentic document AI at enterprise scale.

paper.title: When to Trust: Margin-Calibrated Routing Between LLM-as-a-Judge and Human Experts
paper.abstract: LLM-as-a-judge has become a common approach for comparing candidate answers at scale, but human experts who define what counts as “better” remain a scarce and finite resource. In practice, especially in professional domains, the key question is not whether to use the LLM judge or humans, but **how to combine them into a more efficient evaluation ecosystem**.We study five datasets spanning multiple domains and diverse LLM tasks, and find a consistent pattern: judge–human agreement increases as the margin between two answers grows, while model-produced factuality signals weaken as the margin narrows. This pattern is robust across datasets, different margin signals, and judge model families.We further find that the fact winner is not always the overall winner, and fact-decidable questions are not necessarily decided on factual grounds. Together, these results support a *fact-grounded but not fact-only* interpretation of comparison evaluation.Motivated by these findings, we propose and evaluate a practical *route-by-margin* evaluation strategy: choose a target agreement level T; trust the LLM judge above the corresponding margin threshold; and defer the remaining low-margin cases to human experts, thereby using each resource where it is strongest.

paper.title: DynamicMCPBench: A Trace-Grounded, Effect-Scored Benchmark for LLM Agents over Live MCP Servers
paper.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed over Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, yet the benchmarks used to evaluate them score the final answer or a fixed “ground-truth” list of tools, both of which are fragile once the underlying data is live and stateful. We present DynamicMCPBench, a reusable framework rather than a fixed dataset. A practitioner can run it on their own MCP servers to test models on their own tasks, or let it collect servers automatically to measure a model’s general ability to solve agentic tasks. Given the servers and any set of models, it generates realistic goals, pursues each one live to record a successful trajectory, distills that trajectory into path-agnostic effect checkpoints, and scores an agent on whether it reproduces those effects, never on the final answer. To show what the framework reveals, we run it at scale: 24 models over 121 servers and 750 tasks spread evenly over 15 task categories (50 each), where each category targets a distinct tool-use challenge of the generated questions. Each task is scored by pass^3, it counts as solved only if all three independent attempts succeed. Even the strongest agents solve only about half of the tasks, 31% of tasks are solved by no model at all, and accuracy collapses as the required tool chain grows longer (from 39% on the shortest chains to 13% on the longest). A human validation study confirms the automatic scoring is reliable (chance-corrected agreement of 0.76). DynamicMCPBench thus turns benchmark construction into something practitioners can rerun on their own servers and models, while exposing a consistent inability of current agents to handle long, multi-step agentic tasks.

paper.title: GraphBit: A Graph-based Agentic Framework for Non-Linear Agent Orchestration
paper.abstract: Agentic LLM frameworks that rely on prompted orchestration, where the model itself determines workflow transitions, often suffer from hallucinated routing, infinite loops, and non-reproducible execution. We introduce GraphBit, an engine-orchestrated framework that defines workflows explicitly and deterministically as a directed acyclic graph (DAG). Unlike prompted orchestration, agents in GraphBit operate as typed functions, while a Rust-based engine governs routing, state transitions, and tool invocation, ensuring reproducibility and auditability. The engine supports parallel branch execution, conditional control flow over structured state predicates, and configurable error recovery. A three-tier memory architecture (ephemeral scratch space, structured state, and external connectors) isolates context across stages, preventing cascading context bloat that degrades reasoning in long-running pipelines. Across GAIA benchmark tasks spanning zero-tool, document-augmented, and web-enabled workflows, GraphBit shows excellent performance achieving the highest accuracy, zero orchestration errors, the lowest latency, and the highest throughput. Ablation studies demonstrate that each memory tier contributes measurably to performance with similar configuration due to architectural changes, with deterministic execution providing the greatest gains on tool-intensive tasks representative of real-world deployments.Code and data: https://github.com/InfinitiBit/graphbit

paper.title: REDACT: A Systematically Controlled Multilingual Benchmark for Personal Information Detection

author.affiliation: International Institute of Information Technology, Hyderabad, International Institute of Information Technology Hyderabad

paper.abstract: Benchmark infrastructure for personally identifiable information (PII) detection remains limited: existing corpora cover few entity types, use ad hoc generation conditions, and do not show which surface conditions cause detector failures. We present REDACT, a systematically controlled multilingual PII benchmark with 13,427 records, 324,078 entity annotations, 51 entity types, 4,127 surface-form patterns, and 25 languages across 9 scripts. A strength-2 covering-array sampler controls nine generation axes: domain, format, difficulty, length, density, code-switching, language, adjacency, and co-occurrence. Three entity-level metadata fields (disclosure status, disclosure form, and a GDPR-aligned sensitivity tier) enable stratified evaluation beyond aggregate or per-type F1. From the full benchmark, we evaluate five detectors (Presidio, GLiNER, the OpenAI Privacy Filter, GPT-4.1, and Claude Sonnet 4.6) on a locked, language-stratified sample of 1,000 records. Aggregate F1 masks an architecture-dependent failure structure: the rule-based detector performs poorly on the policy-sensitive data, including HIGH-sensitivity entity types (recall 0.07) and non-verbatim disclosure forms, while the LLM detectors remain more robust, with the HIGH tier as their strongest sensitivity slice. A three-model reference-free LLM-as-judge assessment corroborates that sensitivity-tier assignment is the task’s hardest axis. We release the benchmark, schema, prompts, and stratified evaluation harness.

paper.title: CrisisLink: Closing the Loop between Underspecified Crisis Posts and Humanitarian Coordination
paper.abstract: During disasters, social media becomes a critical channel for identifying urgent needs and mobilizing public and institutional response efforts. Prior crisis-informatics research has mainly focused on detecting or extracting actionable content from disaster-related posts. However, real-world humanitarian response requires structured and operationally complete records, while social media posts are often short, informal, and underspecified.In this work, we present CrisisLink, an LLM-based coordination system that transforms noisy crisis communications into structured crisis records. Unlike prior one-shot extraction systems, CrisisLink dynamically identifies missing operational fields and initiates clarification dialogues with users to repair incomplete records before downstream coordination. The system further grounds resources against a humanitarian taxonomy and supports partial, multi-item matching.Built on the CrisisNLP corpus spanning multiple disaster types, the system is evaluated through human-audited assessments, simulated dispatch workflows, and a pilot evaluation in which trained workers role-play poster replies through a live web-based response interface. Experimental results show that a single clarification round raises end-to-end Offer–Request matching accuracy from 74.0% to 88.3% (a ceiling estimate under full response)while reducing the manual triage burden on responders, demonstrating the potential of interactive LLM systems for real-world humanitarian coordination.

paper.title: How to Speculate about Uncertainty in Agentic Coding? A Draft-Model Gate Method
paper.abstract: LLM agents deployed for software engineering fail expensively: they act confidently wrong, and bad actions are recognized only after costly execution and retry. We present Speculative Uncertainty (SU), a method that recovers a predictive failure signal for a black-box agent from its output tokens alone, with no access to logits, weights, activations, or repeated sampling. Inverting speculative decoding, a small open-weight draft model scores the agent’s already-generated trajectory in a single forward pass. From these speculative cross-likelihoods we extract phase-aware features by separating the reasoning and action spans, and calibrate them against a verifiable objective. SU produces a failure-likelihood score that any downstream policy, such as routing, human intervention, or extra test-time compute, can consume directly. To show the signal is actionable, we instantiate one such policy, a pre-execution veto gate, on software-engineering agents Qwen3-Coder-480B and closed-source Claude 3.5 Sonnet, cutting execution error rate by 6-8 percentage points and token cost by 14-19% in deployment, transferring to out-of-distribution benchmarks without retraining, and generalizing across agent models.

paper.title: Beyond Dense Retrieval: A Structured-Semantic Approach for Conversation Analytics
paper.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) based conversational systems generate vast interaction logs containing critical diagnostic signals such as failure modes and safety violations. However, the cross-turn dependencies, implicit state, and topic drift inherent to these conversations defeat dense retrieval, whose lone embedding cannot concurrently encode discrete structured constraints (e.g., refusal type) and open-ended semantic content. Our central claim is conceptual: conversational retrieval must span two complementary information planes, structured metadata and semantic content, and these are best reconciled by a unified hybrid representation that jointly supports filtering over structured metadata fields and vector similarity search over unbounded open-ended fields. We instantiate this as the Extract-Annotate-Query (EAQ) framework, which derives a metadata taxonomy, applies LLM-driven annotation, and compiles natural-language queries into hybrid graph operations. On the CDR-Benchmark, EAQ lifts NDCG@10 by 30.8% over the strongest dense baseline, with consistent gains across five analytical categories and two external datasets.

paper.title: ProChunker: Self-Optimizing Procedural Chunking for Agent-Ready Workflow Graphs
paper.abstract: Can an LLM read a 30+ page Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) and produce a team of agents that reliably execute it? Industrial SOPs bury workflow logic in prose, leave inter-step dependencies implicit, and scatter referenced entities across sections, forcing planners to parse, sequence, and tool-map within one context window. We argue that the missing primitive is procedural chunking: decomposing a document into self-contained executable units. Unlike RAG-style chunking, each chunk must be independently executable and chunks must jointly form a valid DAG encoding data and process dependencies, turning a prose SOP into a compact orchestrable workflow graph. We present ProChunker, a three-phase self-optimizing LLM pipeline (Boundary Detection, Metadata Extraction, Dependency Construction) with Stochastic Best-of-N prompt exploration guided by five custom metrics (Boundary Clarity, Entity Reference Coverage, Agent Self-Containedness Agreement, Step Coverage, Graph Validity); we then fine-tune Qwen3-1.7B on the pipeline’s own phase outputs, cutting latency by \sim27 min. Across three corpora (500 BioProBench protocols, six Industrial SOPs, 14 SOP-Bench documents), ProChunker improves the five-metric composite over the strongest baseline by +0.036 to +0.111 across corpora. Our study shows ProChunker increases agent construction success rate by +17\% and resolves {>}90\% of procedural ambiguity.

paper.title: RACA-PODS: Reasoning-Informed First-Token Prediction for Query-Document Relevance in WeChat Search
paper.abstract: Applying LLMs to query-document relevance estimation in industrial document retrieval faces two key challenges: the complexity and heterogeneity of Web content, and stringent latency and resource constraints. To address them, we propose an automated framework with two components: **R**eflection-**A**ware **C**ollaborative **A**gent (**RACA**) and **P**rogressive **O**ptimization **D**istillation **S**trategy (**PODS**). RACA uses collaborative reasoning and reflection to produce relevance labels and structured rationales. PODS stratifies training data by difficulty and combines supervised fine-tuning with Reasoning-Informed GRPO. Rationale supervision improves the student’s first-token relevance decision, while deployment stops after that token and avoids explicit rationale generation. Together, these mechanisms enable reasoning-informed first-token prediction that preserves the benefits of structured rationale supervision under stringent latency and resource constraints. Extensive offline experiments and a 10-day online A/B test in WeChat Search demonstrate the resulting accuracy–efficiency trade-off.

paper.title: ONTOFORM: Ontology-Grounded Semantic Data Generation for Enterprise Document Understanding
paper.abstract: Enterprise forms are layout-specific observations of real-world entities whose semantics span fields, recurring sections and related documents. Developing enterprise document-understanding systems requires large-scale supervision, but obtaining authentic forms is constrained by privacy concerns, annotation costs, and organization-specific formats. We present , a semantic-first framework that uses a lightweight, task-specific ontology to generate enterprise form packets. The framework separates domain semantics from layout through ontology maps, hierarchical schemas, dependency-aware entity sampling, deterministic validation, and template bindings. It produces rendered forms with field boxes, ontology-keyed extraction targets, grounded question-answer pairs, and validation metadata. We instantiate the framework on three digitally rendered surrogate insurance form types, producing 706 forms. Finetuned vision-language models improve ontology-keyed extraction F_1 by 4.99 points and grounded-QA ROUGE-L by 44.1 points over their zero-shot baselines. Ontology guidance further improves held-out-form extraction F_1 by 36.05 points overall and by 42.67 points on concepts absent from training, while increasing exact cross-form reasoning accuracy by 34.17 points. These results demonstrate the utility of the generated supervision signals for downstream tasks

paper.title: FedAnchor: Differentially Private Federated LoRA via Weight Anchoring
paper.abstract: Federated learning (FL) with differential privacy (DP) allows several organizations to learn a shared model from user data that only one organization is allowed to see. However, guaranteeing DP requires adding noise to gradients that scales with update dimensionality. While low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is a popular method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning, it is inherently sensitive to DP noise due to the multiplication operator. This noise amplification leads to significant utility degradation, hindering practical deployment in enterprise settings. To overcome this, we propose FedAnchor. Every round, FedAnchor captures compressed information using one of the LoRA matrices A and B, and then decompresses this to the complete adapted weight matrix via singular value decomposition (SVD) at the server. This relieves the model from DP noise exacerbation while maintaining full learning capacity. Experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that FedAnchor matches the strongest baseline in non-private settings and outperforms it by 4.38% under stringent DP constraints (\epsilon = 3). At scale, FedAnchor maintains communication efficiency, computation robustness, and utility under strict privacy budgets, meeting the demands for enterprise-level cross-silo deployments.

paper.title: LLM Post-Training as Brownfield Maintenance: An Industrial Perspective on Dataware Engineering
paper.abstract: Industrial post-training is a brownfield regime. Teams inherit a deployed checkpoint and must land targeted improvements under fixed compute and mixture budgets without regressing the rest. The maintained artifact is increasingly **dataware**: behavior governed by a curated post-training mixture, updated via bounded mixture patches rather than clean-slate retraining. From an industrial code-generation improvement effort, we offer a maintainer’s perspective on why this work is hard in practice, distilling three recurring challenges, **zero-sum mixture design**, **yield as the binding metric**, and **end-to-end integration under uncertainty**, and arguing that progress depends less on one-off recipes than on an engineering discipline for programming dataware. In our case study, interventions that raised the conversion of teacher distillation into usable training data increased accepted supervision by **2.84\times** while using the same solution teacher and four solution attempts per candidate problem. In our primary evaluation, the yield-engineered patch improved CodeForces pass@1 by **+2.59** points (+3.11 pass@3) and held-out LiveCodeBench v6 pass@1 by **+6.11** (+8.05 pass@3), all statistically significant across 16 stochastic evaluations of each benchmark from one fixed checkpoint per condition, with internal AIME and MATH regression suites within tolerance

paper.title: Predicate Importance Estimation and Decoupled Rationale-Score Distillation for Entity Alignment
paper.abstract: Knowledge graphs (KGs) are increasingly used as structured context for Large Language Models (LLMs), but industrial KG-RAG systems often need to integrate public and domain-specific KGs constructed from heterogeneous databases. This integration relies on Entity Alignment (EA), where lexical matching alone is insufficient under predicate-name variation and incomplete local neighborhoods. We address EA for KG integration by constructing a pairwise EA dataset and proposing two complementary modules: Predicate Importance Estimation (PIE) and Decoupled Rationale-Score Distillation (DRSD). PIE is a compact embedding-based approach that removes the subject information from each 1-hop triple, encodes the resulting subjectless triples, and aggregates them with learnable predicate-importance weights to build predicate-aware entity embeddings. DRSD trains a distilled small language model (SLM) with pseudo-answers produced by a teacher LLM through distinct prompts. By converting binary EA labels into text-based supervision and decoupling confidence-score estimation from label-consistent rationales, DRSD enables the SLM to learn task-specific reasoning while retaining a less label-biased confidence signal. Experiments show that PIE and DRSD improve EA classification. Moreover, because DRSD decouples confidence-score estimation from the decision, a division between the two flags an uncertain prediction for human review, thereby enabling a practical discrepancy between automatic acceptance and human-in-the-loop verification.

paper.title: Adapt the Words, Freeze the Model: LLM Prompt Evolution for Domain-Shift-Robust Segmentation
paper.abstract: In specialist industrial imagery the dominant cost is maintenance under domain shift: labeling and fine-tuning must be redone on every new field, and proprietary imagery often cannot leave the operator’s environment. For geological drill-core fracture segmentation we release CoreFrac, to our knowledge the first open pixel-level benchmark on drill-core photographs: 200 expert-annotated full-resolution images with an expert-agreement ceiling (soft-F1 0.86). We retarget a frozen concept segmentor (SAM 3) by evolving only its natural-language prompt — no gradient updates, just a small labeled probe. Under a source-grouped protocol the evolved prompt reaches 0.545 positives-only soft-F1, beating rank-8 LoRA at the same 96-patch cap (0.487; paired +0.058, 95% CI [+0.020, +0.094]) and the best of eight expert prompts by 2.7×. Under a controlled domain shift, re-evolving on a small probe lifts a 0.622 → 0.409 drop back to 0.534. Its masks distill into a small on-premises U-Net (7.8M parameters, 3.8 ms/patch) that retains ≈92% of the teacher’s positives-only soft-F1 (0.501) at ≈1700× lower latency than *unbatched* SAM 3 — a cheaper, leak-free deployment. Code and data are released.

paper.title: AutoGraphQL: A Bring-Your-Own-Schema Framework for Adapting Open-Weight LLMs to GraphQL APIs
paper.abstract: GraphQL has emerged as a widely adopted interface for accessing heterogeneous enterprise data. However, developing Natural Language to GraphQL (NL2GraphQL) systems remains challenging due to the need to rapidly adapt them to proprietary GraphQL schemas.We present AutoGraphQL, a Bring-Your-Own-Schema framework for developing and evaluating NL2GraphQL systems. Given a GraphQL schema, AutoGraphQL synthesizes executable GraphQL queries, generates aligned natural language utterances, and validates them through schema and execution checks to automatically construct high-quality NL2GraphQL datasets. The framework additionally supports human-in-the-loop curation and an end-to-end workflow where the generated datasets are used to fine-tune and benchmark models.Using AutoGraphQL, we construct a corpus of 17,621 NL2GraphQL instances spanning 173 GraphQL schemas and seven major query categories. Empirically, we show that fine-tuning open-weight models on AutoGraphQL-generated datasets substantially improves NL2GraphQL performance. Notably, the best fine-tuned 8B-parameter model achieves 42.57% benchmark accuracy, approaching Claude Sonnet 4.5 at 44.23%, while outperforming it on several GraphQL query categories. These results indicate that AutoGraphQL enables compact open-weight models to approach frontier-level performance on schema-grounded GraphQL generation. To support further research and benchmarking, we are releasing the training and test datasets under the MIT License. The dataset is available at https://nl2graphql-bench.github.io/.

paper.title: Relevance is \mathit{not} enough: A Communication-Oriented Retrieval System for Consequential Scientific Question Answering
paper.abstract: AI systems increasingly answer scientific questions about health, safety, and the environment. But most retrieval-augmented generation systems are tuned to provide factually correct, on-topic answers rather than to help non-experts understand what those answers mean for their lives and decisions. We focus on consequential scientific questions whose results directly shape people’s lives and study them through a public water-quality communication system, where residents and community leaders interpret the findings and choose actions. Their experiences show that on-topic answers can still be insufficient without explanation and context and that the emotional weight of risk information cannot be ignored. Our system first classifies each question by reasoning type (for example, causal versus policy-based), then generates follow-up questions to identify missing evidence and retrieve it. One component clearly distinguishes between what is known and what is uncertain, while another rewrites scientific details into accessible language, using persona-based styles, such as a caring neighbor or an administrative official, to adapt tone and readability. Ablations on over 160 questions show that the system uses an order of magnitude less context and, in several configurations, improves human-rated completeness. A completeness metric co-designed with community members and a fine-tuned learned judge reveal that standard relevance scores explain about 1% of variation in human completeness ratings, and even the tuned judge only moderately aligns with humans, indicating that completeness is a distinct human-centered objective that current metrics do not reliably capture.

paper.title: LDU-Bench: Multimodal LLM Evaluation for Lithography Defect Understanding under Layout-Varying Circuit Backgrounds
paper.abstract: Multimodal large language models have demonstrated strong defect recognition capability in industrial anomaly detection. However, in lithography review, merely determining whether an image contains a defect is insufficient for engineering inspection; models must also understand defect morphology, spatial location, and the potential causes supported by visible evidence. To this end, this paper proposes LDU-Bench, a multi-task multimodal benchmark for lithography defect understanding. Constructed from real lithography and integrated-circuit review images, LDU-Bench decomposes the review workflow into four independent tasks: defect triage, morphology recognition, coarse localization, and image-conditioned cause analysis. It systematically evaluates models using task-level metrics, diagnostic readouts, and the Lithography Closure Score (LCS). Experimental results show that although existing MLLMs can perform defect triage relatively reliably, this ability does not stably transfer to downstream review stages. Morphology alignment, effective localization, and evidence-to-cause mapping remain the major bottlenecks. Further diagnostics indicate that this capability break is not a fluctuation of a single metric, but reflects insufficient structured understanding across semantic levels. Overall, LDU-Bench provides a quantifiable and diagnostic unified platform for evaluating the usability, failure points, and capability boundaries of industrial MLLMs in lithography review chains.

paper.title: MERIT: Mitigating Exposure Bias in Generative XMC for User-Interest Propensity Modeling
paper.abstract: Matching users to interest categories at scale is central to personalized shopping, but the task is challenging in large e-commerce platforms, where label spaces continually evolve and user-interest signals are sparse and long-tailed. Autoregressive language models are appealing because their world knowledge and semantic priors over descriptors generalize across extreme label spaces and accommodate multiple valid label assignments. Yet under teacher-forced fine-tuning, inference-time predictions become part of the conditioning context: early errors steer later outputs toward co-occurring labels, over-generating near-correlates and missing unrelated true interests. We present MERIT, a framework for user-interest propensity modeling that mitigates this exposure bias through a self-correction objective. A permutation-invariant multi-target loss over shuffled mixtures of gold and mined hard-negative labels exposes the generator to erroneous prefixes while preserving the efficiency of teacher-forced training. This training objective concentrates supervision at classification positions, yielding propensity-aligned hidden states powering a lightweight scorer for bidirectional retrieval (interests for users and users for interests). On a proprietary e-commerce dataset with 250k+ interest categories, MERIT improves global recall by at least 11.9% and average Hit@k by 6.1%. In production A/B tests, it achieves +0.26% gain in user conversion.

paper.title: EnterpriseClawBench: Building Enterprise Agent Benchmarks from Real Workplace Sessions
paper.abstract: Enterprise agents increasingly operate in workspaces, read heterogeneous files, use tools, and deliver business artifacts. We introduce EnterpriseClawBench, an internal enterprise agent benchmark constructed from proprietary agent sessions. Starting from a large archive of real workplace sessions, the EnterpriseClawBench pipeline produces 852 reproducible tasks with recovered fixtures, rewritten prompts, role classes, skill subclasses, hard rules, and semantic rubrics. Because the data contain internal enterprise content, the benchmark data are not released; the reusable contribution is the construction and evaluation protocol. On a manually audited 120-task Lite subset, the best score is only 0.663 for Codex with GPT-5.5. The results show that enterprise agent evaluation must report harness–model combinations, artifact delivery, visual quality, cost, runtime, and skill-transfer behavior rather than a single score.

paper.title: Med-GRADE: Medical Grading and Rubric-based Assessment of Doctor-Patient Encounters

author.affiliation: Shanghai University of Traditional Chinese Medicine

paper.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based judges are increasingly used to scale the evaluation and optimization of open-ended medical dialogue systems, making their reliability critical in this high-stakes setting. However, existing medical benchmarks mainly assess their medical knowledge, while general judge benchmarks lack clinically grounded consultation criteria. To address this gap, we introduce Med-GRADE, a benchmark for evaluating LLMs as medical dialogue judges. It contains 2,076 real-world patient–LLM dialogues annotated by 56 physicians with a 23-item rubric adapted from Mini-CEX, covering Medical Interviewing (MI), Humanistic Care (HC), and Diagnosis and Treatment Management (DTM). Experiments on 17 LLMs show that current LLM judges achieve only moderate agreement, with the best model reaching 64.89% Macro-F1 and 68.28% Hamming Accuracy. Besides, more complex prompts may even harm performance: CoT disrupts parsing, while few-shot and self-refine introduce item-level instability. Data and code are available at https://github.com/jyd777/Med-GRADE for reproducibility.

paper.title: SAGE: Stochastic Prompt Optimization via Agent-Guided Exploration
paper.abstract: Context engineering has emerged as a primary lever for improving AI systems without parameter updates. Recent work showing that textual gradients do not function as real gradients motivates treating automatic prompt optimization (APO) as black-box search. We introduce SPO (Stochastic Prompt Optimization), a framework for stochastic search over prompt space, and compare three strategies of increasing sophistication: error-informed random search, a genetic algorithm with evolutionary operators, and SAGE (SPO via Agent-Guided Exploration), a multi-agent pipeline with diagnostic code execution. Across three benchmarks, no single strategy dominates; effectiveness depends on the interaction of landscape structure with error type. We further deploy SAGE on a mental-health chatbot under a continuous optimization paradigm, where it compounds eight cycles of individually-noisy A/B tests into a statistically robust gain in next-day retention. We argue that coupling qualitative diagnosis with quantitative validation is what makes agentic optimization effective for open-ended task-oriented dialogue.

paper.title: Multi-View Structural Interpretability of Agentic Reasoning Traces
paper.abstract: Agentic language models solve tasks through reasoning, tool calls, observations, and terminal answers, exposing rich process information beyond the final answer. For practitioners, knowing which process patterns lead to success or failure is essential to diagnose agent errors and build better process reward models without relying on final-answer supervision. However, existing analyses often evaluate only final outcomes or, when examining traces, flatten them into homogeneous step sequences, fragmenting each reasoning round into disconnected steps. Our key insight is that an agent’s reasoning, action, and observation within a round are better treated as typed segments of a single underlying process state, rather than independent steps. We propose MULTI-VIEW-RA, a reasoning abstraction that represents each round through two complementary views: accumulated state and within-round change. Using unlabeled clustering and binary outcome labels, we apply MULTI-VIEW-RA to two practical use cases: diagnosing failures by surfacing the process states that separate correct from incorrect trajectories, and providing a transition-level correctness signal that is a candidate source of process supervision. Across Math, HotpotQA, and FEVER with multiple Qwen and Llama models, MULTI-VIEW-RA outperforms step-level explainability baselines in cases with sufficient success rates, with particularly strong gains on longer, tool-rich traces.

paper.title: AraDynFact: Dynamic Evaluation of Factual Knowledge in Arabic
paper.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to scale both in size and capabilities, their proficiency in the Arabic Language has seen significant advancement. However, a critical gap remains: the extent of their factual knowledge and cultural sensitivity to the diverse Arabic-speaking world remains largely underexplored. Current evaluation metrics often focus on translation or generic reasoning, failing to capture the rich historical, social, and regional nuances inherent to Arabic culture. In addition, most benchmarks rely on heavy work, with human intervention in some steps, making the evaluation of knowledge coverage expensive and slow. To address this deficiency, we introduce AraDynFact, a novel dynamic evaluation framework designed to rigorously assess the factual Arabic knowledge embedded in LLMs. Unlike static benchmarks, AraDynFact employs a dynamic approach to extract factual information and generate rich and answerable questions in a fast and automatic way. We apply AraDynFact to Arabic Wikipedia and audit the performance of several state-of-the-art models, ranging from Arabic-centric specialized LLMs to high-resource general purpose LLMs. In addition we found high degree of correlation with existing, hand-crafted Arabic-centric benchmarks, confirming the potential of our dynamic approach.

paper.title: Efficient Multi-Tenant LoRA Serving for Encoder Models via Late-Fusion Batched Matrix Multiplication
paper.abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has become a popular method to adapt pre-trained models to specific domains. Applied to encoders in a multi-tenant service, it lets each tenant specialize a shared model for classification, retrieval, or ranking. Existing multi-tenant LoRA serving systems target autoregressive decoders, and for encoders the available tooling supports only per-request adapter swapping, whose cost grows with the number of registered adapters. We observe that, unlike decoder generation, the encoder forward pass is compute-bound and dominated by the shared base projections, so per-tenant adaptation can be expressed as plain batched matrix multiplication with no custom kernels. We present LateFuse, a pure-PyTorch system that serves many different LoRA-adapted encoders in a single shared forward pass on one GPU. LateFuse fuses adapters late, in activation space: the base projections run once over the mixed-tenant batch, while per-sample low-rank deltas and per-tenant classification heads are applied as batched matrix multiplications. Tenant weights are never merged into the shared base, ruling out cross-tenant contamination by construction. Our evaluation shows that LateFuse serving latency stays flat as the adapter pool grows to tens of thousands on a single GPU, and that it achieves 5.6–21.2x higher throughput than HuggingFace PEFT’s native mixed-batch API and up to 521× over per-adapter swapping, while registering new adapters over 299x faster.

paper.title: Uncertainty Guardrails for LLM-Based Medical Diagnostic Systems

author.affiliation: Skolkovo Institute of Science and Technology
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence

paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being adopted in clinical practice, e.g., in medical diagnostic systems. However, their reliability is still a concern, as LLMs are prone to hallucinations and could lead to misdiagnosis, inappropriate treatment decisions, and potential harm to patients. To mitigate these risks, LLM-based medical diagnostic systems should incorporate safety guardrails capable of detecting suspicious predictions and flagging them for human review or further clinical assessment. In this work, we employ uncertainty quantification (UQ) as a safety mechanism within an enterprise diagnostic system. We evaluate 16 UQ methods and propose two task-specific modifications tailored to the medical diagnostic workflow. First, we show that methods based on semantic similarity between generated samples substantially benefit from replacing a general-purpose NLI model with a domain-specific model. Second, we adapt a supervised UQ method that relies on LLM internal states for the detection of erroneous generation from a black-box enterprise LLM accessible only through a text-generation API. Our approach leverages the internal states of an open-source, lightweight proxy white-box model. We demonstrate that this approach outperforms all other UQ methods in the considered setting.

paper.title: Audio Front-End Decoupling: Why Synthetic-Voice Simulators Fail to Predict Real-World Voice Agent Behavior
paper.abstract: LLM-based voice agents are routinely cleared for deployment using synthetic audio regression suites, with engineering teams treating augmented commercial TTS as a safe proxy for real human callers. This paper presents the first systematic approach to quantify the profound behavioral drift that occurs when agents optimized on simulated audio are deployed in the real world. We demonstrate that the assumption of acoustic equivalence fundamentally fails: real production audio triggers 2-13 times more VAD misfires than synthetic data across Silero, WebRTC, and TEN-VAD, while simulated environments cause text-grounded turn detectors to artificially flip decisions 33% of the time, compared to just 3% in reality. A paired four-vendor TTS calibration sweep proves this misranking is structural: on every front-end component, optimizing thresholds for synthetic audio actively degrades real-world performance. To prevent teams from flying blind, we introduce a novel set of signal-layer metrics and an open-source framework to audit any simulator prior to adoption. Rather than testing the agent, our method tests the simulator against real target-domain interactions. By identifying where a simulator’s acoustics deviate from reality, teams can definitively know which front-end tuning decisions are safe to trust.

paper.title: Deploying LLM Agents for Auditable Complaint Investigation in Banking
paper.abstract: Complaint investigation in retail banking requires handlers to synthesise evidence from heterogeneous enterprise systems into policy-aligned summaries. We present a production-deployed tool-augmented LLM agent at a major UK retail bank that assists this process under human review. Given a complaint record, the agent queries 16 typed, schema-validated tools and returns an investigation summary with a source-cited chronological evidence timeline. We evaluate the system using SME assessment, LLM-as-a-Judge monitoring, rework measurement, and downstream impact testing. On 187 paired complaints, SMEs judged the agent to match or exceed historical human-written production investigations in 90% of cases across faithfulness, relevance, completeness, and coherence. Median investigation time falls from 30 minutes to 23 seconds. Operational controls include daily automated monitoring, pre-defined thresholds, hallucination flagging, and periodic human audit. These results demonstrate that constrained single-agent LLMs with typed tools are viable for scalable, auditable complaint investigation in regulated environments.

paper.title: ExhibitionBench: A Multi-Source, Multi-Task Benchmark for Evaluating LLMs as Exhibition Curation Assistants

author.affiliation: The Chinese University of Hong Kong

paper.abstract: Cultural reasoning lies at the core of many emerging AI applications, yet existing benchmarks provide limited insight into how well models understand and contextualize cultural artifacts. We introduce ExhibitionBench, the first benchmark that frames exhibition curation as a high-level evaluation testbed, comprising 300 institution-derived exhibition and thematic collection records, 23,658 artifacts, and three interconnected tasks that evaluate complementary aspects of cultural understanding and reasoning, translating them into user-perceivable utilities. Extensive experiments across 29 systems reveal a significant gap between frontier LLMs and expert-level competence, particularly on tasks that require collection-level coherence and thematic understanding. Performance gains from scaling, prompting, and multimodal inputs are limited and highly model-dependent, whereas tailored model optimizations can equip open-weight models with better capabilities that support on-premise deployment. These findings highlight the difficulty of reasoning over cultural collections and provide a practical benchmark for developing more culturally grounded and reliable AI systems. The full project is released at https://github.com/mengze-hong/ExhibitionBench.

paper.title: CAST: Contrastive Adjudication via Selective Triggering for Clinical LLMs
paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often follow conflicting reasoning paths on difficult tasks, creating uncertainty that is especially dangerous in clinical settings where errors can inform incorrect diagnoses or treatments. Standard self-consistency (SC) improves accuracy by voting over multiple reasoning chains, but it does not resolve the contradictions that produced the uncertainty. We propose Contrastive Adjudication via Selective Triggering (CAST), a lightweight inference-time method that detects disagreement across chain-of-thought samples and triggers contrastive adjudication only when model confidence falls below a threshold. Instead of re-asking the same question, CAST extracts the strongest argument for each competing reasoning path, presents them side by side, and asks the model to resolve the conflict definitively. Across multiple model families and three medical benchmarks, including HealthBench, a physician-rubric clinical task benchmark, CAST outperforms standard SC, compute-matched SC, SC-Max (with the maximum possible number of calls, usually 13), and the pooled CASC variant (which votes across all pre- and post- adjudication votes) across all datasets. Gains are largest on uncertain questions, reaching up to 29% over SC. These results, coupled with selective use of model calls, make CAST practical for clinical deployment where models must be accurate, efficient, and uncertainty-aware.

paper.title: TRACE: Deployable Tree-Relational Structure Enhancement for Oncology LLMs
paper.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used in oncology applications, but their predictions are often weakly grounded in explicit medical structure. We present TRACE, a deployable tree-relational enhancement framework for oncology LLMs. TRACE separates expensive offline structure learning from lightweight online inference: oncology concepts and relations are organized into an updatable tree-relational structure, refined using LM-loss-derived evidence, and retrieved at inference time as compact prompt evidence. This design supports task-adaptive evidence selection without requiring supervised labels in the zero-shot setting. Across ten oncology classification tasks and one MedQuAD CancerGov QA benchmark, TRACE improves both label-free evaluation and supervised fine-tuning. Additional analyses show that TRACE improves over vanilla RAG and generic GraphRAG, remains useful under leakage-controlled METABRIC inputs, and produces interpretable evidence paths aligned with clinical reasoning. These results suggest that explicit, updatable medical structure is a practical path toward more accurate and auditable oncology LLM deployment.

paper.title: From Experts to Open-Weight Models: a Validated LLM Pipeline for Institutional Economic News Annotation
paper.abstract: Economic sentiment plays a central role in shaping perceptions of economic conditions, influencing economic behavior, and policy decisions. Recent advances in large language models have made large-scale sentiment extraction from news increasingly feasible, driving its growing use in economic analysis and forecasting systems across national public-sector institutions. Existing approaches scale mainly through automated or weakly supervised labeling, sacrificing expert alignment and domain nuance, and treat sentiment in isolation, overlooking complementary annotations, such as topic, needed to capture structured economic signals for downstream forecasting. To address these limitations, we introduce a human-annotated dataset of Italian economic news labeled by domain experts for sentiment and topic, and develop a statistically validated pipeline that uses few-shot prompting of commercial large language models to expand coverage while preserving expert alignment at scale. We fine-tune multiple open-weight models on the resulting corpus, yielding language specific annotation models that maintain high expert agreement across architectures and satisfy the reproducibility and governance requirements of national public-sector institutions. Starting from 800 expert-labeled articles, the pipeline produces approximately 9,200 additional expert-aligned labels and trains local models that pass the Alternative Annotator Test for both sentiment and topic classification. A subset of the annotated dataset is publicly released to support further research.

paper.title: When Summaries Distort Decisions: Information Fidelity in LLM-Compressed Financial Analysis

author.affiliation: Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology
Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology
Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Financial decision-makers face more information than they can directly inspect, making context compression necessary. Yet when large language models (LLMs) compress financial source material, they can alter the investment judgment supported by the original source. We frame this problem as information fidelity: compression loses fidelity when it changes the decision induced by the source. In agentic systems, such losses may recur across intermediate steps and amplify throughout the decision process. Across financial filings and earnings-call transcripts, we find that LLM-based compression can produce fluent and factually plausible compressed contexts that nevertheless alter downstream decisions. We analyze two diagnostic patterns associated with fidelity loss: decontextualization, where salient evidence is retained but separated from the caveats and contextual qualifiers needed for correct interpretation, and model dependency, where different compressors expose different views of the same source. We then propose Agentic Context Compression, which generates multiple candidate compressions and audits their disagreements against the original source. Our results suggest that financial compression should be evaluated not only by efficiency or factuality, but also by its ability to preserve decision-relevant context.

paper.title: CapMem: A Benchmark for Caption-Based Episodic Memory in Egocentric Video

author.affiliation: University College London, University of London

paper.abstract: Wearable assistants require episodic memory over egocentric video, yet current vision-language models face bounded frame budgets, growing visual-token costs, and long-context retrieval failures. Under these practical constraints, we study whether textual captions can serve as reusable episodic memory. We define the Episodic Memory Video Caption QA task and introduce CapMem, a human-annotated benchmark with 75 videos totaling 33.7 hours, and 1,000 multiple-choice questions across 16 scenarios. On long videos (>20 min), full-coverage CaptionQA with 30s and 60s caption windows outperforms direct VideoQA for 10/12 and 8/12 models, respectively. On the same video subset, a matched-frame control across six Qwen models retains mean accuracy gains of 3.22 and 2.55 points, respectively. Our caption-guided retrieve-and-verify harness further improves accuracy by up to 5.3 points. These results support the effectiveness of caption memory for episodic reasoning over long egocentric video.

paper.title: ReCAST: Restoration-aware Cascaded Stage-wise Training for Obfuscated SMS Risk Classification

author.affiliation: China United Network Communications Group Co., Ltd.

paper.abstract: Fraudulent messages sent via Short Message Service (SMS) are increasingly obfuscated to evade cost-conscious classifiers in production systems. In Chinese SMS, attackers can exploit a wide range of carefully crafted obfuscation strategies to hide risk-bearing phrases while preserving human readability, making direct classification brittle under real-world latency and throughput constraints. We propose ReCAST, a Restoration-aware Cascaded Stage-wise Training framework for robust obfuscated Chinese SMS classification. ReCAST distills a large teacher model’s de-obfuscation ability into a smaller deployable student model by supervising obfuscated span detection, obfuscation type prediction, and text restoration, and then uses the restoration-aware student for downstream risk classification. Experiments on an internally constructed real-world Chinese SMS benchmark show that ReCAST substantially improves classification performance over directly trained baselines under obfuscation. The results suggest that restoration-aware distillation offers a practical path toward robust SMS risk classification with smaller deployable models under production-oriented constraints.

paper.title: BPCF: A Token-Efficient Process Model Notation for LLM-Based BPMN Generation
paper.abstract: Generating Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) process models with LLMs is costly at the serialization layer. Standard XML and JSON formats consume hundreds to thousands of output tokens per model, creating severe latency and cost bottlenecks for interactive modeling assistants. We present BPCF (Business Process Compact Format), a compact, indentation-based notation designed specifically for LLM emission. BPCF-Full is lossless with respect to the structural constructs found in the PMo benchmark. At 221 tokens per model on average, BPCF-Full is roughly half the size of a Mermaid encoding, 8× smaller than verbose JSON representations (PME JSON) and about 29× smaller than BPMN XML. We evaluated nine BPMN representations across five LLMs and found that BPCF is the most token-efficient format by a wide margin, delivering the lowest cost and latency. Although exact accuracy rankings vary across models, BPCF offers a highly viable accuracy-efficiency trade-off for production systems, successfully modeling complex BPMN constructs where other compact formats fail. In the full-expressivity arm, BPCF-Full+Strict scores 0.469/0.472 on GPT-4o/Gemini at 148–155 visible output tokens. We publicly release our grammar, a dependency-free parser, and the full evaluation pipeline.

paper.title: Reproducing Omitted Temporal Expressions in Japanese News for Retrieval-Augmented Applications
paper.abstract: News articles often contain omitted temporal expressions, such as day-only or month-only mentions, which must be interpreted with reference to the publication date. When such articles are indexed or processed as standalone text in search and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems, these omissions can cause temporal mismatches and unstable interpretation by large language models. We focus on reproducing omitted temporal expressions as concrete dates or intervals using the publication date as external context before the articles are indexed for search and RAG applications. Specifically, building on established temporal-expression extraction and normalization techniques and informed by a manual analysis of Japanese news articles, we propose jaROTE, a rule-based pipeline for Japanese news. Experiments on two news corpora demonstrate that jaROTE achieves high performance, and remains competitive with LLMs while providing a fast, low-cost pipeline. We further show that temporal reproduction improves time-constrained lexical retrieval, demonstrating the practical value of publication-date-grounded normalization for Japanese news retrieval.

paper.title: Multi-Step Tool-Calling over Korean Open Public APIs: A Benchmark and a Data-Synthesis Recipe
paper.abstract: Data-sovereignty regulations increasingly require public institutions to deploy open-source, on-premise LLM agents that chain multiple tool-calls across live government APIs. However, open-source models consistently underperform in this multi-step setting, and no existing benchmark measures the gap. We introduce the Korean Open Public API Benchmark KOPA-Bench, comprising 145 real-world tasks on which open-source models underperform. To close this gap, we present EDGE, an Execution-grounded Dynamic Graph for tool-calling data synthEsis driven by live execution. EDGE builds a graph of how each tool’s output can feed another’s input, keeps only the links that succeed when actually called against the live APIs, and traverses these verified links to synthesize executable multi-step trajectories. Fine-tuned via GRPO on the resulting dataset, our 9B model nearly matches the untuned 27B model from the same family, improving substantially not only on KOPA-Bench but also on the BFCL benchmark.

paper.title: Adapting Technical-Service LLM Agents with Latent Logic Augmentation, Robust Noise Reduction, and Hybrid Reward Modeling
paper.abstract: Technical-service LLM agents are entering production workflows, where value depends on whether engineers adopt generated replies. Service tickets hide decision logic, contain noisy single-reference responses, and make reward evaluation costly, making standard post-training brittle. Existing post-training and LLM-as-a-Judge approaches improve grounding or feedback, but do not jointly model latent decision logic, response diversity, and reward cost. We address this gap by coupling latent logic augmentation, robust noise reduction, and hybrid reward modeling. The framework augments supervised fine-tuning data with Planning-Aware Trajectory Modeling and Reasoning Augmentation, builds dual-filtered Multiple Ground Truths, and trains the policy with a hybrid reward that combines a Reranker with an LLM-as-a-Judge. On real Cloud technical-service tasks, the adapted Qwen3-4B achieves the highest Multi-ECS (0.441), lower reward cost, and the highest production adoption rate (46.63%).

paper.title: MMAI Gym for Science: Training Liquid Foundation Models for Drug Discovery
paper.abstract: General-purpose large language models (LLMs) that rely on in-context learning do not reliably deliver the scientific understanding and performance required for drug discovery tasks. Simply increasing model size or introducing reasoning tokens does not yield significant performance gains. To address this gap, we introduce the MMAI Gym for Science, a one-stop shop molecular data formats and modalities as well as task-specific reasoning, training, and benchmarking recipes designed to teach foundation models the ”language of molecules” in order to solve practical drug discovery problems. We use MMAI Gym to train an efficient Liquid Foundation Model (LFM) for these applications, demonstrating that smaller, purpose-trained foundation models can outperform substantially larger general-purpose or specialist models on molecular benchmarks. Across essential drug discovery tasks - including molecular optimization, ADMET property prediction, retrosynthesis, drug–target activity prediction, and functional group reasoning - the resulting model achieves near specialist-level performance and, in the majority of settings, surpasses larger models, while remaining more efficient and broadly applicable in the domain.

paper.title: TabAutoSyn: A Generator-Agnostic Pipeline for Deployment-Ready Synthetic Tabular Data
paper.abstract: Synthetic tabular data lets organisations share, rebalance, and stress-test sensitive in-house tables-but only if the result is actually fit for the downstream task. Yet a table that matches the real distribution on aggregate statistics can still be unfit for its downstream task: it loses the rare cases that matter, is not optimised for the end task, and silently breaks the deterministic relations that domain data must obey. We present TabAutoSyn, an end-to-end, generator-agnostic pipeline that turns any base generator into deployment-ready synthetic data through four automated stages: generate, verify, augment, and curate. A multi-agent LLM module discovers functional dependencies and domain constraints from the real table and repairs or removes violating rows; a divergence-minimising stage rebuilds under-represented tails; and a curation stage provably never lowers a chosen downstream score. Across 22 public and proprietary datasets and eleven generators spanning five model families (GAN, VAE, diffusion, language-model, and graph), TabAutoSyn delivers the best train-on-synthetic utility and the highest validity while preserving privacy. Because it is generator-agnostic, it attains these results on a commodity GPU at a fraction of the cost of the strongest LLM-based baselines, and it needs no per-dataset tuning-making it practical to run on sensitive, in-house data.

paper.title: Quantizing Masked Diffusion Language Models: Storage-Quality Trade-offs and Runtime Diagnostics

author.affiliation: International Institute of Information Technology Hyderabad
International Institute of Information Technology, Hyderabad, International Institute of Information Technology Hyderabad

paper.abstract: Masked diffusion language models reuse one denoiser across many steps, so post-training quantization (PTQ) must balance predictive quality, serialized storage, and runtime memory. We evaluate LLaDA-8B-Instruct and run transfer checks on Dream-7B, MDLM-OWT, encoder-only masked LMs, LLaDA-MoE, and LLaDA2.0-mini. The 24-text calibration set is distinct from the main n{=}500-example-per-task evaluation. Three findings emerge. First, AWQ-4 is the closest tested 4-bit quality point at the evaluated 1.1–2.3 percentage-point resolution, although ARC-Challenge shows a detectable loss. TurboLDM-(3{+}1) instead provides the smallest serialized checkpoint (4.82 GiB, 3.55 effective bits) while losing quality, making it a storage-compression and diagnostic result, not a live-memory result. NF4 alone reduces peak VRAM from roughly 15 GiB to 6 GiB in our tested PyTorch/bitsandbytes runtime; this is a runtime-specific outcome, not an inherent format advantage. Second, individual attention projections are inexpensive to quantize, whereas jointly quantizing the attention block is damaging. Third, more denoising steps partly recover GSM8K loss but not multiple-choice accuracy.

paper.title: Training Lightweight PII Text Detectors via Rubric-Guided Contrastive Data Synthesis

author.affiliation: The University of Tokyo, The University of Tokyo
The University of Tokyo, The University of Tokyo
The University of Tokyo, The University of Tokyo

paper.abstract: The widespread use of large language models (LLMs) has increased the risk of leaking personally identifiable information (PII), making PII detection increasingly important. PII detection must process large text volumes efficiently, but labeled PII text is difficult to collect, share, and redistribute for privacy reasons. We aim to develop rubric-guided contrastive data synthesis for training lightweight PII text detectors from a few labeled seeds and to determine, through comparative experiments on PII benchmark datasets, whether the proposed method improves PII text detector classification performance. From about ten labeled examples, our method induces explicit criteria for distinguishing the two labels (rubrics), generates contrastive Sensitive/Non-sensitive sentence pairs, verifies and deduplicates them, and trains RoBERTa. Experiments on SPeDaC1 and SPY with Qwen3.5-9B and Gemma-4-26B-A4B showed that our method outperformed four baselines in all four settings and significantly improved Macro F1 over the Self-Instruct-style baseline in three of four settings. Overall, we developed rubric-guided contrastive data synthesis for training lightweight PII text detectors from a few labeled seeds and confirmed through comparative experiments on PII benchmark datasets that the proposed method improves classification performance. Our code is available at https://github.com/ekunish/emnlp2026-code.

paper.title: Verify, Then Argue: Claim Verification in Investment Agent Debates
paper.abstract: Multi-agent debate systems incorporate retrieval-based verification to ground agent reasoning with evidence. However, this approach assumes the availability of data and the informative intent of the source text. These conditions are frequently unmet in venture capital, particularly in early-stage startup evaluation. In this industry, evidence is predominantly private or unavailable, and pitch decks use persuasive rhetoric that prior research shows can shift agent conclusions. To measure how agents navigate these conditions, we evaluate how claim verification alters multi-agent debate using a stratified sample of deals from a real venture fund. We find that verification changes the agent’s final investment decision but not its reasoning. Furthermore, agents are insensitive to which claim a verification label is attached to. Reassigning labels to the wrong claims lowers the decision to the same extent. This indicates that the primary bottleneck in automated screening is fundamental claim verifiability rather than retrieval quality.

paper.title: GRACE-DS: a Guarded Reward-guided Agent Correction Environment in Data Science

author.affiliation: Higher School of Economics, Higher School of Economics
Higher School of Economics, Higher School of Economics

paper.abstract: Evaluating LLM-powered AutoML agents for enterprise data science requires more than final leaderboard scores: agents must deliver reproducible, leakage-free, protocol-valid workflows on organization-specific data before deployment. We introduce GRACE-DS, a Guarded Reward-guided Agent Correction Environment in Data Science for evaluating tabular machine learning agents in real-world-like conditions. GRACE-DS stages the full workflow—planning, data inspection, feature engineering, modeling, validation, code repair, and final submission—inside an isolated sandbox where evaluator-owned labels and hidden tests remain private. Hidden executable validators track both predictive progress and process reliability, including leakage avoidance, reproducibility, validation discipline, correction behavior, reward alignment, and terminal submission validity. Based on 7,000 episodes spanning 8 LLMs, 10 tasks, 15 regimes, ablations, reward-optimization probes, and red-team settings, the structured flexible iterative regime (our approach) achieves the strongest end-to-end normalized hidden-test quality, outperforming single shot, unstructured agent, and restart baselines while improving protocol-valid completion. These results establish GRACE-DS as a controlled pre-deployment harness for diagnosing whether LLM-powered AutoML agents satisfy core enterprise execution constraints, on a deliberately search-free tabular sub-problem that isolates planning, correction, and validation discipline from expensive model search. An earlier version of this paper is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16000v2; code and artifacts are available at https://github.com/Alexx221x/GRACE-DS/tree/archive.

paper.title: Hybrid Generative–Tagging Decoding for Product Attribute–Value Extraction
paper.abstract: Attribute-value extraction is important for building high-quality product catalogs in e-commerce. Existing systems either rely on generative or tagging strategies for extracting the attribute names and their corresponding values. Tagging models directly label spans in the source, making them fast and grounded, but they cannot produce values that require reformatting or generate rare attribute names outside their label space. Generative models avoid these drawbacks by generating both attribute names and values token by token, but this auto-regressive nature makes them slow and limits attribute coverage. We introduce hybrid generative-tagging decoding, a novel model architecture that combines tagging source spans and open-ended generation. For frequent attributes whose values are copyable, a tagging head extracts values directly from the source. This lets the generative head focus on the remainder, rare attributes outside the tagger’s label space and non-copyable values, including implicit or normalized values. Integrated into vLLM inference, the hybrid decoder raises attribute coverage by 10% and extracts 63% more correct attribute-value pairs at no precision cost, while reducing latency by 44%.

paper.title: What Else Needs Fixing? Exploring Cost-Effective Test-Time Compute for Revision Propagation in Artifacts Generated Through Conversation
paper.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often help users generate artifacts through iterative cycles of generation and revision in conversation. A challenge here is that, when users specify only a local change during revision, LLMs must instead identify the relevant dependencies and propagate the revision to all affected parts of the artifact. This paper studies this ability of LLMs on conversationally generated artifacts, where the artifact context and its dependencies may be embedded in the conversation history. Toward practical use, we also explore cost-effective test-time compute for this new setting. Specifically, we introduce a new benchmark for this setting, and evaluate nine revision methods, including sequential reflection and parallel sampling variants, using gpt-oss-20b/120b, gpt-5.4-mini, and qwen3.5-9b/27b/122b on the benchmark. The results show that baselines achieve accuracies of 68.3–93%, and the most cost-effective method is selecting from three parallel samples using either LLM-based or medoid selection, which improves accuracy by 2.2–9.7%. Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/ntt-dkiku/llm-revision-propagation.

paper.title: LatentRiskBench: Measuring State-Dependent Risks in Enterprise Agents
paper.abstract: Enterprise agents face safety risks that cannot be determined from individual actions alone. Existing safety benchmarks largely evaluate action-local risks, overlooking failures whose safety depends on workflow state. In such state-dependent risks, the same action may be safe in one context but violate policy in another. Hence, we introduce LatentRiskBench for evaluating such state-dependent risks in enterprise settings. It pairs risky trajectories with benign counterparts that share the same terminal action but differ in latent policy-relevant states, requiring models to reconstruct workflow context rather than rely on action-level cues. We also introduce new metrics for state-dependent risk evaluation, including a suite of residual risk (RR) measures. Experiments on the benchmark show that action-level evaluation detects only 0.09 of state-dependent violations, whereas state-level evaluation reaches 0.96. Existing guardrail methods largely overlook such risks unless they are explicitly applied to workflow states. Case studies on a commercial deployed scenario further show that the safety metrics embedded in the benchmark provide a more realistic measure of safety for enterprise agents.

paper.title: Certified Cost-Optimal Triage for Suggestion Detection in Reviews

author.affiliation: BITS Pilani, Birla Institute of Technology and Science
Birla Institute of Technology and Science
BITS Pilani, Birla Institute of Technology and Science
BITS Pilani, Birla Institute of Technology and Science

paper.abstract: Detecting suggestions in reviews forces a trade- off: an LLM on every review is slow and costly; a cheap classifier is fast but its error rate is uncontrolled, measurable after the fact, not settable in advance. We present a certified triage layer: a calibration step computes ex- actly where a classifier may act alone so its error there stays below an operator-chosen tar- get α; the rest is escalated. On a 14,995-review gold set over 68 industry categories, natural- weighted to a ∼9.5% deployment positive rate, it auto-handles 74–93% of the stream at cer- tified error for α ∈ 2, 4, 5, 10%. Heuris- tic thresholding violates the α=5% target on 36–49% of draws and an in-expectation con- formal gate on 25–28%; only a betting certifi- cate bounds the violation rate by δ, making a strict 2% SLA rigorous at 74% order-free cover- age. Cost-sensitive training, not threshold tun- ing, lowers the certifiable error floor to 0.39%, and ∼200 target labels restore it under cross- industry shift. Of 13 open-weight LLMs (20B– 675B), 11 are worse detectors than our fine- tuned 435M encoder, supervision, not scale, is why (within-model control, §5.6), and the cer- tificate rides on either backbone. Escalation targets a human: on the deferred slice the best LLM oracle still errs at 21.5%.

paper.title: Fund2Persona: A Framework for Building and Refining Financial Advisor Personas from Fund Disclosure Data

author.affiliation: Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology
Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology
Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Demand for personalized financial advice is growing, yet current LLM-based advisors often fail to provide consistent and specialized guidance. Simple persona prompts rarely specify how a financial advisor should reason and often drift toward generic recommendations. We propose Fund2Persona, a framework that builds financial-advisor personas from real-world fund disclosures and refines them through an actor–scorer–patcher loop. We test whether the resulting personas can predict held-out portfolio changes and produce commentary consistent with fund managers’ own explanations. They outperform generic baselines on both tasks. We further study two downstream diagnostics: market-scenario generation, where persona retrieval broadens plausible investment views, and multi-turn investor–advisor conversations, where matched personas give more specific and useful advice than a generic advisor. These results suggest that real fund data can bring manager-specific investment expertise to LLM advisors rather than merely changing an LLM’s surface style.

paper.title: Cite or Decline: A Strict Course-Grounded Chatbot for STEM Lecture Videos
paper.abstract: Recorded lecture videos, often enhanced with search and summarization features, are a standard study resource. However, students cannot easily ask course specific questions or verify answers against an instructor’s lecture. We report a semester-long deployment of VideoPoints platform with a retrieval-augmented chatbot that answers from course lecture materials and returns timestamped citations. The chatbot retrieves only from the active course, uses chapter summaries to guide transcript ranking, and returns clickable timestamped citations. Students used it for quick lookups and exam review. Across 833 messages, 70.5% included citations, none crossed a course boundary, and when no lecture evidence matched, the chatbot usually declined rather than answering. Among the users, citations were the most consistently useful feature, while practice-question generation was the strongest unmet request. We also evaluated the design on the real-world test split of EduVidQA, a public multimodal benchmark for lecture-video question answering. Our design improved correct-lecture retrieval by 6.3 percentage points over dense-only retrieval. Together, the results show that effective deployment depends on course isolation, supported citations, and alignment with students’ study practices.

paper.title: When Do Prompt-Side Agent Playbooks Transfer?Accuracy, Cost, and Runtime Shift in Agent Deployment
paper.abstract: Prompt-side playbooks can improve tool-using language agents without retraining, but their portability beyond the source setting is unclear. We study frozen playbook transfer under a shared distill–validate–transfer protocol. On ALFWorld, transfer is beneficial under controlled greedy decoding and, in one near-budget-matched comparison, distilled guidance outperforms five fixed demonstrations. On TAU2-Bench, a prespecified aggregate contrast supports a modest average matched-domain advantage, but global Holm correction retains only one of 135 route-level effects; the remaining grid provides descriptive evidence of compatibility-sensitive heterogeneity. On XBench-DeepSearch, one artifact–runtime pairing preserves useful first-try heuristics while producing repeated queries, delayed stopping, and substantial cost inflation after a context-runtime shift. Across benchmarks, transferred and target-derived playbooks both require target-side validation of success, termination, protocol compatibility, and cost. Frozen transfer is therefore a conditional cold-start option, not a reuse-by-default strategy or a universally preferable alternative to target-side redistillation.

paper.title: Calibrated Deferral Routing for Cost-Efficient Guardrails
paper.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance across diverse NLP tasks, but deploying them in real-world scenarios raises concerns regarding safety, reliability, and computational cost. To mitigate the risk of harmful, unreliable, or unfaithful content, LLM pipelines increasingly rely on guardrails. Yet deploying multiple guardrails across different tasks and risk categories introduces significant computational and orchestration overhead. In this work, we propose a calibrated deferral-routing framework for deploying guardrails both accurately and cost-effectively. Our approach arranges guardrails as a cascade of increasing capability and cost: each input is first evaluated by a lightweight guardrail, while only uncertain instances are deferred to a larger, more capable, and more expensive model. We formalize this routing problem and study practical deferral-calibration strategies by applying post-hoc calibration, including isotonic regression, Platt scaling, and temperature scaling. We evaluate 18 guardrail models from four model families (i.e., Granite Guardian, Llama Guard, ShieldGemma, and GuardReasoner) across 10 harm-detection benchmarks. Our experiments show that: (i) all guardrail models are often poorly calibrated out of the box (ECE ranging from 6% to 28%); (ii) post-hoc calibration substantially improves reliability reducing ECE below 2.5% in most cases; (iii) cascade routing yields large cost savings with minimal accuracy loss, while monotone calibration primarily makes routing thresholds deployable rather than improving rank ordering.

paper.title: Not All Fallbacks Are Failures: Understanding and Recovering from Fallbacks in Mobile Voice Assistants

author.affiliation: AIST, National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology

paper.abstract: Robust understanding of user input is a core requirement for voice assistants deployed in real-world environments. In practice, these systems encounter heterogeneous fallback situations caused by noisy audio input, transcription errors, ambiguous requests, incomplete utterances, or unintended activations. Existing systems typically respond with generic fallback messages, which do not resolve the underlying interaction failure and can degrade user experience. We study fallback handling in a deployed smartwatch-based voice assistant for general health support in everyday environments. Our analysis is based on six months of real-world usage data from more than 500 users, yielding a dataset of 3,030 anonymized, naturally occurring fallback-triggering utterances. We contribute (1) an operational taxonomy and the annotated VoxFallbacks dataset of these interactions, (2) a comparative evaluation of different models within a classification pipeline under practical deployment constraints, and (3) practical lessons for designing robust and cost-efficient fallback mechanisms. Results show that lightweight embedding-based classifiers outperform larger generative models on most classification tasks while requiring substantially fewer computational resources.

paper.title: AdCompliance: Towards Automated Compliance Verification in Advertising Operations

author.affiliation: Nara Institute of Science and Technology
Nara Institute of Science and Technology, Japan
Nara Institute of Science and Technology, Japan

paper.abstract: Advertising operations (AdOps) include compliance review processes to ensure that advertisements adhere to applicable laws, platform policies, and industry guidelines. In particular, ads must avoid issues such as overclaiming effectiveness or making definitive assertions about uncertain outcomes. However, these reviews are typically conducted by experts, making them an operational bottleneck. In this paper, we propose the automated ad text compliance verification task and present our classifier-based system. We introduce AdCompliance, a dataset consisting of real pre-submission ad texts annotated by experts. Our experimental results demonstrate practical classification performance, suggesting that non-compliant ads can be effectively filtered while maintaining a low false positive rate.
