These results support practical integration into AdOps workflows.

paper.title: Reading the News: Adapting Large Language Models to Swedish Journalism Through Continued Pre-Training
paper.abstract: Large language models are increasingly capable in general, but their utility can remain modest in niche or understudied areas. One approach to address this limitation is to specialise existing models through additional training on target-domain corpora. In this work, we investigate such continued pre-training for adapting large language models to Swedish journalism, using a high-quality dataset that we curate from millions of news articles. To evaluate the adaptation efficacy, we also construct a novel domain-specific benchmark that covers six editorial tasks. Through full and parameter-efficient fine-tuning across two model sizes, we find that continued pre-training yields benefits in the target domain, but only when paired with experience replay to mitigate forgetting. We observe consistent enhancements in the models’ generation quality and factual knowledge, but not their proficiency in discriminative tasks. Exploring a training-free method to facilitate instruction following, we see further improvements, but exclusively for models trained with low-rank adaptation. Crucially, we demonstrate the importance of targeted evaluation in the adaptation process, as an existing Swedish benchmark largely fails to capture the models’ in-domain performance gains.

paper.title: MotiGAN: Game Theory Meets the Motivated Intruder Test for Re-identification Risk Generation and Annotation in Pseudonymisation
paper.abstract: Re-identification methods serve as a concrete instantiation of the Motivated Intruder Test in privacy-preserving problems, and current state-of-the-art attack techniques are predominantly built upon Large Language Models (LLMs) which are also core components of robust pseudonymized methods. Therefore, it requires the rich training dataset. However, as research demands continue to grow while publicly available data for each domain remains limited and the cost of direct human supervision is high, a central question arises: how can a human-in-the-loop approach be integrated to generate high-quality data and improve the performance of LLMs in psedonymization. To address this limitation, we propose MOTIGAN1 - a gamified framework that transforms the motivated intruder test into a competitive three population tournament. In this game, human characters and AI characters compete to re-identify individuals from each essay. At every stage, players both commit their guesses and contribute to enriching the synthesized dataset. In our experiments, the synthesized dataset contributes to improving the performance of multiple models in several experiments (achieving up to 37.6% improvement on a well-established benchmark).

paper.title: Cost-Efficient Intent Classification via Semantic-Candidate Adaptation and Selective Capability Routing
paper.abstract: Intent classification deployments trade accuracy against retraining effort and inference cost. We study frozen generative reranking and budgeted large-model escalation, introducing Semantic-Candidate Adaptation (SCA): BGE top-5 retrieval followed by joint reranking with one representative training example per candidate. On CLINC150, aligned examples raise Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct from 68.18% label-only accuracy to 76.13% and Gemma-2-2B-it from 66.02% to 76.15%, without LLM parameter updates. CLINC150 wrong-example controls support the role of correct alignment, while BANKING77 and HWU64 provide transfer evidence. Broader comparisons clarify the deployment regimes: direct centroid retrieval reaches 80.71%, while a task-trained MPNet Energy baseline reaches 90.05%; always-on SCA is therefore not a universal replacement for direct or trained classifiers. A validation-selected low-margin SCA fallback provides only a marginal gain at an 8.62% realized test call rate. For real Qwen3.7-Max escalation on CLINC150, routing the lowest BGE top-1 retrieval scores reaches 82.11–82.89% accuracy at a 10% budget and 87.33–88.07% at 20%, with OOS F1 of 70.00–70.13% and 87.47–87.70%, respectively. Learned and token-confidence routing remain alternatives, but no policy dominates every evaluated point.

paper.title: What Should Be Fixed? Rule-Grounded Corrective Actions for Reworkable Logical Anomalies in Industrial Inspection
paper.abstract: Logical anomalies in industrial inspection are rule violations: an object count is wrong, an item is misplaced, a component type does not match, or a required relation is broken. Existing anomaly understanding systems usually stop at diagnosis, answering whether an image is anomalous, where the anomaly is, or why it violates a rule. Reworkable inspection workflows require the next question: What should be fixed? We introduce an industry-oriented benchmark and training pipeline for rule-grounded corrective actions. The task asks a model to produce an operator-facing action that supports one of three downstream decisions: no action, rework, or reject/manual review. This setting exposes a Diagnosis-Action Gap: identifying an abnormal object does not imply knowing the valid, minimal action that restores normality. We construct from MVTec LOCO and from VID-AD, adding correction-oriented annotations that connect normal rules, visual evidence, repairability, corrective actions, and verification targets. The datasets support multiple-choice correction selection, structured JSON action prediction, and open-ended correction generation. We further train ReworkVLM, a Qwen3-VL-based model optimized with , which combines semantic correctness, trace-answer alignment, and minimal-edit rewards. Experiments on both benchmarks show that correction-oriented evaluation reveals failures hidden by diagnosis alone, including wrong action direction, unnecessary repair, and non-minimal edits, while ReworkVLM improves structured corrective success and open-ended correction quality over general and anomaly-specific VLM baselines.

paper.title: Catching AI-Generated Code at Scale: A Lightweight and Interpretable Detector for the LLM Era

author.affiliation: Indraprastha Institute of Information Technology, Delhi
Indraprastha Institute of Information Technology, Delhi
Indraprastha Institute of Information Technology, Delhi
Indraprastha Institute of Information Technology, Delhi

paper.abstract: As LLMs become everyday creative partners in software development, code is no longer a purely human artefact; it emerges from an increasingly hybrid human-AI process. Understanding who contributed which parts of a codebase has become a foundational question of creative attribution, touching on authorship, trust, and the integrity of co-created work. Yet existing detectors exceed 100M+ parameters, are too slow for practical deployment, and offer no insight into what distinguishes human from AI creative contributions. We present NanoDroid, a backbone-free detector with only 5.1M parameters that runs \mathbf{20\times} faster than 125M-parameter UniXcoder (SOTA) and is fully interpretable: per-stream attribution scores explicitly expose which stylistic evidence (token statistics, transition patterns, surface style) distinguishes human from AI authorship in code. On the challenging 4-class DroidCollection benchmark (Human / Machine / Refined / Adversarial), NanoDroid achieves 90.77% weighted F1, within 2.6% of SOTA, on the CodeT-M4 benchmark, NanoDroid achieves SOTA performance, while providing the kind of transparent decision decomposition that black-box models cannot. Beyond a detection tool, we argue NanoDroid offers a lens for studying how human and AI creativity differ stylistically, and where they blur.

paper.title: Phoenix-VL 1.5 Medium: Continued Pre-Training of Sovereign Multimodal AI for On-Premises Public-Sector Deployment

author.affiliation: national university of singaore, National University of Singapore

paper.abstract: Sovereign AI deployments often require foundation models to operate under constraints overlooked by standard benchmarks: adherence to legislation, multilingual and multimodal grounding in local contexts, institution-specific safety behaviors, and on-premises deployment on power-constrained infrastructure. We present a production case study detailing the multi-stage engineering pipeline that spans trillion-token-scale continued pretraining, multi-billion-token alignment and post-training for a 123B-parameter natively multimodal foundation model, *Phoenix-VL 1.5 Medium*, optimized for Singapore public-sector use. On our novel localized evaluation suite and behavioral safety framework, the model substantially improves localized multimodal, statutory, and public-safety capability (a +0.118 average gain over the strongest baselines) while retaining broad general capability. We also share empirical analysis from a full production deployment currently serving over 30,000 users and processing \sim1 billion tokens over a two-month period. Ultimately, our findings demonstrate that sovereign AI is best approached as an end-to-end systems problem, where data curation, domain training, institutional alignment, and hardware layout interact and cannot be optimized in isolation.

paper.title: Graph-Guided Selective Unlearning for Language Models: Controlling Support Routes Beyond Forget Seeds
paper.abstract: Enterprises fine-tune language models on proprietary data that may later require removal due to privacy, contractual, or compliance obligations. Selective unlearning removes requested knowledge while preserving model utility, offering a practical alternative to full retraining, but existing methods treat the explicitly identified forget examples as the complete deletion scope. This is insufficient when target knowledge remains recoverable through paraphrases, aliases, or neighboring training examples. We propose GraphSU, a graph-guided controller that expands the deletion scope beyond forget seeds by constructing a weighted support-route graph, propagating deletion pressure through it, and applying graded forgetting strengths to high-risk neighbors. On TOFU and PISTOL with GPT-2 Medium and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, GraphSU achieves the lowest utility-feasible soft leakage across all deletion settings, reducing leakage by up to 49.5 percentage points over a matched seed-only baseline, demonstrating that effective enterprise unlearning requires controlling support routes, not just forget seeds.

paper.title: DiffResearch: Accelerating Deep Research with Diffusion Language Models

author.affiliation: Moscow State Institute of Steel and Alloys

paper.abstract: Deep research systems iteratively plan, gather evidence, synthesize, and revise, making end-to-end latency a key bottleneck for interactive use. Almost all production systems are built on autoregressive (AR) language models and inherit left-to-right decoding in planning and long-form writing. We present DiffResearch, an open multi-agent deep research framework that places a diffusion language model (dLLM) at the core of every stage, and measure how a diffusion backbone changes latency and report quality. Holding the agentic scaffold, retrieval code, prompts, and evaluation fixed, we swap the backbone between an open diffusion model and a comparable AR model. Across 100 Deep Research Bench tasks, the diffusion backbone is roughly 6× faster end-to-end, driven by order-of-magnitude reductions in planning and writing. We further introduce dFast, a decomposition mode that reads intermediate denoising states and extracts subqueries before generation finishes, providing a 1.99× median speedup for decomposition in isolation with no loss of report quality. On the benchmark’s RACE rubric, dFast obtains the best overall score among the three configurations. Finally, in a public system-level leaderboard snapshot, an instance built on a stronger diffusion model ranks above several commercial systems. We release DiffResearch under an Apache-2.0 license.

paper.title: CARE: Bounded Selective Evidence-to-Judgment Routing for Cost-Aware Document Security Classification

author.affiliation: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST)

paper.abstract: Enterprise document security classification is a selective-decision problem. Rare high-risk labels require evidence and auditability, yet judging every document with an LLM is costly and adds model-specific variance to cases that precedents already settle. We introduce CARE (Cost-Aware Resource-adaptive Evidence), a bounded, fixed commit–verify–adjudicate controller that routes each case by precedent trust. It forms a zero-LLM evidence vote, commits when a learned reliability gate predicts low vote-error risk, verifies uncertain cases through verifier–evidence agreement, and spends heterogeneous panel judgment only on the residual conflicts where evidence and verification disagree. Across two contrasting evidence regimes that defeat different fixed baselines, the same controller selects route depth document by document. On WikiLeaks, where contrastive retrieval already supports strong performance without LLM calls, CARE preserves the zero-call evidence endpoint within bootstrap uncertainty while staying above every always-LLM decoder. It reaches 0.9824 Macro-F1 and 0.9624 SECRET F1, with only 44 of 2,863 documents reaching any LLM stage. This requires 55 invocations in total, 1.9% of a one-call-per-document budget. On DISC, where the rare TOP SECRET tail destabilizes sparse and LLM decoders, it gives the strongest row in our controlled comparison (0.8785 Macro-F1, 0.8444 TOP SECRET F1) using 496 physical model invocations against 789 for a same-evidence always-LLM policy, 63% of that budget, with only 81 documents reaching the panel. CARE thus turns security classification into an auditable policy for deciding when evidence is enough and when judgment is worth spending.

paper.title: SKILL.state: Scalable Long-Horizon Agent Skills
paper.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly act as autonomous agents executing complex, long-running procedural skills. Existing agent runtimes maintain execution by continually appending observations, actions, and intermediate reasoning traces to an ever-growing conversation history, causing latency degradation and context-poisoning failures over long horizons. We present SKILL.state, a runtime architecture that replaces append-only conversational history with an explicit, mutable execution state. At each execution step, the model receives only the immutable skill specification, the current structured execution state, and the latest observation. Intermediate reasoning is discarded immediately after producing a validated state update, preventing prompt growth with execution history. Across diverse datasets, models, and execution environments, SKILL.state improves task accuracy while substantially reducing cumulative token consumption. Our results demonstrate that explicit execution state is an effective and architecture-agnostic abstraction for scalable long-horizon agent skills.

paper.title: Trace-GRAF: Trace-Guided Granularity Routing for Sequential Agentic Workflows
paper.abstract: Multi-agent LLM results can conflate decomposition with roles, communication, parallelism, and extra compute. We study strictly ordered tool-use workflows of dependent state-changing steps, where segmentation may also support auditing and handoff constraints. We introduce Trace-GRAF, a granularity selector that aligns one single-agent trace to target workflow steps, converts order violations and unrelated drift into split pressure, and selects the smallest granularity on the minimum-pressure plateau. It executes balanced contiguous segments because boundary ablation finds no significant success difference from semantic segmentation; pressure-minimizing partitions characterize cuts. Across held-out cohorts spanning two benchmarks and three executors, fixed decomposition sometimes improves and sometimes reduces success, while greater granularity both rescues failures and regresses solved runs. When SA success is observable, the pressure route preserves successful runs by construction. Across validation resplits on TerminalWorld, the calibrated extension’s mean recovery is 2.3–3.0% for GPT-OSS, 0.0–0.1% for Gemini, and 2.3–4.9% for DeepSeek. Simple fixed fallbacks match much of the observed gain. Trace-GRAF therefore provides a risk-aware routing diagnostic with benchmark- and split-dependent gains.

paper.title: Cloud and On-Premises Deployment of Uzbek Legal RAG via Targeted Retriever Fine-Tuning
paper.abstract: Deploying large language models for legal question answering raises challenges that general-purpose leaderboards do not capture, particularly for low-resource languages and under hard operational constraints. We report on building and operating a retrieval-augmented (RAG) legal assistant for Uzbek that must run in two regimes: a managed cloud service that maximizes answer quality within a per-token cost ceiling, and an on-premises deployment for clients whose legal data may not leave their infrastructure, restricting us to open-weight models on limited local hardware under latency constraints. Because no evaluation existed for this setting, we build two domain benchmarks: a retrieval benchmark of 178 expert-annotated legal queries with gold provision spans, and an end-to-end benchmark of 504 expert-curated question–answer pairs scored by an LLM judge whose ratings we validate against human judgments and against an independent-family judge. Applying these benchmarks under each regime, we find the open-versus-proprietary gap is small and cheaply closed by fine-tuning. Therefore, we train UTE-1, which is a state-of-the-art text embedder among open models for Uzbek. We also demonstrate that closing the performance gap via fine-tuning is both impractical due to the intensive hardware demands of long-context legal Q&A and unnecessary, given that legal acts change frequently. We support this by reporting a negative result from a QLoRA experiment. We distill practical guidance for similar deployments, drawn from a system serving real users in production. We release our benchmarks, evaluation code and the fine-tuned embedder (UTE-1) at this https URL to support future work on low-resource legal NLP.
